In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat "al-An'am"

It is said: all of it is Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: it was revealed at Mecca, at night, all at once, except six verses, and they are: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you"﴾ [al-An'am: 151]; and His saying, ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am: 91]; and His saying, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ [al-An'am: 93]; and His saying, ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands﴾ [al-An'am: 93]; and His saying, ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 114]; and His saying, ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it﴾ [al-An'am: 20].

Al-Kalbi said: "al-An'am" is entirely Meccan except for two verses, which were revealed at Medina concerning Finhas the Jew, and they are: ﴿Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?"﴾ [al-An'am: 91], together with what is connected to this verse. That is because Finhas said: "Allah did not send down anything upon any human being."

Ibn 'Abbas also said: Surat al-An'am was revealed with seventy thousand angels around it, having a loud chanting, crying out in glorification.

Ka'b said: the opening of the Torah is the opening of al-An'am: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, up to ﴿they ascribe equals﴾; and the close of the Torah is the close of Hud: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Hud: 123]. It was also said: its close is ﴿And say, "Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son and has had no partner in dominion"﴾ [al-Isra': 111], up to ﴿glorify Him with great glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 111].

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "al-An'am" is among the choicest of the Qur'an.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: whoever recites Surat al-An'am has attained the good pleasure of his Lord.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ ﴿He it is who created you from clay, then decreed a term; and a specified term is with Him; then you still doubt.﴾

This is a declaration that Allah, exalted is He, is the one who deserves all praise in its entirety, because the alif and lam in "al-hamd" (praise) are for the comprehensiveness of the category. He, exalted is He, possesses the lofty attributes: knowledge, power, comprehensiveness, and bounty. So He is worthy of praise in all its kinds, and to Him belongs the praise that encompasses thanks specifically for blessings.

When this statement was given, it was followed by mention of some of His attributes that necessitate praise, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth, the sustainers of people and their provisions. "al-Ard" (the earth) here is for the category, so its singular form in wording is equivalent to its plural.

What is apparent from this order is that the heaven was created before the earth; al-Tabari related this from Qatadah. But that is not so, because the conjunction "wa" does not establish sequence of meanings. What is derived from the totality of the Qur'anic verses is that Allah, exalted is He, created the earth but did not spread it out; then He turned to the heaven and created it; then He spread out the earth after that.

"Ja'ala" here means "khalaqa" (created); nothing other than that is permissible. Reflect: why were the heavens and the earth specified with "khalaqa," while the darknesses and the light were specified with "ja'ala"? al-Tabari said: "wa ja'ala," this is the one that varies in the ways of speech, as you say: "I began to do such-and-such," so it is as if He said: "and He made their darkening and their illumination."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is not sound, because "ja'ala," when it is in this manner, must be linked with another verb, as occurs with verbs of approximation, such as your saying: "Zayd almost died," "Zayd began to come and go." But when no verb is linked with it, it is not valid that it is what al-Tabari mentioned.

al-Suddi, Qatadah, and the majority of the exegetes said: "al-zulumat" (the darknesses) is the night, and "al-nur" (the light) is the day. A group said: "al-zulumat" is disbelief, and "al-nur" is faith.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is not sound, because it removes a word that is clear in the language from its real apparent meaning to an inner meaning without necessity; and this is the method of riddles from which the Qur'an is free. Also, "al-nur" here is for the category, so its singular form is equivalent to its plural.

His saying, Exalted is He: "thumma" (then) indicates the ugliness of the act of those who disbelieve, because the meaning is that His creation of the heavens and the earth and other things has been established, His signs have shone forth, and His bounty through that has become clear; then after all this they ascribe equals to their Lord. This is like your saying: "O so-and-so, I gave you, I honored you, and I did good to you; then you insult me?" meaning: after an interval from the occurrence of all this. Had the conjunction in this and similar cases been "wa," the reproach would not have been necessary as it is with "thumma."

"Alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieve) in this place means everyone who worships anything besides Allah. Qatadah said: they are specifically the people of polytheism. Whoever among the exegetes specified it for some and not others has not been correct; however, the prior context of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) indicates that the reference is to idol-worshippers, because of their proximity to him. The wording of the verse also alludes to the Manichaeans, who are called "al-mananiyya," worshippers of light, who say that good comes from the action of light and evil from the action of darkness. The statement of Ibn Abza that the intended ones are the People of the Book is far-fetched.

"Ya'dilun" means: they equate and liken. The "'adl" of a thing is its equal and its like. The Manichaeans are Magians. A hadith occurs in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, and it is: "The Qadariyya are the Magians of this Ummah," and its meaning is severe condemnation of them and blame for them in likening them to the Magians. The point of resemblance is that the Magians say: actions, their good is the creation of light and their evil is the creation of darkness; so they made a creator other than Allah. And the Qadariyya say: man creates his actions; so they made a creator other than Allah, exalted is He, according to their statement. Abu al-Ma'ali held that the comparison with the Magians is only the statement of the Qadariyya that good is from Allah and evil is from Him but He does not will it; and we only said in the hadith that it is an intensification because it has stated that they are of the Ummah; had he made them literal Magians he would not have added them to the Ummah. All of this is if the hadith is sound; and Allah is the Granter of success.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾, etc. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and others said: the meaning is that He created Adam from clay, and mankind is from Adam; therefore He said: ﴿created you from clay﴾. al-Mahdawi related from a group that they said: rather, the meaning is that the drop from which a human is created originally comes from clay; then Allah transforms it into a drop. Makki and al-Zahrawi also mentioned this. The first view is more fitting with the Shari'a, because the second view is only grounded on the view of one who says that clay returns, after generation and many transformations, to a drop; and that is rejected among the scholars of legal theory.

The exegetes differed concerning the two terms. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak said: "ajalan" is the term of a person from his birth until his death; and "al-ajal al-musamma 'indahu" is from the time of his death until his resurrection; He described it as "specified with Him" because He alone has knowledge of the time of the Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "ajalan" is the worldly life; and "ajal musamma" is the Hereafter. Mujahid said: "ajalan" is the Hereafter, and "ajal musamma" is the worldly life, the reverse of the previous view. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "ajalan" is a person's death by sleep, and "ajal musamma" is his death by dying. Ibn Zayd said: the first term is at the time of the taking of the covenant from the children of Adam, when He brought them out from Adam's back; and one term remains specified in this worldly life. al-Mahdawi related from a group: "ajalan" is what people know of the terms of the crescents, years, and occurrences; and "ajal musamma" is the establishment of the Hour. It is also related from a group: "ajalan" is what we know of the fact that there is no prophet after Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace); and "ajal musamma" is the Hereafter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: One should reflect upon the word "qada" (decreed) in this verse, for it bears two meanings. If it is taken to mean "qaddara" (measured out) and "kataba" (wrote), and it refers back to His prior knowledge and decree, then we say that this is necessarily before His creation of Adam from clay; and "thumma" (then) is removed from its customary sequence regarding the order of the times of the two matters, and it retains the order of the times of the reporting of it, as if He said: "He informed you that He created you from clay; then He informed you that He decreed a term." And if "qada" is taken to mean "awjada" (brought into existence) and "azhara" (made manifest), and that returns to an attribute of action, then it is valid that He created Adam from clay before the manifestation and disclosure of this term, and "thumma" remains in its proper sense regarding the order of the times of the occurrence of the two matters.

"Tamtarun" means: you doubt; and "al-mirya" is doubt.

His saying: ﴿"thumma antum"﴾ is like His saying: ﴿then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾, in reproach for evil conduct, after an interval from the clarity of the proofs.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 3–5:

His - Mighty and Majestic is He - saying:

﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾ ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿So they have denied the truth when it has come to them, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾

The principle of discussion regarding this verse is that the indwelling of Allah the Exalted in places is impossible; likewise His contact with bodies, or His facing them, or His being confined to a direction, because it is impossible for these to be permissible for Him - Blessed and Exalted is He. Once this is established, it is clear that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾, is not in the sense of our saying "Zayd is in the house"; rather, it is according to another mode of interpretation. A group said: this is according to a attribute omitted from the wording, present in the meaning; as if He said: "And He is Allah, the one worshipped, in the heavens and on the earth." Some expressed it by estimating: "He is Allah, the one who manages the affair in the heavens and on the earth." Al-Zajjaj said: "fi" (in) is connected to what the name of Allah the Exalted includes of meanings, as one says: "the Commander of the Faithful, the Caliph, in the east and the west."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad - may Allah have mercy on him - said: This, in my view, is the best of the opinions and the most comprehensive in securing the eloquence of the wording and the forcefulness of the meaning. Its clarification is that He intended to indicate His creation, His power's preference, His encompassing, His dominion, and similar attributes; so He gathered all of these in His saying: "And He is Allah," i.e., "the One to whom all of these belong in the heavens and on the earth," as if He said: "And He is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, the Encompassing, in the heavens and on the earth." Just as you say: "Zayd is the sultan in Syria and Iraq." If you intended the essence of "Zayd," you would be speaking nonsense; but if the intent of your saying "Zayd is the commander, the forbidder, the decisive one who dismisses and appoints, in Syria and Iraq" is conveyed by your placing "the sultan" in place of these, it is eloquent and correct. Likewise in the verse, He placed the word "Allah" in place of those mentioned attributes.

A group said: ﴿And He is Allah﴾ is a beginning and a predicate, and the speech is complete at that point; then He began anew, and His saying ﴿in the heavens﴾ is connected to the object of "He knows": as if He said: "And He is Allah; He knows your secret and your open, in the heavens and on the earth." With this connection it is not permissible for "Huwa" to be a pronoun of the matter and affair, because that would make "Allah" the subject of a beginning and "He knows" in the place of the predicate; and ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ would have separated the beginning from the predicate, which is a strange placement within the sentence. Those who hold this view must also hold that the address in the kaf of ﴿your secret and your open﴾ is to all created beings, both jinn and angels, because humans have no secret or open in the heaven; so the arrangement of the speech according to this view is: "And He is Allah; He knows, O all created beings, your secret and your open, in the heavens and on the earth."

Another group said: "Huwa" is a pronoun of the matter and affair, and ﴿Allah in the heavens﴾ is a beginning and a predicate, the speech being complete at that point; then He began anew, as if He said: "And He knows in the earth your secret and your open." This view, since it escapes the necessity of addressing the angels, also escapes the doubt of being in the heaven, by estimating the omission of "the worshipped" or "the manager," as previously mentioned. His saying the Exalted: ﴿He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn﴾ is a statement containing a warning and a deterrence; and "taksibun" (what you earn) is a general term for all beliefs, deeds and sayings.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And there does not come to them﴾ - the verse: "ma" is a negation; the first "min" is the extra one which enters upon the genera after a negation, so that it is as if it encompasses the whole genus; and the second "min" is for partitive. "Ayah" means the sign, the proof and the argument; its morphological form has already been discussed at the beginning of the book. This verse contains a rebuke of those who equate others with Allah, in that they turn away from every sign that reaches them. Then the "fa" in His saying "faqad" requires that their turning away from the signs has resulted in their denying the truth, which is Muhammad - peace and blessings be upon him - and what he brought. Then He threatened them that there would come to them the punishment of their mockery. "Ma" here means "alladhi" (that which), and it may also be verbal (masdariyya); in the speech there is an omitted modifier, its estimate being: "there will come to them the content of the news of the Quran which they used to mock"; and if "ma" is made verbal, the estimate is: "there will come to them the news of their being mockers," i.e., "a punishment they will be informed is due for that mockery." These punishments with which they were threatened encompass the punishments of this world, such as Badr and others, and the punishments of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 3–5:

His - Mighty and Majestic is He - saying:

﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾ ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿So they have denied the truth when it has come to them, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾

The principle of discussion regarding this verse is that the indwelling of Allah the Exalted in places is impossible; likewise His contact with bodies, or His facing them, or His being confined to a direction, because it is impossible for these to be permissible for Him - Blessed and Exalted is He. Once this is established, it is clear that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾, is not in the sense of our saying "Zayd is in the house"; rather, it is according to another mode of interpretation. A group said: this is according to a attribute omitted from the wording, present in the meaning; as if He said: "And He is Allah, the one worshipped, in the heavens and on the earth." Some expressed it by estimating: "He is Allah, the one who manages the affair in the heavens and on the earth." Al-Zajjaj said: "fi" (in) is connected to what the name of Allah the Exalted includes of meanings, as one says: "the Commander of the Faithful, the Caliph, in the east and the west."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad - may Allah have mercy on him - said: This, in my view, is the best of the opinions and the most comprehensive in securing the eloquence of the wording and the forcefulness of the meaning. Its clarification is that He intended to indicate His creation, His power's preference, His encompassing, His dominion, and similar attributes; so He gathered all of these in His saying: "And He is Allah," i.e., "the One to whom all of these belong in the heavens and on the earth," as if He said: "And He is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, the Encompassing, in the heavens and on the earth." Just as you say: "Zayd is the sultan in Syria and Iraq." If you intended the essence of "Zayd," you would be speaking nonsense; but if the intent of your saying "Zayd is the commander, the forbidder, the decisive one who dismisses and appoints, in Syria and Iraq" is conveyed by your placing "the sultan" in place of these, it is eloquent and correct. Likewise in the verse, He placed the word "Allah" in place of those mentioned attributes.

(p-316)

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, generations We had established on the earth in ways We have not established you? We sent the sky down upon them in abundant rain, and made rivers flow beneath them. Then We destroyed them for their sins and brought into being after them other generations.﴾

This is an exhortation to take lesson (ʿibrah). The seeing here is seeing of the heart (ruʾyat al-qalb). The word "kam" (how many) is in the accusative position, governed by "ahlakna" (We destroyed).

"Al-qarn" (a generation, a community of people who coexist in a span of time) is the community that lives together in a period of time. From it is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The best of people is my generation (qarni)," and the rest of the hadith. People have differed over how long a qarn lasts. The majority hold it is one hundred years. What supports this is the hadith in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you see this night of yours? Within a hundred years from it, none of those who are upon the earth today will remain." Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "He meant that it will sweep away that generation." It is also reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to ʿAbd Allah ibn Bashir: "You will live a qarn," and he lived one hundred years.

It was said that the qarn is eighty years. It was also said seventy, and it was said sixty. Those who held these figures relied on the (common) experience of life spans. Al-Naqqash related forty. Al-Zahrawi mentioned concerning this that it is from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Naqqash also related thirty and related twenty, and related eighteen. All of this is weak. These are (merely) strata (tabaqat), not generations. The qarn is rather the passing away of the elders and then the birth of the children. This is evident from the Exalted's saying: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 31]. Ibn al-Majishun, in al-Wadiha, pointed to observing these strata and the extinction of people through them, in permitting "testimony based on hearsay" (shahadat al-sama', i.e., testimony based on what one has heard from others) when a matter has been long past, fifteen years or more.

It was also said that qarn is the time itself. It is then an elided construction, its estimated form being "from the people of a qarn." The pronoun in "makkannahum" (We established them) refers to the qarn. The address in "lakum" (for you) is to the believers and to all contemporaries of those (generations) among the rest of mankind. It is as if He said: "What We have not established for you, O people of this age." This is the clearest of what is said about it.

It is also possible to estimate in the verse the sense of saying directed at these disbelievers, as if He said: "O Muhammad, say to them: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, generations We established on the earth in ways We have not established for you?﴾" When you report that you said something to an absent person, or that it was said to him, or that you ordered that it be said, then in eloquent Arabic speech you may relate the words exactly as spoken, bringing the address form (khitab), or you may convey the meaning in the wording by mentioning an absent party without direct address.

"Al-sama'" (the sky) here means the rain, and from it is the poet's saying:

"When the sky (rain) descends upon a people's land,
we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

"Midrar" (abundant, copious) is a form of intensification, like "midhkar" and "mi'nath" (intensive forms of male and female). Its meaning is that it pours upon them according to benefit, because the context of the verse is only enumerating blessings. Otherwise its outward meaning allows for blessing and allows for destruction. The verse may also intend the known sky, with the estimate "and We sent the rain of the sky," because "midrar" is only applied as a description to rain.

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿So We destroyed them﴾, its meaning is: "They disobeyed and disbelieved, so We destroyed them."

﴿And We brought into being﴾ means: We created and originated. "Akharin" (others) is in the plural because it is construed according to the sense of "qarn" (generation).

(p-317) His saying, may He be glorified and exalted:

﴿And if We had sent down to you a Book upon paper, so that they could touch it with their hands, those who disbelieved would surely have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would certainly have been decided, and they would not then be reprieved.﴾ ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them about what they are already confusing.﴾

When He, may He be glorified and exalted, informed about them that they had denied every sign that came to them, there followed a statement containing exaggeration, implying that if something more monstrous than what had come to them had come, they would have denied that too. The meaning: ﴿"And if We had sent down"﴾ before their eyes ﴿"upon you a Book"﴾ — i.e., written speech — ﴿"upon paper"﴾ — i.e., upon a sheet; it is said "qirtās" (with the qāf vowelled with a ḍamma) — ﴿"so that they could touch it with their hands"﴾ — meaning that they exaggerated in examining and turning it over, so that every doubt would be removed; still they would have been obstinate about it, persisted in their disbelief, and said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."

It seems that the occasion of this verse was the proposal and obstinacy of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Umayya, when he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will not believe in you until you ascend into the sky, and then descend with a book in which there is: From the Lord of Might to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Umayya, commanding me to believe in you"; and I do not think that, even with this, I would have believed you." Afterwards, ʿAbd Allāh embraced Islam and was killed as a martyr at al-Ṭāʾif.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"And they say, 'Why has an angel not been sent down to him?'"﴾ — the verse — is a report about those among the Arabs who went to excess, in that they asked that an angel descend to confirm Muḥammad in his prophethood and inform them from God, may He be glorified and exalted, that it is true. God answered them with His saying: ﴿"Had We sent down an angel, the matter would certainly have been decided"﴾. Mujāhid said: its meaning is that the Resurrection would have been established.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is weak.

Qatāda, al-Suddī and Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: there is an ellipsis in the speech; its implied sense is: "And if We had sent down an angel and they denied him, the matter would have been decided by their punishment, and they would not have been reprieved, as occurred with every community that asked for a sign and denied after it was shown to them." This is a good view.

Another group said: ﴿"the matter would have been decided"﴾, i.e., they would have died from the terror of seeing the angel in his form. This interpretation is supported by what follows, His saying: ﴿"And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man"﴾, for the people of interpretation are agreed that this was because they could not endure seeing the angel in his form. So the more apt reading of His saying "the matter would have been decided" is: they would have died from the terror of seeing him.

"Yunẓarūn" means: they would be delayed; and "al-naẓra" is delay.

(p-318) As for His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿"And had We made him"﴾ — the verse — the meaning is: "Indeed, if We had made him an angel, We would certainly have made him, in creation, a man, because they have no capacity to see the angel in his form." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda and Ibn Zayd.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: What supports this meaning is the report concerning the two men who climbed the mountain on the day of Badr in order to watch what would happen in the war of the Prophet (peace be upon him) against the polytheists; they heard the sound of the angels and a speaker in the sky saying, "Advance, Ḥayzūm!" One of them died from the terror of that. How then would it be with seeing an angel in his own creation? This is not contradicted by the Prophet's (peace be upon him) seeing Gabriel (peace be upon him) and others in their forms, because the Prophet (peace be upon him) was given a strength other than all of these — may God bless him and grant him peace.

﴿"And We would have confused"﴾, i.e., "We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves and for their weak-minded followers"; that is, We would have done to them a confusing act which would have led them to be confused by it; and that is not fitting. The statement may also bear another purpose, namely: "We Ourselves would have confused them just as they confuse their weak followers; so We would forbid them from confusion and do it to them." It is said: "The man confused the matter (labasa al-amr, yalbisuhu, labsan)" when he mixed it up. Ibn Muḥaysin read "wa-labbasnā" with a fatḥa on the lām and a shadda on the bā'.

Some people mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book; but the context and meanings of the speech require that it concerns the disbelieving Arabs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 10–11:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encompassed by that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the end of the deniers."﴾

It is recited "wa-laqadu" (with a ḍammah on the dal), because of the ḍammah following the sukūn that comes after the dal. It is also recited with a kasrah on the dal, according to the customary usage of assimilation of consecutive sounds (al-iltiqā'). This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the example of the messengers, a strengthening of his own resolve in disputing with the polytheists, and an announcement that contains a warning to those who deny him and to the mockers.

"Fa-ḥāqa" means: it descended upon, and encompassed. It is specific to evil. One says: "ḥāqa, yaḥīqu, ḥayqan." From this is the saying of the poet:

"He trampled the swift horses upon the sanctuary of their homes, and there encompassed them, from the might of Ḍabba, an encompassing (ḥāʾiq)."

Some people said: the origin of "ḥāqa" is "ḥaqqa," and one of the two qāfs was replaced, just as the nūn was replaced in "taẓannantu."

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak.

The "mā" in His saying, "mā kānū" [al-An'ām: 5 (sic)], may be a relative pronoun meaning "that which," and it may be with the verb in the sense of a verbal noun, as if He had said: "their mockery." This is an allusion to the punishment, just as when you threaten a person and say: "Your deed will overtake you," meaning: its consequence. "Sakhirū" means: they mocked.

His exalted saying, "Say, travel..." to the end of the verse, is an exhortation to take lesson from the traces of those who passed before, of those who did their deeds. He said "kāna" and did not say "kānat," because the feminine marking of "al-ʿāqibah" is not real; it has the meaning of "al-ākhir" (the last) and "al-ma'āl" (the outcome).

The meaning of the verse is: "Travel and receive [knowledge] from those who have traveled," because obtaining the lesson from the traces of those who passed only rests upon sensory sight of the eye.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 10–11:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encompassed by that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the end of the deniers."﴾

It is recited "wa-laqadu" (with a ḍammah on the dal), because of the ḍammah following the sukūn that comes after the dal. It is also recited with a kasrah on the dal, according to the customary usage of assimilation of consecutive sounds (al-iltiqā'). This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the example of the messengers, a strengthening of his own resolve in disputing with the polytheists, and an announcement that contains a warning to those who deny him and to the mockers.

"Fa-ḥāqa" means: it descended upon, and encompassed. It is specific to evil. One says: "ḥāqa, yaḥīqu, ḥayqan." From this is the saying of the poet:

"He trampled the swift horses upon the sanctuary of their homes, and there encompassed them, from the might of Ḍabba, an encompassing (ḥāʾiq)."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 12–13:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah." He has prescribed for Himself mercy. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. Those who have lost their souls—they do not believe.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

(p-320) Some of the people of ta'wil (interpretation) said: there is an omission in the speech; its implied meaning is: "Say: 'To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?' Then, when they are bewildered and do not answer, [say:] 'Say: To Allah.'" Another group said: the meaning is that he was commanded to pose this question; as if they, when they did not answer and were not certain, were asked, and so it was said to him: "Say: To Allah." The correct view is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) to make them certain by this clear proof and this decisive demonstration, against which there is no objection among them or among anyone, so that they would hold this belief which lies between him and them; then his argument against them would be built upon it. This came in the form of an interrogative and an affirmation in His saying: ﴿To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾. The manner of disputation, when a person asks his opponent about a matter which the opponent cannot contest, is that he should, after the affirmation, anticipate him to the proof, hastening to the argument, just as you say to one whom you wish to defeat with a verse by which you argue against him: "How did Allah, Exalted, say in such-and-such?" Then you yourself anticipate him to the verse and state it plainly to him. Thus it is as if the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said to them: "O disbelievers who associate others with your Lord, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Then he anticipated them and said: "To Allah"; meaning: there is no contest in this for you, nor for anyone.

Then He began to inform about Himself, Exalted: ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾. Its meaning: He decreed it and executed it. On this meaning there are hadiths from the Prophet (peace be upon him) which contain the prescribing of mercy. It is known from more than one place in the Sharia that this (mercy) is for the believers in the Hereafter, and for all people in this world. Among them is: "Indeed Allah, Exalted, created one hundred mercies, and placed one of them on the earth; by it the beasts show compassion to one another, and the mare lifts her hoof lest it trample her foal, and by it the birds and the fish show compassion. He has ninety-nine mercies with Him; and when the Day of Resurrection comes, He will make that mercy together with the ninety-nine and disperse them among His servants."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: How wretched is the one whom these mercies do not encompass! May Allah cover us with His grace.

(p-321) Among them is another hadith: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wrote a book with Him, and it is with Him above the Throne: that My mercy precedes My wrath"; and it is narrated: "has overtaken My wrath." Its meaning: it precedes. And Thabit ibn Qasim recited as evidence:

"O sons of Kulayb, indeed my two paternal uncles
Attained the kings and unfastened the shackles."

This report about Allah, Exalted, that He prescribed mercy, includes reassurance to the disbelievers and the negation of their despair of Allah's mercy if they repent, and that the door of their repentance is open. Al-Zajjaj said: "Mercy" here means the granting of respite to the disbelievers and the lengthening of their lives so that they may repent. Al-Mahdawi related that a group of grammarians said: "la-yajma'annakum" is the explanation of "mercy"; its implied form is "an yajma'akum" (that He gather you), so "la-yajma'annakum" is in the accusative position as a substitute for "al-rahmah"; and it is like His saying: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time﴾ [Yusuf: 35]; the meaning being: "an yasjununhu" (that they imprison him).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It follows from this view that the heavy nun would enter an affirmative statement, and this is rejected; it enters only in commands and prohibitions, and in a restricted way in the oath of necessity.

Another group said—and this is the more apparent view—that the lam is the lam of oath and the statement is a new sentence; and this can be construed in "la-yasjununnahu." Another group said: "ila" (to) is in the sense of "fi" (in); it was also said that it retains its original meaning of limit (end point), and this is the more preponderant view.

And ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾: that is, it in itself and its essence is free of doubt.

As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾, etc.: it was said that "alladhina" is a vocative (munada).

(p-322) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is invalid, because the particle of address does not drop with the indefinite pronouns.

It was said that it is an adjective (na't) of "al-mukadhdhibin" (the deniers) previously mentioned. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) of the pronoun in "la-yajma'annakum." Al-Mubarrad said: That is not permissible, just as it is not permissible to say: "I passed by you, Zayd."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: His saying in the verse, "la-yajma'annakum," differs from this example, because the benefit of a substitute is expected from the second term; whereas when you say "I passed by you, Zayd," there is no benefit in the second term. And His saying "la-yajma'annakum" is suitable for addressing people in general; so "alladhina" from the pronoun informs us that they are the ones specifically addressed here, and they are singled out by way of warning; and the warning becomes clear if we make the lam one of oath, which is the correct view; and this comes as a substitute of part from the whole.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Alladhina" is in the nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿so they do not believe﴾; and this is a good view; and the fa' in His saying "fahum" is a response on the view that "alladhina" is nominative as the inceptive, because the sense of the conditional is present; its implied form is: "whoever loses his soul, then he does not believe."

On the view that "alladhina" is a substitute of the pronoun, it is a conjunction of one sentence to another sentence; and "khasiru" (they lost) means: "they cheated themselves in that there became incumbent upon them the punishment of Allah, Exalted, and His wrath"; and from it is the saying of the poet:

"He does not take a bribe in his judgment,
And does not care about the loss of the one who loses."

(p-323) His saying, Exalted: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests﴾, etc.: "wa lahu" is conjoined to His saying "li-Llah"; and the lam is for ownership; and "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi"; and "sakana" is from residing and the like; that is, what has become settled and established; so said al-Suddi and others. Another group said it is from stillness (sukun); and some said: because what is still among things is more than what moves; and other sayings besides this, which are confused. The intent of the verse is the generality of everything, and that is not realized except if "sakana" means "settled and established"; otherwise, what moves among created things is more than what is still. Do you not see the celestial sphere, the sun, the moon, the swimming stars, the angels, and the kinds of animals? And night and day are the two limits of time.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: these are two attributes fitting the tenor of the verse, because what was mentioned before of the disbelievers' wicked sayings, the disbelievers who associate others with Allah, He hears them, knows their places, and will requite them for them; so in the pronoun there is a warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 14–16:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Say: Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, while He feeds and is not fed? Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first to submit, and do not be of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ ﴿Whoever is spared it that day, He has had mercy upon him, and that is the clear triumph.﴾

Al-Tabari and others said: He was commanded to say this statement to the disbelievers who invited him to worship their idols; thus, according to this view, the verse comes as a response to their speech.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This interpretation requires a chain of transmission establishing that this was revealed as a response; otherwise, the apparent meaning of the verse does not contain it. The sound view is that when He had established with them that to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day, and that He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, he was commanded to say to them, by way of rebuke and interrogation: "Shall I take as a protector other than this One whose attributes are these?" meaning that this would be an error, clearly so, if I did it. The force of the speech indicates that whoever among the rest of mankind does it is clearly in error. And "atakhidhu" (I take) governs both "ghayra" (other than) in His saying "aghayra" and "waliyyan" (a protector); one of the two objects has been placed first.

The "waliyy" (protector) is a general term for one who is worshipped, and for other than that of the means connecting the servant with his Lord, may He be exalted. Then he proceeded to the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted, saying: "Fatiri" (Originator), with the "ra'" in the genitive, as a description of Allah, may He be exalted. "Fatara" means: he originated, created, and brought into being. "Fatara" also means in the language: he split; and from it: ﴿Do you see any rifts?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, any cracks; and from this is the cleaving (infitar) of the sky. In this sense the saying "fatara nab al-ba'ir" (the camel's tooth broke through) is established, when it emerges, because it splits the gum. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "I did not know the meaning of ﴿Originator of the heavens﴾ until two Bedouins disputed before me over a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who fatarahā' (originated it), that is, I invented it and brought it into being."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Ibn 'Abbas took it in this sense, and it is valid to take it in the other sense: that He split the earth and the well when He dug it.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "Fatiru" with the "ra'" in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject, or as an inchoative.

﴿He feeds and is not fed﴾: what is meant by it is: He provides sustenance and is not provided for. He singled out feeding from among the kinds of sustenance because of the strong need for it, its prominence, and its being specific to humans. Yaman al-'Ammani and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "yut'imu" with a dammah on the "ya'" and a kasrah on the "'ayn" in the second as in the first, meaning the idol: that it does not feed. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' (in one narration from him) read in the second: "wa la yut'amu" with a fatha on the "ya'", as the imperfect of "ta'ima" (to eat); so it is an attribute containing disculpation, that is: He does not eat, and is not like created beings.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded﴾ up to ﴿tremendous﴾, the exegetes said: the meaning is: "the first to submit from this community, and by this law"; and the speech contains nothing beyond that. A group said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimate being: "and it was said to me: 'Do not be of the polytheists.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The summary of this is that he (peace be upon him) was commanded, and it was said to him: "Be the first to submit, and do not be of the polytheists." When he was commanded in the verse to say what he was commanded, some of that came in meaning and some of it in the very same wording.

The word "'asaytu" (I disobey) is general to all kinds of disobedience; but here it refers only to the polytheism that he was forbidden. The tremendous day is the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "man yusrafu 'anhu" with a dammah on the "ya'" and a fatha on the "ra'"; the object to which the verb is attributed is the pronoun referring to the punishment, which is thus implied. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim also read "man yasrif 'anhu," attributing the verb to the pronoun referring to "my Lord," and governing the pronoun of the punishment mentioned just before, but it is an elided object. It is reported that it appears in the reading of 'Abd Allah: "man yasrifhu 'anhu yawma'idhin"; and in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "man yasrifhu Allahu 'anhu"; and it is said that it is "man yasrifi Allahu 'anhu." Abu 'Ali said: The omission of this pronoun is not good, as the omission of the pronoun from the relative clause is good, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]; and His saying: ﴿Peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ [al-Naml: 59]; meaning "sent him" and "chose them." This is good because of length, as Sibawayh explained; but this is not good because of the absence of a relative clause. Some people said: the reading with a fatha on the "ya'", "man yasrif," is better, because it corresponds with ﴿then He has had mercy upon him﴾; and on the other reading it would have been better to say "fa-qad ruhima" so that the two verbs correspond.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a verbal justification whose connection is weak; as for the meaning, the two readings are one. A group preferred the reading with a dammah on the "ya'," because it involves less implied pronoun. Abu 'Ali pointed to the goodness of the reading with a fatha on the "ya'" for the reason we have mentioned. As for Makki ibn Abi Talib (may Allah have mercy on him), he was confused in his book "al-Hidayah" in preferring the reading with a fatha on the "ya'," and in his argument he gave corrupt examples; and Allah, may He be exalted, is the Guardian of success.

"Rahima" governs the attached pronoun, which is the pronoun of "man," and it is attributed to the pronoun referring to "my Lord." His saying "wa dhalika" (that) refers to the averting of the punishment, and to the mercy, the triumph, and the salvation.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "Fatiru" with the "ra'" in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject, or as an inchoative.

﴿He feeds and is not fed﴾: what is meant by it is: He provides sustenance and is not provided for. He singled out feeding from among the kinds of sustenance because of the strong need for it, its prominence, and its being specific to humans. Yaman al-'Ammani and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "yut'imu" with a dammah on the "ya'" and a kasrah on the "'ayn" in the second as in the first, meaning the idol: that it does not feed. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' (in one narration from him) read in the second: "wa la yut'amu" with a fatha on the "ya'", as the imperfect of "ta'ima" (to eat); so it is an attribute containing disculpation, that is: He does not eat, and is not like created beings.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded﴾ up to ﴿tremendous﴾, the exegetes said: the meaning is: "the first to submit from this community, and by this law"; and the speech contains nothing beyond that. A group said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimate being: "and it was said to me: 'Do not be of the polytheists.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The summary of this is that he (peace be upon him) was commanded, and it was said to him: "Be the first to submit, and do not be of the polytheists." When he was commanded in the verse to say what he was commanded, some of that came in meaning and some of it in the very same wording.

The word "'asaytu" (I disobey) is general to all kinds of disobedience; but here it refers only to the polytheism that he was forbidden. The tremendous day is the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "man yusrafu 'anhu" with a dammah on the "ya'" and a fatha on the "ra'"; the object to which the verb is attributed is the pronoun referring to the punishment, which is thus implied. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim also read "man yasrif 'anhu," attributing the verb to the pronoun referring to "my Lord," and governing the pronoun of the punishment mentioned just before, but it is an elided object. It is reported that it appears in the reading of 'Abd Allah: "man yasrifhu 'anhu yawma'idhin"; and in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "man yasrifhu Allahu 'anhu"; and it is said that it is "man yasrifi Allahu 'anhu." Abu 'Ali said: The omission of this pronoun is not good, as the omission of the pronoun from the relative clause is good, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]; and His saying: ﴿Peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ [al-Naml: 59]; meaning "sent him" and "chose them." This is good because of length, as Sibawayh explained; but this is not good because of the absence of a relative clause. Some people said: the reading with a fatha on the "ya'", "man yasrif," is better, because it corresponds with ﴿then He has had mercy upon him﴾; and on the other reading it would have been better to say "fa-qad ruhima" so that the two verbs correspond.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a verbal justification whose connection is weak; as for the meaning, the two readings are one. A group preferred the reading with a dammah on the "ya'," because it involves less implied pronoun. Abu 'Ali pointed to the goodness of the reading with a fatha on the "ya'" for the reason we have mentioned. As for Makki ibn Abi Talib (may Allah have mercy on him), he was confused in his book "al-Hidayah" in preferring the reading with a fatha on the "ya'," and in his argument he gave corrupt examples; and Allah, may He be exalted, is the Guardian of success.

"Rahima" governs the attached pronoun, which is the pronoun of "man," and it is attributed to the pronoun referring to "my Lord." His saying "wa dhalika" (that) refers to the averting of the punishment, and to the mercy, the triumph, and the salvation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 14–16:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Say: Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, while He feeds and is not fed? Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first to submit, and do not be of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ ﴿Whoever is spared it that day, He has had mercy upon him, and that is the clear triumph.﴾

Al-Tabari and others said: He was commanded to say this statement to the disbelievers who invited him to worship their idols; thus, according to this view, the verse comes as a response to their speech.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This interpretation requires a chain of transmission establishing that this was revealed as a response; otherwise, the apparent meaning of the verse does not contain it. The sound view is that when He had established with them that to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day, and that He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, he was commanded to say to them, by way of rebuke and interrogation: "Shall I take as a protector other than this One whose attributes are these?" meaning that this would be an error, clearly so, if I did it. The force of the speech indicates that whoever among the rest of mankind does it is clearly in error. And "atakhidhu" (I take) governs both "ghayra" (other than) in His saying "aghayra" and "waliyyan" (a protector); one of the two objects has been placed first.

The "waliyy" (protector) is a general term for one who is worshipped, and for other than that of the means connecting the servant with his Lord, may He be exalted. Then he proceeded to the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted, saying: "Fatiri" (Originator), with the "ra'" in the genitive, as a description of Allah, may He be exalted. "Fatara" means: he originated, created, and brought into being. "Fatara" also means in the language: he split; and from it: ﴿Do you see any rifts?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, any cracks; and from this is the cleaving (infitar) of the sky. In this sense the saying "fatara nab al-ba'ir" (the camel's tooth broke through) is established, when it emerges, because it splits the gum. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 17–18:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿If Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things Competent.﴾ ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

"Yamsaska" (touches you): its meaning is "reaches you and attains you." The real meaning of al-massu (touching) is the meeting of two bodies, as if the human being and the harm were touching one another.

Al-durr (with a dammah on the dad) is bad condition in the body and other than it, while al-darr (with a fatha on the dad) is the opposite of benefit. In this verse, al-durr takes the place of al-sharr, although al-sharr is more general than it, so it is set against al-khayr (good). This is part of eloquence, a departure from the rule of artificial contrivance. The method of contrivance and of rhetorical balancing (tarsi') in speech is that a thing is paired with that which is specifically associated with it, by some kind of association, either in agreement or in opposition. Among examples is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is [promised] for you that you will not be hungry therein or be unclothed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118] ﴿And that you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119]. He placed hunger with nakedness, whereas the proper pairing would have been with thirst. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,
And never poured out the wine-skin's contents, nor said to my horses: 'Turn back for a second charge after the rout.'"

(p-327) And this is abundant.

Al-Suddi said: "Al-durr here is sickness, and al-khayr is health."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an example. The meaning of the verse is the report that all things are in the hand of Allah: if He inflicts harm, none other than He removes its harm; and if He bestows good, likewise there is none to turn it back or prevent it. This is the statement of the meaning. But in place of this implied meaning He placed a more general expression that encompasses it and other things, namely His saying: ﴿over all things Competent﴾; and the apparent wording of the speech indicates the implied meaning within it. His saying ﴿over all things Competent﴾ means: over every thing that it is permissible for Allah, Exalted is He, to be described as having power over.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Subduer﴾, etc., means: He, Exalted and Majestic, is the Dominant, the Powerful. "Fawqa" (over) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, not of physical place, but in the meaning contained in the word "al-Qahir," as you say: "Zayd is above 'Amr in rank." The literal meaning of "fawqa" concerns places, and in meanings it is used metaphorically. It is applied to one who is higher in rank in some respect, since in physical places it truly indicates the higher. Al-Mahdawi related that it is by way of an implied circumstantial clause, as if he said: "And He is the Subduer, dominating."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This too is not free from objection, and the first view is, in my opinion, more correct.

Al-'ibad means the same as al-'abid; both are plurals of al-'abd. Yet we find the word "al-'ibad" used in the Qur'an and elsewhere in contexts of exaltation, elevation, or honour, while the word "al-'abid" is used in contexts of contempt, weakness, or reproach. Do you not see the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Say to Dudan, slaves of the staff..."

It would not be fitting to say here "'ibad al-'asa." Likewise those who are called "al-'ibad" cannot fittingly be called "al-'abid," because they are more exalted than that. Similarly the saying of Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him: "Are you not but slaves to my father?" — "'ibad" would not fit there.

(p-329) And "al-Hakim," in the sense of "al-Muhkim," and "al-Khabir," both indicate intensity of knowledge; and these are two attributes fitting to the pattern of the verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "Allah is witness between me and you. This Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby, and whomever it reaches. Do you really bear witness that there are other gods with Allah?" Say: "I do not bear witness." Say: "He is only one God, and I am innocent of what you associate."﴾

"Ayyu" (which): an interrogative; it is declinable (mu'rab) despite its ambiguity. This is because it necessarily takes an annexed genitive (iḍāfa), and because it implies knowledge of a part of what is asked about, though not specified. For when you say, "Which of the two men came to us?", you already know that one of them came, but not which one. These two features removed it from the murkiness of ambiguity, so it was declined (i'rab).

This verse implies that Allah, exalted is He, may be described as "a thing," just as He may be described as "existent"; but "nothing is like His likeness" (42:11), blessed and exalted is He.

"Shahādatan" (as testimony) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). It may also be in the accusative as an object, by taking "akbar" as an imitation of the attributive adjective of the active participle.

This verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah."﴾ (6:12), in that He asks in the manner of establishing and affirming, then hastens to the answer, since no contention is conceivable in it. This is like when you say to someone you are disputing with and complaining against: "Who is the most powerful in the land?", then you hasten and say: "The sultan; for he stands between us," and similar examples. So the sense of the verse is that He said to them: "What thing is greatest as testimony? Allah is greatest as testimony; He is witness between me and you." So "Allah" is raised as the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is elided, indicated by the apparent meaning of the speech as we have estimated, and "witness" is the predicate of an elided subject.

Mujahid said: the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, said to His Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him: "Say to them: 'What thing is greatest as testimony?' And say to them: 'Allah is witness between me and you,' since they were unable to answer." So "witness," according to this interpretation, is the predicate of "Allah"; and in this interpretation there is no hastening by the questioner to the answer intended by His saying: ﴿witness between me and you﴾; i.e., in my conveying.

One group recited: "wa-Ūḥiya ilayya hādhā al-Qur'ān" with the verb in the active past and "al-Qur'ān" in the accusative; in "wa-awḥā" there is a pronoun referring to Allah, exalted is He, from His saying ﴿Say: "Allah"﴾. Another group recited: "wa-Ūḥiya" with the verb in the passive, "al-Qur'ān" in the nominative.

"Li-undhirakum" (that I may warn you): its meaning is that I may frighten you thereby with punishment and the Hereafter. "Wa-man" (and whomever) is conjoined to the kāf and mīm in His saying "li-undhirakum." "Balagha" (reaches), according to the majority, means: the reaching of the Qur'an; i.e., that I may warn you and warn whomever it reaches. So in "balagha" there is an elided pronoun, because it is in the relative clause of "wa-man," and it was elided due to the length of the speech. Another group said: "wa-man balagha al-ḥulum" (whoever reaches maturity), so in "balagha" according to this interpretation there is an implied pronoun referring back to "man."

Hadiths have been related in support of the first interpretation, among them that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O people, convey from me even a single verse; for whoever has a verse of the Book of Allah conveyed to him, the command of Allah has reached him, whether he takes it or leaves it." And similar to this are hadiths such as his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever has this Qur'an reach him, I am his warner."

One group recited: "Āyinnakum" with an added alif between the first hamza and the second, softened hamza, treating it after this softening as it was treated before softening. Another group recited: "Ayinnakum" with two hamzas, the second softened, without an alif between them. Another group recited: "Ā'innakum" — they found the joining of the two hamzas burdensome, so they added an alif between the two hamzas. Another group recited: "Innakum" affirmatively, without estimation.

The purpose of this verse is rebuke and the exposure of the folly of their opinion.

"Ukhrā" (other) is an attribute of "ālihatan" (gods); and the attribute of a plural of non-rational things is treated in the singular as a feminine singular, like His saying: "other uses" (mā'ārib ukhrā) (20:18); similarly, addressing a plural of non-rational things, like His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ (34:10), and similar. And since these gods were stones and wooden idols, they were treated in this manner.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to disavow their testimony and to proclaim the Oneness of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, and to disavow their associating partners.

"Wa-innanī" (and indeed I): an affirmative in which the nūn is appended that attaches to the verb, so that its vowel remains when the pronoun is attached to it, as in your saying "wa-ḍaraban-ī" and similar.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that it concerns worshippers of idols. Al-Ṭabarī mentioned that it has been transmitted by a route whose soundness is not established that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews. It is attributed to Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Al-Naḥḥām ibn Zayd, Qardam ibn Ka'b, and Baḥrī ibn 'Umayr came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know of any god with Allah other than Him?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: 'There is no god but Allah; I have been commanded with this.' So the verse was revealed concerning them."

(p-332) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book know it as they know their own sons. Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe.﴾ ﴿And who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against God or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.﴾

"Alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative case, as the mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). Its khabar (predicate) is "yaʿrifunahu" (they know it). "Al-Kitab" (the Book) means the Tawrat (Torah) and the Injil (Gospel). It is a singular noun that denotes a genus. The pronoun in "yaʿrifunahu" refers, according to some opinions, to Tawhid (the Oneness of God), because of the nearby saying: ﴿Say: He is only one God﴾ [6:19]. On this reading, the verse cites the People of the Book as evidence against the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs.

On this interpretation, "alladhina khasarū" (those who have lost) is a new, independent clause, in the nominative as a subject. It is not a qualifier of the first "alladhina," because it is not valid to cite the People of the Book as evidence and blame them in the same verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It may well be valid, because the matter for which they are cited as evidence differs from the matter for which they are blamed, and the blame and the citing do not come from the same aspect.

Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj said: the pronoun in "yaʿrifunahu" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his message. This is in line with what is said in: ﴿This Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you﴾ [6:19]. It is as if He said: "And the People of the Book know this from my warning and from the revelation made to me." Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, interpreted it this way. This is shown by his saying to Abdullah ibn Salam: "God revealed to His Prophet in Mecca that you know him as you know your sons. So what is this knowledge?" Abdullah ibn Salam replied: "Yes, I know him by the description with which God described him in the Torah, so I have no doubt about him. As for my son, I do not know what his mother has done."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Ibn Salam, may God be pleased with him, interpreted "knowing" in the case of the son as confirming the validity of his lineage. The purpose of the verse is only to identify his form, so the father does not err about him.

Another group said: the pronoun in "yaʿrifunahu" refers to the Qur'an mentioned before.

(p-333) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is also valid to refer the pronoun to all of these together, without restriction. It is as if He described many things and then said: "The People of the Book know it," that is, what We have said and what We have related.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 22–24:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And on the Day We shall gather them all together, then We shall say to those who associated partners with Allah, "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿Then their temptation will be only that they will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who associated partners."﴾ ﴿Look how they lied against themselves, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾

A group said: ﴿The wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-An'am: 21] is a complete sentence, meaning: "The wrongdoers will not succeed at all." Then He began anew and said: "And mention the Day We shall gather them..." Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: "The wrongdoers will not succeed today in this world, and [mention] the day We shall gather them," as a conjunction with the supposed adverbial phrase, and the speech is continuous.

A group recited "nahshuruhum" and "naqulu" with the nun (first person plural). Humayd and Ya'qub recited both with the ya' (third person). 'Asim recited here and in Yunus (before the thirtieth verse) "nahshuruhum" and "naqulu" with the nun, and recited the rest of the Qur'an with the ya'. Abu Hurayra recited "nahshiruhum" with a kasra on the shin, so the verb according to this would be: "hasara, yahshuru, and yahshiru."

He attributed the partners to them because there is in reality no partnership between the idols and anything; rather, the name of "partner" was applied to them merely by the naming of the unbelievers, so they were attributed to them for this relation.

"Taza'mun" means: you claim that they are [partners] of Allah, the Exalted. Al-za'm is the saying that inclines towards falsehood and lying, in most of their speech; and it may be said "za'ama" in the sense of "mentioned," without inclination towards lying. On this basis Sibawayh says: "Za'ama al-Khalil" (al-Khalil claimed). But that is only used of a strange matter, the responsibility for which remains upon its speaker.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then their temptation will be only that they will say﴾, etc.: Ibn Kathir, in the narration of Shibl from him, and 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, and Ibn 'Amir recited "takun fitnatuhum" with the fitna in the nominative; and "illa an qalu" is in the accusative position as a predicate; the estimate being: "illa qawluhum" (except their saying). This is correct, because it made the feminine marker on the verb when it attributed it to a feminine noun, namely fitna. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Kathir also recited "takun fitnatahum" with the fitna in the accusative; the name of "kana" is "an qalu," and in this reading the "an qalu" is feminine; and this was permissible because fitna is feminine in meaning. Abu 'Ali said: This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So for him is ten times the like thereof﴾ [al-An'am: 160]; He made "amthal" feminine, since the good deeds are in meaning. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "yakun" with the ya', "fitnatahum" with the accusative; the name of "kana" is ﴿illa an qalu﴾. This is correct, because it masculinized the verb marker when it attributed it to a masculine. Al-Zahrawi said: A group recited "yakun fitnatuhum" with the fitna in the nominative; in this reading a masculine verb is attributed to a feminine noun, and this came according to meaning, because fitna is in the sense of testing, or love of a thing, or admiration [for it].

Abu Ubayy ibn Wakī', Ibn Mas'ud, and al-A'mash recited "wa ma kana fitnatuhum"; and Talha ibn Musarrif recited "thumma kana fitnatuhum."

Fitna in the speech of the Arabs is a shared term; it is said in the sense of loving a thing and being admiring of it, as you say "futintu bi-kadha" (I have become enamoured with such-and-such). The verse here may bear this meaning: i.e., "Their love for the idols, their admiration of them, and their following of them was not, when they were asked about them and were made to stand before their impotence, [anything] except disavowing them and denying them." This is a rebuke to them, as you say to a man who used to claim affection for another and then turned away from him and became hostile to him: "O so-and-so, your affection for so-and-so was not except that you insulted him and became hostile to him." It is also said that "al-fitna" in the speech of the Arabs means testing, as Allah, Exalted and Majestic, said to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And We tested you with many trials﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]; and as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We did test Sulayman and We placed upon his throne a body﴾ [Sad: 34]. The verse here may bear this meaning too, because their being questioned about the partners and their being made to stand is a test; so the meaning is: "Then Our testing of them was not — since it yielded nothing and bore no fruit — except their denial of associating partners."

Fitna comes in the language with meanings other than these two, which have no place in the verse. And whoever said: "The origin of fitna is testing, from 'fatantu al-dhahab fi al-nar' (I tested the gold in the fire), and then it is used figuratively in other than that" — he has erred, because a noun is not judged to be figurative until its literal meaning is certainly impossible in the place where it is used figuratively, as in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"......... and dawn wrapped the Pleiades in its cloak"

and the like; and fitna is not impossible to be literal in every place where it is said.

And Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Umar recited "wallahi rabbina" with the genitive, as an epithet of the name of Allah, Exalted; Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "rabbana" in the accusative, as a vocative; and it is permissible in it to estimate a praise. 'Ikrima and Sallam ibn Miskin recited "wallahu rabbuna" with both nouns in the nominative; this is on the estimate of an inversion and postponement, as if they said: "We were not associators; and Allah is our Lord." "We were not associators" means the denial of their associating in the world. It is narrated that when they see those from the people of the Fire who are of the believers being brought out, they cry out, and they are made to stand, and it is said to them: "Where are your partners?" and they deny, out of hope that they will be treated as the people of faith were treated. A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: I heard Allah, Exalted, say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not associators﴾; and in another place: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "When they saw that none enters Paradise except a believer, they said: 'Come, let us deny'; and they said: 'We were not associators.' So Allah, Exalted, sealed upon their mouths, and their limbs spoke, so they do not conceal from Allah any statement."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Some of the exegetes expressed the fitna here by their saying "their excuse"; this was said by Qatada. Others said: "their speech"; this was said by al-Dahhak. Other things have been said, all of which are within what we have mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Look how they lied﴾, etc.: the address is to Muhammad, peace be upon him; and the looking is the looking of the heart. He said "kadhabu" (they lied) regarding a matter that had not yet occurred, since it is a narration of the Day of Resurrection; so there is no difficulty in using the past tense there in place of the future; and the use of the past tense gives us the affirmation and confirmation of the action; and this is a well-trodden path in the language. From it is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Dabu' al-Fazari:

"I have become one who does not carry a weapon, nor possess the head of a camel if it bolts."

He means: "if it bolts."

﴿"And what they had invented has gone astray from them"﴾: its meaning is: "their fabrication in the world went away, and their lying by ascribing partners to Allah, blessed and exalted is He."
