'Ikrima and Sallam ibn Miskin recited "wallahu rabbuna" with both nouns in the nominative; this is on the estimate of an inversion and postponement, as if they said: "We were not associators; and Allah is our Lord." "We were not associators" means the denial of their associating in the world. It is narrated that when they see those from the people of the Fire who are of the believers being brought out, they cry out, and they are made to stand, and it is said to them: "Where are your partners?" and they deny, out of hope that they will be treated as the people of faith were treated. A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: I heard Allah, Exalted, say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not associators﴾; and in another place: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "When they saw that none enters Paradise except a believer, they said: 'Come, let us deny'; and they said: 'We were not associators.' So Allah, Exalted, sealed upon their mouths, and their limbs spoke, so they do not conceal from Allah any statement."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Some of the exegetes expressed the fitna here by their saying "their excuse"; this was said by Qatada. Others said: "their speech"; this was said by al-Dahhak. Other things have been said, all of which are within what we have mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Look how they lied﴾, etc.: the address is to Muhammad, peace be upon him; and the looking is the looking of the heart. He said "kadhabu" (they lied) regarding a matter that had not yet occurred, since it is a narration of the Day of Resurrection; so there is no difficulty in using the past tense there in place of the future; and the use of the past tense gives us the affirmation and confirmation of the action; and this is a well-trodden path in the language. From it is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Dabu' al-Fazari:

"I have become one who does not carry a weapon, nor possess the head of a camel if it bolts."

He means: "if it bolts."

﴿"And what they had invented has gone astray from them"﴾: its meaning is: "their fabrication in the world went away, and their lying by ascribing partners to Allah, blessed and exalted is He."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 25:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is not but the fables of the former peoples."﴾

The pronoun in His saying "wa minhum" (and among them) refers to the disbelievers who were mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And the Day We gather them all together﴾ [al-An'am: 22]. He used the singular "yastami'u" (listens), though it is a verb of a plural subject, in keeping with the wording of "man" (whoever). "Akinna" is the plural of "kinan," which is the all-encompassing covering, and from it comes "kinanat al-sihām" (the quiver of arrows). "Al-kinn" (a shelter or protective cover) is also from this root, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Like hidden eggs﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]. From it is also the saying of the poet:

"When they draw them in battle from their sheaths, you think the lightning flashes of rain are stirred up by their clouds."

The patterns "fi'āl" and "af'ila" are common in their speech.

"An yafqahūhu" (that they understand it) is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: "out of aversion that they understand it." It has also been said that the meaning is: "lest they understand it," and this view requires the implied omission of the negative particle. "Yafqahūhu" means "yafhamūhu" (they comprehend it). It is said "faqiha al-rajul" (with a kasra on the qaf) when a man comprehends a thing; "fuqiha" (with a damma) when he becomes a jurist possessing that faculty; and "faqaha" (with a fatha) when he surpasses others in jurisprudence.

Al-waqr is the heaviness in hearing. It is said "waqirat udhunuhu" and "waqarat" (with a kasra or fatha on the qaf). From it is the saying of the poet:

"And a foul speech, my ear was burdened by it, and there is no deafness in me."

It has also been heard as "udhunun mawquratun" (an ear that is burdened), so the verb in this case is "wuqirat." Talha ibn Musarrif recited "wiqran" (with a kasra on the waw), as if he took it to mean "in their ears," and that they were burdened with deafness, just as a beast is loaded with a burden. This is an irregular (shadhdh) recitation. This expression refers to what Allah, Exalted is He, placed in the souls of these people of error and aversion from accepting good, not that they were not hearing His words.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they see every sign﴾; "al-ayah" (the sign): the seeing here is seeing with the eye, meaning like the splitting of the moon and its like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The purpose of this verse is that they are at the lowest degree of incapacity, and they tried to reject the truth with bare claims. The "wa" in His saying "wa ja'alna" (and We placed) is the waw of circumstance (hal), and the rule is that it be accompanied explicitly by "qad," though it sometimes comes with "qad" implied. The clarification of this is that He, Exalted is He, said: Among these disbelievers is one who listens to you, while in the extent of his dullness his heart is within coverings and his ear is deaf, and he sees the signs but does not believe in them. Yet, despite reaching the extreme of this deficiency, when he comes to dispute he responds with bare claims.

"Al-mujadala" (disputation) is the confrontation in argument, derived from "al-jadal" (contention). "Hadha" (this) in their saying refers to the Qur'an.

"Al-asatir" is the plural of "usṭār," like "aqwāl" and "aqāwīl" and similar. "Asṭār" is the plural of "saṭr" or "saṭar." It has also been said: "al-asatir" is the plural of "isṭāra," which means trifles. It has also been said it is the plural of "usṭūra" like "u'jūba" and "udhḥūka." It has also been said it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like "‘abābīd" and "shamāmīs." The meaning is: the reports of the former peoples, their tales and narratives, which are written down and related, and are not verified, like histories. The disbelievers only likened them to the stories of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, Rustam, and al-Sindbad. The disputing of the disbelievers was their attempt to extinguish the light of Allah with their false mouths. Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he gave an example of such, their saying: "You who follow Muhammad eat what you slaughter with your own hands, and you do not eat what Allah kills," and similar confusion from which no proof can be composed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a dispute over a ruling, whereas what is in the verse is a dispute aimed at repelling the Qur'an. So in my view the verse is not to be explained by the matter of slaughter.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 6, verses 26–27:**

His words, exalted is He:

﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it, and they destroy none but themselves, yet they perceive not.﴾ ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire, and they say: "Would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers!"﴾

The pronoun in His words "wa-hum" ("and they") refers to those mentioned before. As for the pronoun in "ʿanhu" ("from it"): Qatadah and Mujahid said it refers to the Qur'an, previously mentioned in His words "that they should understand it." Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah and al-Dahhak said it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is that they forbid others (from him), while they themselves keep far away. *Al-nayʾ* (distancing) means remoteness.

As for "and they destroy...": its meaning is that they destroy none but themselves, through the disbelief that enters them into Hell. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, as did al-Qasim, Habib ibn Abi Thabit and ʿAta' ibn Dinar, that what is meant by His words "and they forbid it" is Abu Talib and those with him, in protecting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while remaining persistent in disbelief. The meaning is: "They forbid from him those who wish to harm him, and they keep away from him by not believing in him and not following him; so they do one thing and its opposite." This view is weakened by the fact that the pronoun "wa-hum" is then returned to the whole group of disbelievers mentioned earlier, because not all of them were forbidding the harming of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This can be explained, and it is good, if you take the intended meaning to be the mention of a faction within the group, the whole of which is united in disbelief. The expression then refers to a part of the group with a term that encompasses the entire group, because rebuke in this form is more severe for them. Just as you say, when you denounce a group among whom are adulterers, thieves and drinkers of wine: "These people commit adultery, steal and drink wine." The real meaning of your words is that some of them do this and some of them do that. It is as if He said: "Among these disbelievers is one who listens while they forbid harm to him, and who does not believe in him," meaning: "Among them there are those who do this."

As for "wa-ma yashʿurun" ("yet they perceive not"): its meaning is "they do not know with sensory knowledge." It is derived from *al-shiʿar* (the undergarment, which lies next to the body of a person), and *al-shiʿar* is derived from *al-shaʿr* (hair). The negation of perception is a severe reproach, since animals perceive and sense. When you say, "So-and-so does not perceive," you have negated knowledge from him in the general sense, which implies that he knows neither knowable things nor sensible things.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: al-Hasan read "wa-yanawna ʿanhu," moving the vowel of the hamza onto the nun, by the regular easing (*al-tasḥil al-qiyasi*, the systematic softening of the hamza).

As for His words, exalted is He, "And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire...": the address in it is to Muhammad (ﷺ). The response to "law" ("if") is omitted. Its implied sense at the end of this verse is: "You would see a terrible thing, or hardships," or something similar. Omitting its response in such a context is more eloquent, because the addressee is left with the fullest scope of his imagination.

The word "idh" is used in the place of "idha," which refers to the future. This is permissible because a matter whose occurrence is certain is expressed in the way that a past event is expressed. "Wuqifu" ("they were made to stand") means "they were detained." The form of this verb, whether transitive or intransitive, is the same: you say, "I stopped" (*waqaftu*), and "I stopped another" (*waqaftu ghayri*). Al-Zahrawi said: They have been distinguished by the verbal noun: in the transitive form it is *waqftuhu waqfan*, and in the intransitive it is *waqaftu wuqufan*. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' said: I have not heard in the speech of the Arabs "awqaftu fulanan" (I made so-and-so stand), but if I met a man standing and said to him, "What made you stop here?" it would seem good to me. His words "wuqifu ʿalā al-nār" may mean "they entered it," so that their standing over it means their standing in it. This was said by al-Tabari. It may also mean "they came to its edge and beheld it."

Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisaʾi, and ʿAsim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, read "wa-la nukadhdhibu" and "wa-nakunu" with the *raf*ʿ (nominative) in both. This is according to the intention of *isti'naf* (resumption) and *qat'* (cutting off) in His words "wa-la nukadhdhibu," and "wa-nakunu," meaning: "Would that we were returned; and we, in every state, would not deny, and we would be..." They informed about themselves of this, and because of this information their later denial was valid. Sibawayh preferred this reading and illustrated it with your saying, "Leave me, and I will not return," meaning: "And I, in every state, will not return." This may also be explained by another view, namely that "wa-la nukadhdhibu" and "wa-nakunu" are included in the wish (*tamannī*), in the same way that "nuradd" is included in it. It is as if they said: "Would that we were returned; and would that we did not deny; and would that we were..." This interpretation is objected to on the grounds that one who wishes for something cannot be called a liar, since only one who makes a statement can lie.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This objection can be answered by taking His words, "And indeed they are liars" (Qur'an 6:28), as a statement cut off from what precedes it, describing their state in this world. There is also another answer: when the one who wishes has a disposition and way of life that opposes what he wishes for and is far from it, it is valid to say to him, "You have lied," in a figurative sense. This is because whoever wishes for something, his wish implies a statement that this desire suits him and he suits it, so the denial falls on that statement implied by the wish. An example is a wicked man saying, "Would that I performed pilgrimage, fought in holy war, and stood in prayer through the night." It is permissible to say to such a man, in a figurative sense, "You have lied," meaning: "You are not fit for this, and it is not fit for you."

It is transmitted from Abu ʿAmr that he assimilated the *bāʾ* of "nukadhdhiba" into the following *bāʾ*. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, and ʿAsim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "wa-la nukadhdhiba" and "wa-nakūna" with the *naṣb* (accusative) in both verbs. This is like the *fāʾ* taking the accusative in the response of a wish. The *wāw* in this case and the *fāʾ* hold the same position. This is according to the supposition of mentioning the verbal noun of the first verb, as if they said: "Would that there were for us a return, and a non-denial, and an existence among the believers."

Ibn ʿAmir, in the transmission of Hisham ibn ʿAmmar from his companions, from Ibn ʿAmir, read "wa-la nukadhdhibu" with the *raf*ʿ and "wa-nakūna" with the *naṣb*. This can be understood in light of what preceded, in the codex of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud: "Would that we were returned, so that we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and would be..." with a *tā'* (feminine form). In the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "Would that we were returned, so that we would never deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be..." Abu ʿAmr related that in Ubayy's reading it is: "the signs of our Lord, and we, we are..."

His word "nuradd" ("we be returned") in all these statements means: to the world. Al-Tabari related another interpretation, namely: "Would that we were returned to the Hereafter," meaning: "We would be raised and made to stand over the Fire that we were made to stand over, as deniers. Would that this happened, while we were in a state of not denying and of being..." The meaning then is: "Would that we were made to stand this standing, not denying the signs of our Lord, being among the believers."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is weak on several grounds, and His words refute it: "And if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden" (Qur'an 6:28). Nor is denial valid in this wish, because it is a wish for what has already passed. The denial that we mentioned earlier is valid only in a figurative sense regarding the wish for future matters.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 28–30:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before. And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿And they say, "There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say, "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve."﴾

The pronoun in "lahum" (to them) refers to those mentioned in His saying "wuqifu" (they are made to stand), and "qalu" (they say). This statement implies that they used to conceal something in the world, and it became apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection; or, what became apparent to them was its harm and its consequence, so the genitive noun (mudaf) was omitted and the genitive complement (mudaf ilayhi) was put in its place. Al-Zahrawi related from a group that they said: the verse concerns the hypocrites, because they used to conceal disbelief; so there became apparent to them its harm on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The expression becomes strained according to this interpretation, because He said "wuqifu" meaning a group of disbelievers, then He said "bada lahum" meaning the hypocrites among these disbelievers; and the speech does not allow this except with great strain. Al-Zahrawi said: It has also been said that when the Prophet (ﷺ) admonished the disbelievers, they would fear, and they would conceal that fear so that their followers would not perceive it; so that became apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is valid that the purpose of the verse is to inform of the terror of what they encountered and to magnify what they suffered; so He expressed this by saying that their hidden matters in the world became apparent to them, such as sins and other things. How then, according to this, is the assumption regarding what they used to openly declare, such as disbelief and the like? This interpretation is supported by His saying, Exalted is He, magnifying the matter of the Day of Resurrection: ﴿On the Day when secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9]. It is also valid to estimate that what they used to conceal in the world was the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his sayings; for they used to conceal it in the world by belittling him in the presence of those who came to them, describing him with other than his attributes, and intercepting people on the roads, saying to them: "He is a sorcerer; he separates between relatives," intending by that to hide his matter and nullify it. The meaning of this verse, according to this, is: "Nay, there has become apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection your matter, your truthfulness, your warning, and your informing of the punishment of those who disbelieved, which they used to conceal in the world"; and the concealment would be as we have described.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "What the misguided ones used to conceal of the resurrection became apparent to those who followed them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Thus the two pronouns according to this do not refer to one thing. Al-Mahdawi related something similar to this from al-Hasan.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-Nakha'i, and al-A'mash read "wa-law riddu" with a kasra on the ra', according to transferring the vowel of the dal from "ruddidu" into it.

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before. And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿And they say, "There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. Al-Zahrawi related from a group that they said: the verse concerns the hypocrites, because they used to conceal disbelief; so there became apparent to them its harm on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The expression becomes strained according to this interpretation, because He said "wuqifu" meaning a group of disbelievers, then He said "bada lahum" meaning the hypocrites among these disbelievers; and the speech does not allow this except with great strain. Al-Zahrawi said: It has also been said that when the Prophet (ﷺ) admonished the disbelievers, they would fear, and they would conceal that fear so that their followers would not perceive it; so that became apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 31:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost, until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they say, "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens on their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they carry.﴾

This is a resumed statement informing of the loss of the deniers. It implies the magnification of the calamity that befell them. The word "loss" (khasara) is used in such a context, because whoever takes disbelief and follows it, it is as if he has given up faith and discarded it, so it resembles a transaction of taking and giving.

The reference in this verse is to those who said, "There is only our life of this world." His saying, ﴿"the meeting with Allah"﴾, means: by returning to Him, and to His judgments, and His power, as you say, "So-and-so met his deeds," meaning, "he met their consequences and their outcome." And "the Hour" (al-sa'a) is the Day of Resurrection. The definite article (ta'rif al-'ahd) was applied to it without prior mention of it, because of its fame, its settlement in souls, and the spread of its matter. Also, His saying, ﴿"the meeting with Allah"﴾, has already included it.

And "suddenly" (baghtatan) means: unexpectedly. You say, "The matter took me by surprise" (baghatanī al-amr), meaning, "it came upon me unexpectedly." From it is the saying of the poet:

"But they repented, and I did not fear a sudden [attack], and the most dreadful thing is when the sudden event overtakes you."

Its accusative form is as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl), as you say, "I killed him patiently" (qataltuhu ṣabran). Sibawayh does not permit analogy based on it; and you do not say, "So-and-so came quickly" (sur'atan) or similar.

The calling out of regret (nidā' al-ḥasra) is for the magnification and condemnation of the matter. Sibawayh said: It is as if the one who calls out to regret, or wonder, or joy, or woe, says, "Draw near, or present yourself, for this is your time and your moment." In this there is a magnification of the matter, both for the speaker himself and for his listener, if there is a listener. This magnification for the self and the listener is also the intended meaning in calling out to inanimate things, as in your saying, "O house!" or "O abode!" and in calling out to what does not understand, as in their saying, "O camel!" and the like.

And "we neglected" (farraṭnā) means: we fell short while having the ability to avoid falling short. This is the true meaning of tafrīṭ. The pronoun in His saying, "concerning it" (fīhā), refers to the Hour, meaning: in preparation for it. This is the view of al-Ḥasan. Al-Ṭabarī said: it refers to the transaction implied by the mention of loss at the beginning of the verse. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the world (al-dunyā), since the meaning requires it, and the sense of place (ẓarfiyya) is more apt, like: "Zayd is in the house." Its reference to the Hour means only: in its affairs and preparation for it, like: "Zayd is occupied with knowledge."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿while they carry their burdens on their backs﴾, the waw is the waw of the circumstantial state (wāw al-ḥāl). The word "awzār" is the plural of "wizr" with a kasra on the waw, and it is the weight of sins. You say from it, "wazara, yazir," when he carried. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. And you say, "wazara al-rajul, fa huwa mawzūr" (the man was burdened with sin). Abū 'Ubayda said: the common people say "ma'zūr," but when this is paired with "ma'jūr" (rewarded), the Arabs say "ma'zūr." The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to women whom he met coming back from the graveyards: "Return burdened with sin, not rewarded." Abū 'Alī and others said: this is for verbal conformity (al-itbā' al-lafẓī). The "wizr" here is a metaphor and figurative comparison to the weight of loads, and the comparison is strengthened by placing it on the backs, since that is customarily the place where heavy loads are carried. As for one who says it derives from "al-wazar" (the mountain one takes refuge in), from which comes "al-wazīr" (minister), meaning "helper," that is an unclear statement. Al-Ṭabarī and others said: this is in the literal sense, and they related in this regard a report that the believer will meet his deed in its most beautiful and fragrant form, and he will greet him and say, "I rode you much in the world and wore you out, so ride me today." He said: so the image of the deed carries him. And that the disbeliever will meet his deed in its ugliest and most foul form, and it will revile him and say, "I am your wicked deed; you rode me much in the world with your desires, so I will ride you today." He said: so he carries the image of his deed and his burdens on his back.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they carry﴾, it is information about the evil of what they incur as sin, containing the magnification of that and the proclaiming of it. This is like the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Unquestionably, let the present one convey it to the absent one," and his saying: "Unquestionably, have I conveyed?" He only intended proclamation and calling to witness. All of this is included in "unquestionably" (alā). As for ﴿"evil is what they carry"﴾, it is a plain statement, like the saying of the poet:

"I was pleased with a plan of humiliation, not of any benefit, so evil is this pleasure, O Qays of 'Aylan!"

"Sā'a" is a past-tense verb, and "mā" is its subject, as you say, "The matter of such-and-such displeased me." It is also possible that "sā'a" here is treated like "bi'sa," and what is applied to "bi'sa" is applied to it, since it has come in the Book of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Evil is the example of the people﴾ [al-A'rāf: 177].

Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 6, verses 32–33:

(p-349) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement. But the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of Allah. Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah.﴾

This is the beginning of a report about the state of this world. The meaning is: since it is transient, finite, and without any benefit, it resembles play and amusement, which have no benefit once they are over.

The six readers recited "wa-la-dāru" (وَلَلدّارُ) with two lām's, and "al-ākhiratu" (اَلْآخِرَةُ) as an adjective of "al-dār." Ibn ʿĀmir alone recited "wa-ladāru" (وَلَدارُ) with a single lām, and so it is written in the codices of Syria, with "al-dār" in an idafa to "al-ākhira." This is like "masjidu l-jāmiʿ" (مَسْجِدُ الجامِعِ), meaning "the masjid of the congregational day," so likewise here: "wa-ladāru l-ḥayati l-ākhira" (وَلَدارُ الحَياةِ الآخِرَةِ).

Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, recited "ya'qilūna" (يَعْقِلُونَ) with the third person, intending the absent party. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, recited "taʿqilūna" (تَعْقِلُونَ) with the second person, intending those addressed. So also in al-Aʿrāf and at the end of Yūsuf; Abū Bakr agreed with them at the end of Yūsuf. As for "a-fa-lā yaʿqilūna" (أفَلا يَعْقِلُونَ) in Yā-Sīn, Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān recited it with a tāʾ, and the rest with a yāʾ.

This verse contains a refutation of their saying: "There is nothing but our life of this world" (Q. 6:29), and that is its intended purpose. It is also possible that His saying "Will you not then reason?" means: "Say to them, O Muḥammad, since the situation is of this description: will you not reason?"

As for His saying, "We certainly know" (قَدْ نَعْلَمُ), the verse: "qad" (قَدْ), which accompanies the verb, is a particle that comes with expectation, either on the part of the speaker or the hearer, or assumed to be in the hearer's mind. When the verb is purely future, the expectation is from the speaker, as in your saying "Zayd may come" (قَدْ يَقُومُ زَيْدٌ) and "rain may fall in such-and-such a month" (قَدْ يَنْزِلُ المَطَرُ في شَهْرِ كَذا). When the verb is past, or a present verb with the meaning of the past, like this verse of ours, the expectation is not from the speaker; rather, the speaker affirms what he reports, and the expectation lies with the hearer, so the speaker informs him of one of the two expected outcomes.

"We know" (نَعْلَمُ), when it is from Allah Exalted, implies the continuity and eternity of knowledge; it therefore encompasses past, present, and future. The particle "inna" (أنَّ) enters for emphasis in the strongest sense.

Nāfiʿ alone recited "la-yuḥzinuka" (لَيُحْزِنُكَ), from "aḥzana" (أحْزَنَ); the rest recited "la-yaḥzunuka" (لَيَحْزُنُكَ), from "ḥazina al-rajulu" (حَزِنَ الرَجُلُ). Abū Rajāʾ recited "li-yuḥzinka" (لِيُحْزِنْكَ) with a kasra on the lām and the zāy, and a jazm on the nūn. Al-Aʿmash recited (p-350) "annahu" (أنَّهُ) with a fatḥa on the hamza, and "yaḥzunuka" (يَحْزُنُكَ) without a lām. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The Arabs say "ḥazina al-rajulu" (حَزِنَ الرَجُلُ) with a kasra on the zāy, "yaḥzanu, ḥazanan wa-ḥuznan"; and "ḥazantuhu anā" (حَزَنْتُهُ أنا). It is related from al-Khalīl that their saying "ḥazantuhu" is not an alteration of "ḥazina" in the manner of "dakhala" and "adkhaltuhu," but means "I made him have grief," as you say "kaḥaltuhu" (I applied kohl to him) and "dahantuhu" (I anointed him with oil). Al-Khalīl said: Had you wished to alter "ḥazina," you would say "aḥznatuhu." Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī, in his book Khabʾa, related from the Arabs: "aḥznatu al-rajul." Abū ʿAlī said: "ḥazantu al-rajul" is more commonly used among them than "aḥznatuhu." Whoever recited "la-yuḥzinuka" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, it is by the analogy of alteration; and whoever recited "la-yaḥzunuka" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the zāy, it is by the frequency of usage.

"Alladhī yaqūlūna" (الَّذِي يَقُولُونَ) is an expression encompassing all their sayings which contain a rejection of the Prophet (ﷺ) and an attack upon the beginning of his prophethood, such as the saying of some of them: "He is a liar, a fabricator, a sorcerer"; and the saying of some of them: "He is mad, bewitched"; and the saying of some of them: "He has a jinn companion," and the like of these.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza recited "lā yukadhdhibūnaka" (لا يُكَذِّبُونَكَ) with a shadda on the dhāl and a fatḥa on the kāf. Ibn ʿAbbās recited it "yukadhdhibūnaka" (يُكَذِّبُونَكَ) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, and rejected it when a reader recited it to him that way, and said: They used to call him "the Trustworthy." Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī recited it with a sukūn on the kāf and a lightened dhāl. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) also recited it thus. These are two well-known and sound readings. The interpreters differed about their meanings. One group said: they have the same meaning, as you say "saqaytu" and "asqaytu" (I gave to drink), "qallaltu" and "aqlaltu" (I made little), "kaththartu" and "akthartu" (I made much). Al-Kisāʾī related that the Arabs say "kadhdhabtu al-rajul" (كَذَّبْتُ الرَجُلَ) when they find him to be a liar, just as they say "aḥmadtuhu" (أحْمَدْتُهُ) when they find him praiseworthy. The meaning according to the reading of whoever recited "yukadhdhibūnaka" with a shadda on the dhāl is: "Do not grieve, for they do not deny you in a way that harms you, since you are not a liar in your reality; so their denial is as if it were no denial." It may also be meant: "they do not deny you" as a report about them, that they do not deny, and that they know his truthfulness and his prophethood (ﷺ), but they deny out of obstinacy and wrongdoing. According to this, the verse does not encompass all the disbelievers, but specifies the group of whom it is reported that they used to say: "We indeed know that Muḥammad is truthful, but if we believe in him, the Banū Hāshim will surpass us in prophethood, so we will never believe in him." This saying is related from Abū Jahl and those who went his way. al-Naqqāsh related that the verse was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf, for he used to deny openly and affirm in secret, and would say: "We fear that the Arabs will snatch us away, and we are the eaters of heads." (p-351) The meaning according to the reading of whoever recited "yukdhibūnaka" with a lightened dhāl includes what we mentioned first for "yukadhdhibūnaka," namely: "they do not find you a liar in your reality." It also admits the two aspects that I mentioned for "yukadhdhibūnaka" with a shadda on the dhāl.

"Āyāt Allāh" (آياتُ اللهِ) means His signs and the evidences of His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ). "Yajḥadūna" (يَجْحَدُونَ), its true meaning in the speech of the Arabs, is denial after knowledge; it is the opposite of affirmation. Its meaning, according to the interpretation of those who take the verse as referring to the obstinate opponents, follows its literal sense; this is the view of Qatādah, al-Suddī, and others. According to the view of those who take the verse as referring to the disbelievers as a whole, without specifying the people of obstinacy, there is a figurative usage in the word. That is because when they denied his prophethood and sought to refute him by claims unsupported by any proof, he expressed their denial with the most severe form of denial, namely jaḥd, as a way of intensifying the censure of them and condemning their act, since his miracles and signs are radiant, and it is incumbent upon every person of sound nature to know them and acknowledge them.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of these interpretations concerning the negation of denial refer only to their inner belief. As for all their statements, they are denials, either of him or of what he brought.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Disbelief out of obstinacy is possible to occur according to rational consideration, and the apparent texts of the Qur'an indicate it, such as His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ (Q. 27:14), and others. Some of the theologians went so far as to forbid its possibility, holding that knowledge necessitates faith and denial necessitates disbelief, and that there is no way for the two to coexist. They interpreted the apparent texts of the Qur'an, saying, regarding His saying Exalted "and they denied them" (Q. 27:14): "It refers to the rulings of the Torah which they altered, such as the verse of stoning, and others."

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him: (p-352) Refuting what is conceived and understood as the possibility of disbelief out of obstinacy along this line of reasoning is difficult. However, that disbelief out of obstinacy from one who knows Allah Exalted and prophethood is remote, because there is no motive for disbelief out of obstinacy except envy; and whoever knows Allah Exalted and prophethood, and that Muḥammad (ﷺ) is visited by an angel from heaven, there is no way for envy to remain alongside that. As for its being possible, Abū Jahl saw, over the head of the Prophet (ﷺ), a great stallion camel that had resolved to attack Abū Jahl, yet he disbelieved nonetheless. al-Ṭabarī related with a chain: "Jibrīl (ʿalayhi al-salām) found the Prophet (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wa-al-salām) grieved, and asked him, and he said: 'These people have denied me.' He said: 'They do not deny you; rather they know that you are truthful; but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah.'"

What I hold regarding the disbelief of Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and those who went his way is that they used to see the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) and recognize them, or most of them; then they would see from his signs something beyond what they had; so they would cling, in deceiving themselves, to every doubt, on the flimsiest pretext, and their opinions would waver: sometimes saying "he is that one," and sometimes "perhaps he is not." Then their envy would be added to this, and their loss of leadership; so their aversion and disbelief would grow and become firmly established. Thus they, although they recognized some things and were obstinate about them, have cut themselves off through this from reaching the full extent of knowledge, and they remain in the darkness of ignorance; so they are ignorant of some things and obstinate about others. I, for my part, consider obstinacy alongside complete knowledge to be unlikely.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 6, verses 32–33:

(p-349) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement. But the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of Allah. Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah.﴾

This is the beginning of a report about the state of this world. The meaning is: since it is transient, finite, and without any benefit, it resembles play and amusement, which have no benefit once they are over.

The six readers recited "wa-la-dāru" (وَلَلدّارُ) with two lām's, and "al-ākhiratu" (اَلْآخِرَةُ) as an adjective of "al-dār." Ibn ʿĀmir alone recited "wa-ladāru" (وَلَدارُ) with a single lām, and so it is written in the codices of Syria, with "al-dār" in an idafa to "al-ākhira." This is like "masjidu l-jāmiʿ" (مَسْجِدُ الجامِعِ), meaning "the masjid of the congregational day," so likewise here: "wa-ladāru l-ḥayati l-ākhira" (وَلَدارُ الحَياةِ الآخِرَةِ).

Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, recited "ya'qilūna" (يَعْقِلُونَ) with the third person, intending the absent party. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, recited "taʿqilūna" (تَعْقِلُونَ) with the second person, intending those addressed. So also in al-Aʿrāf and at the end of Yūsuf; Abū Bakr agreed with them at the end of Yūsuf. As for "a-fa-lā yaʿqilūna" (أفَلا يَعْقِلُونَ) in Yā-Sīn, Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān recited it with a tāʾ, and the rest with a yāʾ.

This verse contains a refutation of their saying: "There is nothing but our life of this world" (Q. 6:29), and that is its intended purpose. It is also possible that His saying "Will you not then reason?" means: "Say to them, O Muḥammad, since the situation is of this description: will you not reason?"

As for His saying, "We certainly know" (قَدْ نَعْلَمُ), the verse: "qad" (قَدْ), which accompanies the verb, is a particle that comes with expectation, either on the part of the speaker or the hearer, or assumed to be in the hearer's mind. When the verb is purely future, the expectation is from the speaker, as in your saying "Zayd may come" (قَدْ يَقُومُ زَيْدٌ) and "rain may fall in such-and-such a month" (قَدْ يَنْزِلُ المَطَرُ في شَهْرِ كَذا). When the verb is past, or a present verb with the meaning of the past, like this verse of ours, the expectation is not from the speaker; rather, the speaker affirms what he reports, and the expectation lies with the hearer, so the speaker informs him of one of the two expected outcomes.

"We know" (نَعْلَمُ), when it is from Allah Exalted, implies the continuity and eternity of knowledge; it therefore encompasses past, present, and future. The particle "inna" (أنَّ) enters for emphasis in the strongest sense.

Nāfiʿ alone recited "la-yuḥzinuka" (لَيُحْزِنُكَ), from "aḥzana" (أحْزَنَ); the rest recited "la-yaḥzunuka" (لَيَحْزُنُكَ), from "ḥazina al-rajulu" (حَزِنَ الرَجُلُ). Abū Rajāʾ recited "li-yuḥzinka" (لِيُحْزِنْكَ) with a kasra on the lām and the zāy, and a jazm on the nūn. Al-Aʿmash recited (p-350) "annahu" (أنَّهُ) with a fatḥa on the hamza, and "yaḥzunuka" (يَحْزُنُكَ) without a lām. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The Arabs say "ḥazina al-rajulu" (حَزِنَ الرَجُلُ) with a kasra on the zāy, "yaḥzanu, ḥazanan wa-ḥuznan"; and "ḥazantuhu anā" (حَزَنْتُهُ أنا). It is related from al-Khalīl that their saying "ḥazantuhu" is not an alteration of "ḥazina" in the manner of "dakhala" and "adkhaltuhu," but means "I made him have grief," as you say "kaḥaltuhu" (I applied kohl to him) and "dahantuhu" (I anointed him with oil). Al-Khalīl said: Had you wished to alter "ḥazina," you would say "aḥznatuhu." Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī, in his book Khabʾa, related from the Arabs: "aḥznatu al-rajul." Abū ʿAlī said: "ḥazantu al-rajul" is more commonly used among them than "aḥznatuhu." Whoever recited "la-yuḥzinuka" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, it is by the analogy of alteration; and whoever recited "la-yaḥzunuka" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the zāy, it is by the frequency of usage.

And messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over being denied and harmed until Our help reached them. None can alter the words of Allah. And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers. And if their turning away is difficult for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign, [then do so]. And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant.

This verse contains the model (al-Uswah) that should be followed set before Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hope that he would receive the same help that came to them when he adopted the same patience. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj said: Allah consoled His Prophet (ﷺ) with this verse.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he recited "wa-udhu" (وَأُذُوا) without a waw after the hamza.

Then He strengthened this hope with His words: ﴿None can alter the words of Allah﴾; that is, none can repel His command, nor His preceding words concerning what will happen, nor deny what He has reported. The meaning is as if it said: "So be patient as they were patient, await what is coming, and trust this report, for none can alter it." Thus the purpose here is this report (p-353). The wording is general, covering all of Allah's preceding words, the Exalted. As for the speech of Allah, the Exalted, in the Torah and the Gospel, the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that none can alter them, and that the Jews only distorted them through interpretation, not by changing letters and words. Many scholars permitted that they had changed the wording, because they were entrusted with preserving it, and this is the more apparent view. As for the Qur'an, Allah has guaranteed its preservation, so alteration in it is not possible. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]; and He said concerning those [earlier peoples]: ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44].

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾; that is, in what We have sent down and related to you is what settles the matter of what We have reported to you. The subject of "jā'aka" (came to you) is implied, according to what al-Tabari and al-Rummani held; its estimated form is: "And there has certainly come to you a news report, or reports."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The correct meaning in my view is to estimate it as "jalā'" (clarification) or "bayān" (explanation).

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: His saying ﴿min naba' al-mursalin﴾ is in the position of a nominative (raf') with "jā'a" (came); and the particle of genitive (min) entered upon the subject. This is according to the view of al-Akhfash, who permitted the insertion of "min" in an affirmative sentence. The view of al-Rummani is that "min" is not added in an affirmative sentence.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And if their turning away is difficult for you﴾, and the rest of the verse, is a verse in which the proof is established against the Prophet (ﷺ) and the states are divided for him, until it becomes clear that there is no course but patience and proceeding with the command of Allah, the Exalted. The meaning is: "If you greatly magnify their denial and disbelief upon yourself, and commit yourself to grief over it, then if you are able to enter a passage into the depths of the earth, or to climb a ladder into the sky, then go ahead and do so." That is: "You are not able to do any of this, and you must commit to patience, endure hardship, and confront them with the signs that Allah has set up for the observers who reflect. For He, there is no god but Him, did not intend to gather them upon guidance; rather, He intended to set up from the signs what some people will be guided by through reflecting upon them, while others will go astray. He created them upon the fitrah (natural disposition) and guided them to the path, and His mercy precedes His wrath. To Him belongs all of that by right of His dominion, the Exalted. So do not be among the ignorant by grieving and sorrowing over a matter that Allah, the Exalted, willed and executed, and knew the benefit in it."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the style of the meaning of the verse.

The subject of "kāna" (was) may be the matter or the affair (al-amr wa-al-sha'n), and ﴿kabura 'alayka i'rāḍuhum﴾ would be its predicate. It is also possible that "i'rāḍuhum" is the subject of "kāna", and a pronoun is implied in "kabura", so that "kabura" is in the position of the predicate. The first of the two possibilities is more analogical.

"Al-nafaq" (tunnel) is a passage in the earth, and from it comes "nāfiqā' al-yarbū'" (the hidden exit of the jerboa). "Al-sullam" (ladder) is the thing by which one ascends and climbs; its name may be derived from "al-salāmah" (safety), because it is its cause. Its plural is "salālīm". From it comes the saying of the poet:

No barriers of lands restrain a man, nor are ladders built for him in the heavens.

"Fa-ta'tiyahum bi-āyah" (so that you bring them a sign) means: with a sign, a mark. He intends either: in your doing that, that is, the sign would be the very act of your entering the earth or your ascending into the sky; or that you bring them a sign from one of the two directions. The answer to the condition was omitted earlier in His saying "fa-in istaṭa'ta" (if you are able) for brevity, since the hearer understands it. Its estimated form is: "Then do it, or go ahead," as previously mentioned.

"La-jama'ahum" (He would have gathered them) allows two meanings: either that He would create them as believers, or that He would bestow faith upon them after their disbelief by expanding their hearts. "Al-hudā" (guidance) is guidance. This verse refutes the deviant Qadariyyah (a sect that denied divine predestination), who say: "Power does not require that the disbeliever believe, and whatever a person does of all his actions, Allah, the Exalted, has no creation in it." Allah is exalted above what they say.

His saying "min al-jāhilīn" (among the ignorant) may be understood as: not knowing that Allah, the Exalted, if He willed, would have gathered them; and it may be understood as: that you should be concerned with the existence of their disbelief, which He decreed and willed, and that you take it upon yourself to something Allah has not decreed.

There appears a difference between His saying, the Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾, and His saying, the Exalted, to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46]. It has been established that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the prophets. Makki and al-Mahdawi said: "The address in His saying ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾ is to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and what is meant by it is his community." This is weak and is not required by the wording. Some said: Noah was excused because of his age and his gray hair. Others said: the reprimand was more severe upon Muhammad (ﷺ) because of his nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and his high station with Him, just as one bears reproach from a close relative more than from strangers.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The strongest view in my opinion regarding the verse is that this was not according to the rank of the two prophets; rather, it came according to the two matters over which the prohibition and reproach occurred. It is clear that the matter from which Muhammad (ﷺ) was forbidden is greater in importance and more dangerous in its occurrence than the matter that Noah (peace be upon him) committed.

Many scholars permitted that they had changed the wording, because they were entrusted with preserving it, and this is the more apparent view. As for the Qur'an, Allah has guaranteed its preservation, so alteration in it is not possible. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]; and He said concerning those [earlier peoples]: ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44].

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾; that is, in what We have sent down and related to you is what settles the matter of what We have reported to you. The subject of "jā'aka" (came to you) is implied, according to what al-Tabari and al-Rummani held; its estimated form is: "And there has certainly come to you a news report, or reports."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The correct meaning in my view is to estimate it as "jalā'" (clarification) or "bayān" (explanation).

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: His saying ﴿min naba' al-mursalin﴾ is in the position of a nominative (raf') with "jā'a" (came); and the particle of genitive (min) entered upon the subject. This is according to the view of al-Akhfash, who permitted the insertion of "min" in an affirmative sentence. The view of al-Rummani is that "min" is not added in an affirmative sentence.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And if their turning away is difficult for you﴾, and the rest of the verse, is a verse in which the proof is established against the Prophet (ﷺ) and the states are divided for him, until it becomes clear that there is no course but patience and proceeding with the command of Allah, the Exalted. The meaning is: "If you greatly magnify their denial and disbelief upon yourself, and commit yourself to grief over it, then if you are able to enter a passage into the depths of the earth, or to climb a ladder into the sky, then go ahead and do so." That is: "You are not able to do any of this, and you must commit to patience, endure hardship, and confront them with the signs that Allah has set up for the observers who reflect. For He, there is no god but Him, did not intend to gather them upon guidance; rather, He intended to set up from the signs what some people will be guided by through reflecting upon them, while others will go astray. He created them upon the fitrah (natural disposition) and guided them to the path, and His mercy precedes His wrath. To Him belongs all of that by right of His dominion, the Exalted. So do not be among the ignorant by grieving and sorrowing over a matter that Allah, the Exalted, willed and executed, and knew the benefit in it."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the style of the meaning of the verse.

The subject of "kāna" (was) may be the matter or the affair (al-amr wa-al-sha'n), and ﴿kabura 'alayka i'rāḍuhum﴾ would be its predicate. It is also possible that "i'rāḍuhum" is the subject of "kāna", and a pronoun is implied in "kabura", so that "kabura" is in the position of the predicate. The first of the two possibilities is more analogical.

"Al-nafaq" (tunnel) is a passage in the earth, and from it comes "nāfiqā' al-yarbū'" (the hidden exit of the jerboa). "Al-sullam" (ladder) is the thing by which one ascends and climbs; its name may be derived from "al-salāmah" (safety), because it is its cause. Its plural is "salālīm". From it comes the saying of the poet:

No barriers of lands restrain a man, nor are ladders built for him in the heavens.

"Fa-ta'tiyahum bi-āyah" (so that you bring them a sign) means: with a sign, a mark. He intends either: in your doing that, that is, the sign would be the very act of your entering the earth or your ascending into the sky; or that you bring them a sign from one of the two directions. The answer to the condition was omitted earlier in His saying "fa-in istaṭa'ta" (if you are able) for brevity, since the hearer understands it. Its estimated form is: "Then do it, or go ahead," as previously mentioned.

"La-jama'ahum" (He would have gathered them) allows two meanings: either that He would create them as believers, or that He would bestow faith upon them after their disbelief by expanding their hearts. "Al-hudā" (guidance) is guidance. This verse refutes the deviant Qadariyyah (a sect that denied divine predestination), who say: "Power does not require that the disbeliever believe, and whatever a person does of all his actions, Allah, the Exalted, has no creation in it." Allah is exalted above what they say.

His saying "min al-jāhilīn" (among the ignorant) may be understood as: not knowing that Allah, the Exalted, if He willed, would have gathered them; and it may be understood as: that you should be concerned with the existence of their disbelief, which He decreed and willed, and that you take it upon yourself to something Allah has not decreed.

There appears a difference between His saying, the Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾, and His saying, the Exalted, to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46]. It has been established that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the prophets. Makki and al-Mahdawi said: "The address in His saying ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾ is to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and what is meant by it is his community." This is weak and is not required by the wording. Some said: Noah was excused because of his age and his gray hair. Others said: the reprimand was more severe upon Muhammad (ﷺ) because of his nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and his high station with Him, just as one bears reproach from a close relative more than from strangers.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The strongest view in my opinion regarding the verse is that this was not according to the rank of the two prophets; rather, it came according to the two matters over which the prohibition and reproach occurred. It is clear that the matter from which Muhammad (ﷺ) was forbidden is greater in importance and more dangerous in its occurrence than the matter that Noah (peace be upon him) committed.

God says, may He be exalted:

﴿Only those who listen will respond. As for the dead, God will raise them up, and then to Him they will be returned.﴾ ﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed God is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾ ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its wings, but they are communities like yourselves. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.﴾

This belongs to the pattern already mentioned concerning consolation (tasliyah, consoling the Prophet). That is: "Do not concern yourself with those who turn away. Only those who respond to the call of faith will respond, those who establish the signs and receive the proofs with acceptance." He expressed all of this by "they listen," because listening is the path to knowledge of prophethood and the miraculous signs. The Sufis use this expression too: when an admonition reaches someone in a fully effective way, they say, "He heard."

Then He said, "and the dead" (wal-mawta), meaning the disbelievers. He described them with the opposite of what He used for the believers, using a description that resembles their state: blindness to the light of God, and deafness to understanding His words. This was said by Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan.

"God will raise them" (yab'athuhumu Allah) may carry two meanings. al-Hasan said: its meaning is that God will raise them by making them believe when He causes them to stand [before Him]."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: On this interpretation, metaphor (isti'arah) appears in both respects: in calling them "dead," and in calling their faith and guidance "raising" (ba'th). The waw (and) on this reading shares the same governing verb, joining "the dead" to "those who," and "God will raise them" stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The sense of the verse is then: "Only those who are guided respond, when they hear and believe. As for the disbelievers, when God guides them by His will, do not grieve over them, and do not hasten what has not been decreed."

al-Hasan recited "then to Him they will return" (yarji'un), so the verse is consistent. Mujahid and Qatada said: "the dead" means "the disbelievers," meaning that they are like the dead when they see no guidance and hear nothing that they understand. "God will raise them" means "He will gather them on the Day of Resurrection." "Then to Him" means "to His might and punishment they will be returned." This group read "yurji'un" with the letter ya', and on this reading the waw joins one complete sentence to another: "the dead" is the subject (mubtada') and "God will raise them" is its predicate (khabar). The sense of the verse is then: "Only those who listen and understand will respond. As for the disbelievers, God will raise them and bring them back to His punishment." On this reading the verse includes a threat against the disbelievers. The returning pronoun referring to "those who" is the pronoun in "they listen." The pronoun in "they said" refers to the disbelievers. "Why not" (lawla) is a form of urging, meaning "why not" (halla). The poet said:

﴾Do you count the slaughter of she-camels the best of your glory, Banu Dawtara, if not the hidden, veiled [one]?﴿

The sense of the verse is: "Why has not a clear proof been sent down to Muhammad, peace be upon him, leaving no room for hesitation on anyone's part, such as an angel bearing witness for him, or more than that, or other excessive demands of theirs that are known in this matter?" So the Prophet, peace be upon him, was commanded to reply that God, may He be exalted, has the power to send down that sign, but most of them do not know that if it were sent down and they did not believe, they would be hastened to punishment. It may also mean, "But most of them do not know," that God has placed the benefit in signs that are open to reflection and consideration, so that some people may be guided and others go astray.

As for God's words, "There is no creature," the meaning of this verse is to draw attention to the signs of God that exist in the varieties of His creatures. That is: "Say to them: God is able to send down a sign, but you do not know the wisdom in His not sending down a sign in a ready-made form. Rather, He refers to the signs set out for one who reflects and takes heed, such as the beasts and birds, which together comprise all animals. They are communities (umam), that is, groups similar to humans in creation, sustenance, life, death and gathering." It is possible that by similarity he means only that they are communities, as when you say, "I passed by a man like you," meaning that he is a man. It is also valid to take it in other respects of description. However, the benefit of this verse lies in similarity in attributes other than being communities. Al-Tabari and others said: the similarity lies in the fact that their deeds are taken into account, they are called to account, and retribution is exacted for some of them from others, as related in the hadiths. That is: if He does this with the animals, then you are more deserving of it, since you are responsible and rational. Abu Dharr related that two goats butted each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Do you know why they butted?" We said: "No." He said: "God knows, and He will judge between them." Makki said: "The similarity lies in their knowing God and worshipping Him." This is the view of Khalaf.

The word "dabbah" (creature) is of the form fa'ilah. It is an adjective placed in the position of a noun, as they said "al-a'raj" and "al-abraq." The sense of adjective has been removed from it. It is not like the dominant adjective in our saying "al-'Abbas" and "al-Harith," because the sense of the adjective remains in the dominant adjective.

A group read "wa-la ta'ir" (nor bird) in the genitive, by conjunction to the wording. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read "wa-la ta'irun" in the nominative, by conjunction to the sense. A group read "wa-la tayr," which is the plural of "ta'ir."

As for His words, "with its wings," it is an emphasis, an explanation, and a removal of the metaphor commonly associated with this word. It is said "the bird of good fortune and misfortune," and God the Exalted said: ﴿We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra' 17:13], meaning his deed. It is also said, "the bird of such-and-such fell to so-and-so," meaning his share in the allotments. So His words "with its wings" remove the bird from all of this.

'Alqama and Ibn Hurmuz read "farratna" (we neglected) with a light r. The meaning is the same. al-Naqqash said: "farrata," lightened, means "we delayed," as they say, "God made the illness pass from you," meaning He removed it. The first is more correct. Tafrit (neglect) is falling short regarding a thing while having the power to avoid falling short. "The Book" is the Qur'an, and this is what the structure of meaning in these verses requires. It was said that it is the Preserved Tablet. According to this view, "anything" is general, covering all things. According to the view that it is the Qur'an, it is specific to things that contain benefit for the addressees and the ways of their guidance.

"They will be gathered" (yuhsharun): one group said: the gathering of the beasts is their death. Another group said: their gathering is their resurrection. They argued with the hadiths that include the statement that God will exact retribution for the hornless animal from the horned. [And the statement in the hadiths that include the claim that God will exact retribution for the hornless from the horned] "is only a figure of speech for justice, not a literal reality." This is a rejected view, leaning toward the view of symbols and the like.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 6, verses 39–41:

(p-359)

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darknesses. Whomever Allah wills, He leaves astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path.﴾ ﴿Say: "Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills, and you forget what you associate.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 42–45:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they would humble themselves.﴾ ﴿So why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they had been doing.﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

There is an ellipsis in the speech, indicated by the apparent meaning; its estimated form is: "So they denied, and We seized them." Its meaning is: "We pursued them and followed up on them, one thing after another."

"Al-ba'sa' (ٱلْبَأْسَاءُ)" means calamities in wealth; "al-darra' (ٱلضَّرَّاءُ)" means calamities in bodies. This is the view of the majority. It was also said that each may be used in place of the other. Allah, exalted, disciplines His servants through al-ba'sa' and al-darra'; and from here the worshippers disciplined their souls through al-ba'sa', in distributing wealth, and al-darra', in imposing upon the body, through hunger and nakedness.

The expectation in "la'alla" (لَعَلَّ) in this place is only according to the belief of humans; that is: "If anyone saw that, he would hope that they would humble themselves because of it." "Al-tadarru' (ٱلتَّضَرُّعُ)" means humbling oneself and submission. There is a saying: "Indeed, fever has humbled me before you." The meaning of the verse is a warning to the disbelievers and a striking of an example for them. "Fa-lawla (فَلَوْلا)" is an urging reproach, and it is the one that precedes the verb with the meaning of "hal-la" (why not); and this is in the manner of reproaching an absent guilty person, and showing the evil of his action, along with regret over it. The meaning: "When the first signs of might came upon them, and its marks, which is the recurrence of al-ba'sa' and al-darra'." "Qasat (قَسَتْ)" means became hard; and it is an expression for disbelief. He attributed the adornment to Satan; and Allah, exalted, said in another verse: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾ [al-An'am: 108]; because Satan's causing and whispering bring about the attractiveness of disbelief in their hearts; and that which is brought about is created by Allah. So if it is attributed to Allah, exalted, it is because He is its Creator; and if to Satan, it is because he is its cause.

As for His statement, exalted, ﴿So when they forgot﴾, etc.: He expressed abandonment by forgetting, when it reaches the aspects of abandonment that accompany forgetting and the departure of what is abandoned from the mind.

It is reported from Ibn 'Amir that he read "fattahna (فَتَّحْنا)" with a doubled ta'; and "kulli shay' (كُلِّ شَيْءٍ)" means: "from what had been closed off to them through al-ba'sa' and al-darra', of worldly blessings"; so it is a general term whose meaning is specific. "Farihu (فَرِحُوا)" means: they became insolent, exulted, were pleased with themselves, and thought that this would not perish, and that it indicated Allah's approval of them; and it is an enticement from Allah, exalted. It has been reported from some scholars that he said: "May Allah have mercy on a servant who reflects upon this verse: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾." Muhammad ibn al-Nadr al-Harithi said: "The people were given respite for twenty years." 'Uqba ibn 'Amir narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you see Allah giving His servants what they wish despite their sins, that is an enticement," then he recited ﴿So when they forgot﴾, the whole verse.

"Akhadhnahum (أَخَذْنَاهُمْ)" in this place means: We uprooted them and struck them down; and "baghtatan (بَغْتَةً)" means: suddenly; the operator of it is "akhadhnahum"; and it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); it is not analogized upon according to Sibawayh. "Al-mublis (ٱلْمُبْلِسُ)" is the grieved, the confounded, the one despairing of good, who cannot find an answer, because of the severity of the bad state that has befallen him.

As for His statement, exalted, ﴿So the last remnant of the people was cut off﴾, etc.: "Al-dabir (ٱلدَّابِرُ)" is the last of the matter, the one who follows it; that is, comes from behind it; and from it is the statement of the poet:

"So they were destroyed by a punishment that encompassed their last remnant, and they could not repel it nor be victorious."

And the statement of another:

"And 'Ulya claimed, with hostility, and her lips... that I am alone, and my last remnant has been cut off."

This is a metaphor for the uprooting of their root and the erasing of their traces, as if they came to the punishment until their last one, who followed them, came. 'Ikrima read "faqata'a (فَقَطَعَ)" with a fatha on the qaf and the ta'; and "dabira (دَابِرَ)" in the accusative.

Praise was fitting after this verse because of the beauty of the actions mentioned before: that Allah, exalted, sent the messengers, and was gentle in seizing them with al-ba'sa' and al-darra', so that they would humble themselves before Him, that He would have mercy, bestow blessings; and He cut off at the end the root of their wrongdoing. This is good in itself and a blessing upon the believers; so praise is fitting after these actions; and with the praise of Allah, exalted, every action and every statement should be concluded, there being no lord besides Him.

It was also said that each may be used in place of the other. Allah, exalted, disciplines His servants through al-ba'sa' and al-darra'; and from here the worshippers disciplined their souls through al-ba'sa', in distributing wealth, and al-darra', in imposing upon the body, through hunger and nakedness.

The meaning of the verse is a warning to the disbelievers and a striking of an example for them. قَوْلُهُ - عَزَّ وجَلَّ -:

﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal over your hearts, what god other than Allah could bring them back to you? Look how We vary the signs, yet they turn away.﴾ ﴿Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly, will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾ ﴿We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners. Whoever believes and reforms, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ ﴿As for those who deny Our signs, the punishment will touch them for what they used to defiantly disobey.﴾

This is the beginning of an argument against the disbelievers. "Akhadha Allah" (Allah took) means: He removed it and took it away by His power, exalted is He. He used the singular "al-sam'" (hearing) because it is a verbal noun (masdar) in singular form that indicates a plural. The pronoun in "bihi" (by it/him) refers to what was taken. It was also said that it refers to hearing, and it was said that it refers to the guidance that the meaning implies. Al-A'raj and others read "bihi unzur" with a dammah on the ha', and al-Musayyabi and Abu Wajza narrated it from Nafi'. "Yasdifun" (they turn away) means: they turn aside and flee. From it is the verse of the poet:

When they mention a saying, they say the best of it,
and they are among the chaste women who guard against every evil.

Al-Naqqash said: The verse contains evidence for the preference of hearing over sight, because it is mentioned first here. He then argued for this with the words of the Exalted, ﴿Only those who listen respond﴾ [al-An'am: 36], and with other things.

The interrogative in His words "man ilah" (who is a god) means reproach and admonition, i.e., "there is no god besides Him; so what is the matter with your attachment to idols and your clinging to them, when they neither repel harm nor bring any good?" The "tasrif al-ayat" (varying of the signs) is the setting forth of lessons, and the coming of the Qur'anic signs with warning, admonition, good news and the like.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Have you considered﴾ [al-An'am: 40], to the end of the verse, are a threat and a warning. "Baghtatan" (suddenly) means: no prior knowledge of it reaches you. "Jahratan" (openly) means: its signs and beginnings appear to you, then they follow one another until it descends. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "Baghtatan" is suddenly, and "jahratan" is by day. Mujahid said: "baghtatan" is suddenly while you are secure, and "jahratan" is while you are watching.

Ibn Muhaysin read "hal yahlik" (will [anyone] perish), with the verb in the active voice, and the meaning is: "Will you perish, except you, because wrongdoing has become evident in your domain?" The particle "hal" apparently has the form of a question, but its meaning is equalization (taswiyah) implying negation. Equalization with it occurs only in negation, and it may occur with the alif (interrogative) in negation and in affirmation.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿We send the messengers only﴾, to the end of the verse: The meaning is: "We only send the prophets who have been specially chosen for the message, so that they may give good news of Our bounty and mercy to whoever believes, and warn of Our punishment and retribution whoever denies and disbelieves. We do not send them so that signs are demanded of them, or so that they follow the deviations of every extremist who oversteps the bounds." Then He promised those who took the path of good news and believed and reformed, by performing acts of obedience, and He threatened those who took the path of warning and denied the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and transgressed, i.e., went beyond the limit in their disbelief and disobedience. Ibn Zayd said: "Every instance of fisq (transgression) in the Qur'an means lying." Al-Tabari transmitted this from him with a chain. "Yamassuhum" (touches them) means: it reaches them and clings to them. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "al-'adhabbima" with the assimilation of the ba' into the ba', and it was narrated from Abu 'Amr. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "yafsiqun" with a kasrah on the sin, and this is a dialect (lughah).

"Yamassuhum" (touches them) means: it reaches them and clings to them. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "al-'adhabbima" with the assimilation of the ba' into the ba', and it was narrated from Abu 'Amr. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "yafsiqun" with a kasrah on the sin, and this is a dialect (lughah).

(p-365) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasures of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I follow only what is revealed to me. Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Will you not then reflect?﴾ ﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having besides Him no protector and no intercessor, so that they may be God-fearing.﴾

This is part of the refutation of those who said: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him?", and of those who demanded that an angel be sent down, or that he have a garden, or more than that, or the like. The meaning is: "I am not characterized by these attributes, so it is not incumbent upon me to answer your proposals."

His saying: ﴿I do not tell you that with me are the treasures of God, nor do I know the unseen﴾ admits of two meanings. The more apparent of them is that he intends: he is a human being; nothing with him of the treasures of God the Exalted, nor of His power, and he knows nothing of what is hidden from him. The other is that he is not a god; it is as if he said: "I do not tell you that I possess the attributes of a god, in that I have His treasures and that I know the unseen." This is the view of al-Tabari.

The force of the wording in this verse suggests that the angel is superior to the human being; yet this does not necessarily follow from this passage. What follows from it is only that the angel is greater in standing in their souls and nearer to God the Exalted. The preference is conveyed by the meaning in a subtle way, and it is evident from other verses; but it is a matter of disagreement.

"What is revealed" (ma yuha) means: the Qur'an and all that the angel brings. That is, in this there are lessons and a sign for whoever reflects and considers.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: Are they alike?﴾ and the rest of the verse: that is, "Say to them: Indeed, the one who looks and reflects upon the signs is not alike to the one who turns away, the disbelieving one who neglects consideration." So the blind and the seeing are two examples of the believer (p-366) and the disbeliever. That is: "So reflect and consider yourselves." The command to reflect came in the form of an offer and urging (al-'ard wa al-tahdid).

"And warn" is conjoined to "Say." The Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, is commanded to warn all creatures; the urging here came according to the meaning intended. That is because in the preceding verses there is a kind of despair, for the most part, regarding these disbelievers, of whom it was also said: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. So it is as if it were said to him here: "Say to these disbelieving deniers: such-and-such... and leave them and their opinion to themselves; and warn with the Qur'an those others who are the likely ones for faith and fit to benefit." He did not intend that he warns no one else; rather the general warning is established and firm. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "what is revealed." "Yakhafuna" (they fear) retains its ordinary sense of fear: that is, "those who fear what they have come to know, namely being gathered, and prepare themselves for it; and many a person who knows of a frightening thing, yet due to little reflection and resolve, does not fear it and does not prepare for it."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: al-Tabari said: It has been said that "yakhafuna" here means "they know"; but this is not necessary. His saying: ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ encompasses, by the wording itself, every believer in the resurrection: Muslim, Jew, and Christian.

His saying: ﴿having besides Him no protector and no intercessor﴾ admits of two meanings. If we take it as included within the fear, it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, "they fear being gathered in a state where they have no protector and no intercessor." In that case it is specific to the believing Muslims, because the Jews and Christians claim that they have intercessors and that they are the sons of God the Exalted, and similar falsehoods. If we take His saying ﴿having besides Him no protector and no intercessor﴾ as God the Exalted's report about the state of affairs on that day, then it is general to the Muslims and the People of the Book. "So that they may be God-fearing" is an expression of hope, according to what humans see and what their consideration yields.
