(p-367) His words, exalted is He:

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. Nothing of their reckoning falls upon you, and nothing of your reckoning falls upon them, so that you would drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others, so that they say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" Is Allah not most knowing of the grateful?﴾

What is meant by "those who" are the weaker believers at that time, in worldly matters: Bilal, 'Ammar, Ibn Umm 'Abd (Ibn Mas'ud), Marthad al-Ghanawi, Khabbab, Suhayb, Subayh, Dhu al-Shimalayn, al-Miqdad, and others like them.

The occasion of the revelation was that some of the disbelievers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Because of our nobility and our rank, it is not possible for us to mix with these people. So if you drive them away, we will follow you and sit with you." A report on this subject has been transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud. It is also said that this statement was made only by Abu Talib, by way of advice to the Prophet (ﷺ); he said to him: "If you removed these people, the nobles of your people would follow you." It is also narrated that the chiefs of Quraysh gathered before Abu Talib concerning this matter; the apparent matter is that they intended by it deception. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and others among the believers approved of this opinion from Abu Talib, and so the verse was revealed.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: some of the disbelievers only sought that these people be delayed from the first row in the prayer, and that they themselves occupy their place, and that they would believe if these were driven from the first row; so the verse was revealed. al-Tabari attributed, through a chain reaching Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, that "al-Aqra' ibn Habis and whoever resembled him from the nobles of the Arabs said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Make for us from yourself a sitting-place which the slaves and the allies do not mix with us in, and write for us a document.' The Prophet (ﷺ) then intended to do that, so this verse was revealed."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This interpretation of the occasion of revelation is far-fetched, because the verse is Meccan, and these nobles only came to [the Prophet] in Medina. It is possible that this statement was made by them, but if it was made, it was some time after the revelation of the verse, unless the verse is Medinan. Khabbab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Then there was revealed: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-An'am: 54], and so on. We would come, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would say to us: "Peace be upon you," and we would sit with him (ﷺ). When he wished to rise, he (ﷺ) would rise and leave us. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and so on. So he (ﷺ) would sit with us, and when the time came for him (ﷺ) to rise, we would rise and leave him until he (ﷺ) rose.

As for ﴿call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾: al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: what is meant by it is the prayer of Mecca, which was twice a day, at morning and at evening. It is also said: rather, his words ﴿morning and evening﴾ are an expression for the continuity of the act, and that time is filled with it, as you say: "Praise be to Allah morning and evening," meaning: "Praise be to Allah Exalted at every time." According to this interpretation, it is said that what is meant is the five prayers; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibrahim. It is also said: it is supplication and the remembrance of Allah Exalted, and the word is on its literal sense. Some storytellers (qussas) said: it means gathering with them morning and evening; but Ibn al-Musayyab and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Amra and others denied this, and said: the verse is only about the prayers in congregation. It is also said: the recitation of the Qur'an and learning it; Abu Ja'far said: al-Tabari mentioned it. It is also said: worship; this was said by al-Dahhak.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Malik ibn Dinar, al-Hasan, Nasr ibn 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "bil-ghudwati wal-'ashiyyi" (with the ghudwa and the 'ashiyy). It is narrated from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman: "bil-ghuduww" without the ta' marbuta. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "bil-ghudawati wal-'ashiyyati" (with the plural forms, with alif in both), in the plural. "Ghudwa" is definite, because it has been made a proper name for a particular time of that same day; and it is permissible to attach the alif and lam to it, as Abu Zayd related: "laqitu-hu faynata" (I met him at a time), and "al-faynata ba'da al-faynati" (the time after the time), so they attached the definite article to what is used as definite. And in accordance with what al-Khalil related, that it is said: "laqitu-hu al-yawma ghadwatan" (I met him today in the morning), indefinite; and because in it, along with specifying the day, there is the possibility of estimating the meaning of generality; mentioned by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi.

And "wajhahu" in this place means: the direction of drawing near to Him, as you say: "So-and-so went out in the direction of such-and-such," i.e., "toward a purpose and a direction."

As for ﴿Nothing of their reckoning falls upon you﴾: its meaning is: you are not charged with anything other than calling them, so that you should advance or delay [anyone]. It appears that the pronoun in "their reckoning" and "upon them" refers to the disbelievers who wished to drive away the believers; i.e., "Nothing is upon you from them, whether they believed or disbelieved, so that you should drive these away out of regard for that." The pronoun in "so that you would drive them away" refers to the weaker believers. What supports this interpretation is that what follows the fa' is always the cause of what precedes it, and that would not be clear if all the pronouns referred to the believers. al-Tabari related that the reckoning here is only in worldly provision; i.e., "You do not provide for them, nor do they provide for you."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: According to this, all the pronouns refer to the believers; al-Mahdawi mentioned it. He also mentioned from al-Hasan that it is from the reckoning of their deeds, as the majority said. The first "min" is partitive, and the second is superfluous, for emphasis. His words ﴿"so that you would drive them away"﴾ are the answer to the negation in his words ﴿"Nothing is upon you"﴾; and his words ﴿"and thus be"﴾ are the answer to the prohibition in his words ﴿"do not drive away"﴾; and ﴿"among the wrongdoers"﴾ means: "those who place a thing other than in its proper places."

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others﴾, etc.: "tried" (fatana) in this verse means: We tested. The testing of the believers by the polytheists is what they suffer from them of harm; and the testing of (p-370) the polytheists by the believers is that a noble man among the polytheists sees people without nobility whom this religion has honoured and whom it has given standing and rank with its Prophet. The indication of "thus" refers to what was mentioned of their request that he drive away the weak; and "so that they say" means: "so that by the decree of destiny their matter comes to the point that they say..." So it is the lam of result, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]; i.e., so that the outcome would be that he became an enemy to them. The statement of the polytheists, according to this interpretation, ﴿"Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾ is by way of contempt and mockery. The sentence may bear another meaning, namely that the lam in "so that they say" is in its original sense of the lam of "in order that," and the statement from them is a question addressed to themselves and a discussion among them, and it becomes a cause of faith for those among them whose faith had preceded. So the meaning of the verse according to this interpretation is: "And thus We tested the nobles of the disbelievers with the weak believers, so that they would wonder in their souls at that, and it would be a cause of reflection for whoever is guided."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The first interpretation is more prior, and the second is derivable. And "favour" (mann), according to both interpretations, is only from the belief of the believers; i.e., "These are those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, by their claim that their religion is a favour."

As for His words ﴿Is Allah not most knowing of the grateful?﴾: i.e., "O you who mock — or who wonder, according to the other interpretation — the matter is not one of mockery nor of wonder; Allah the Exalted is most knowing of who gives thanks for His blessing, and of the places in which it should be placed." Their being informed of this came in the form of a question, since it is clear, and in which no obstinacy is open to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 54–55:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: that whoever among you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, then indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, and that the way of the criminals may become clear.﴾

The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: "Those who..." refers to the people whose expulsion (from the assembly) had been proposed; so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forbade their expulsion, and He reinforced this by commanding the Prophet (ﷺ) to greet them with peace and to make them feel at ease.

'Ikrimah and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: "Those who..." refers to a group of believers who had endorsed the opinion of Abu Talib concerning the expulsion of the weak. So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to greet them with peace and to inform them that Allah the Exalted forgives them, together with their repentance from that evil and other things.

al-Tabari transmitted, via Maham, that he said: The verse was revealed concerning a group of believers who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about sins they had committed in the past, so the verse was revealed on account of them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: According to this, it applies to all believers without pointing to any particular group.

al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "A people said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'We have committed sins, so ask forgiveness for us.' The Prophet (ﷺ) turned away from them, and so the verse was revealed."

Abu ʿAli said: this is not permissible, because "man" is either a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi," in which case it needs a predicate, or it is a conditional, in which case it needs an apodosis. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 56–58:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those you call upon besides God. Say: I will not follow your desires; I would then have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it. What you are impatient for is not with me. Judgment belongs only to God; He relates the truth, and He is the best of deciders.﴾ ﴿Say: If what you are impatient for were with me, the matter would have been decided between me and you. And God knows best the wrongdoers.﴾

God, Blessed and Exalted, commanded His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, to declare openly his disavowal of what they were engaged in. The phrase "an a'bud" (that I worship) is in the form of a verbal noun (masdar) by interpretation, and the sense is "from the worship of," then the preposition was deleted, so the verb took direct effect. Then "an a'bud" was placed in the position of the verbal noun. He referred to the idols with "alladhina" (those who), according to the claim of the disbelievers, since they had treated them as though they were rational beings. "Tad'una" (you call upon) means "you worship." It is also possible that it means "you call upon in your affairs," and that this is part of the meaning of worship and of believing them to be gods.

The majority of readers recited "qad dalaltu" (I have indeed gone astray) with a fatha on the lam. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Talha ibn Musarrif recited "dalilt" with a kasra. Both are dialectal forms. The word "idhan" (then) in this place is mediate (mutawassita), and what follows it depends on what precedes it. It is therefore not governing, but it implies the meaning of a condition, so its sense is "if you were to do that." "Ahwa'" is the plural of "hawa," which is will and love for things that lead to ruin. This is the usual use of hawa, and it has been mentioned previously.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon a clear proof from my Lord﴾, to the end of the verse. This verse elaborates on his distinction from them. The meaning is: "Say: I am upon a clear matter," so the described noun was deleted, then the intensive ha' (ha' al-mubalagha) entered, as in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself﴾ [al-Qiyama: 14]. It is also valid for the ha' in "bayyina" to be merely the feminine marker, and for it to mean clarity (bayan), as He said: ﴿that whoever perishes might perish by clear proof, and whoever lives might live by clear proof﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. The intended meaning of the verse is: "I, O deniers, in my belief, my certainty, and the knowledge that has settled in my soul, am upon a clear proof from my Lord." As for "wa kadhdhabtum bihi ma" (and you have denied it, what), the pronoun in "bihi" refers either to "bayyin" in the sense of the intensive ha', or to "al-bayan," which is "bayyina" in its meaning in the other interpretation, or to the Lord. It has also been said that it refers to the Qur'an, and although no clear mention of it has preceded, it is part of the clarity from which the belief and certainty of the Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, arose, so the return of the pronoun to it is valid.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, has other matters besides the Qur'an, from which knowledge also came to him, such as the stones speaking to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, his seeing the angel before revelation, and other things.

Some exegetes (mufassirun) said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma," and what is meant by it is the proposed signs (al-ayat al-muqtaraha), according to what some exegetes said. It was also said that what is meant by it is the punishment. This is preferred on two grounds. The first is from the standpoint of meaning: His words "and you have denied it" imply that you have committed what makes you deserving of punishment, except that it is not with me. The second is from the standpoint of wording: the "impatience" (isti'jal) that appears in the Qur'an as "their impatience" is only for punishment, because their demand for signs was not with impatience.

His words: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, that is, the decision and the execution. "He relates the truth" means He informs of it, and the meaning is: He relates the true accounts (al-qasas al-haqq).

This is the reading of Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Nafi' and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir recited "yaqdi al-haqq," that is, He executes it. This reading is preferred on account of His words "the deciders" (al-fasilin), because decisiveness (al-fasl) is suited to judgment. Decisiveness and detailing have also come together with narrating accounts. In the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, it reads: "and He is the swiftest of deciders." Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: 'Abd Allah, Ubayy, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Talha and al-A'mash recited "yaqdi bil-haqq," with the added preposition ba'. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "yaqdi al-haqqa wa huwa khayru al-fasilin."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If indeed what I have were﴾, to the end of the verse. The meaning is: "If the proposed signs were with me, or the punishment, according to the other interpretation, the matter would have been decided." That is, the separation would have taken place and the dispute would have been concluded, because of the manifestation of the proposed sign, or because of the descent of the punishment, according to the two interpretations. Al-Zahrawi reported that the meaning is "the Resurrection would have been established." Al-Naqqash narrated it from 'Ikrima. Some people said: the meaning of "the matter would have been decided" is that death would have been slaughtered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a very weak statement, because its speaker took this meaning from His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And warn them of the Day of regret, when the matter is decided﴾ [Maryam: 39]. The slaughter of death is appropriate here, so he transferred it to this place without any resemblance. Al-Tabari attributed this statement to Ibn Jurayj without restricting it to this surah, and the assumption about Ibn Jurayj is that he was only explaining what is in the Day of regret.

﴿And God knows best the wrongdoers﴾ includes a warning and a threat.

It is also valid for the ha' in "bayyina" to be merely the feminine marker, and for it to mean clarity (bayan), as He said: ﴿that whoever perishes might perish by clear proof, and whoever lives might live by clear proof﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. The intended meaning of the verse is: "I, O deniers, in my belief, my certainty, and the knowledge that has settled in my soul, am upon a clear proof from my Lord." As for "wa kadhdhabtum bihi ma" (and you have denied it, what), the pronoun in "bihi" refers either to "bayyin" in the sense of the intensive ha', or to "al-bayan," which is "bayyina" in its meaning in the other interpretation, or to the Lord. It has also been said that it refers to the Qur'an, and although no clear mention of it has preceded, it is part of the clarity from which the belief and certainty of the Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, arose, so the return of the pronoun to it is valid.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, has other matters besides the Qur'an, from which knowledge also came to him, such as the stones speaking to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, his seeing the angel before revelation, and other things.

Some exegetes (mufassirun) said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma," and what is meant by it is the proposed signs (al-ayat al-muqtaraha), according to what some exegetes said. It was also said that what is meant by it is the punishment. This is preferred on two grounds. The first is from the standpoint of meaning: His words "and you have denied it" imply that you have committed what makes you deserving of punishment, except that it is not with me. The second is from the standpoint of wording: the "impatience" (isti'jal) that appears in the Qur'an as "their impatience" is only for punishment, because their demand for signs was not with impatience.

His words: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, that is, the decision and the execution. "He relates the truth" means He informs of it, and the meaning is: He relates the true accounts (al-qasas al-haqq).

This is the reading of Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Nafi' and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir recited "yaqdi al-haqq," that is, He executes it. This reading is preferred on account of His words "the deciders" (al-fasilin), because decisiveness (al-fasl) is suited to judgment. Decisiveness and detailing have also come together with narrating accounts. In the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, it reads: "and He is the swiftest of deciders." Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: 'Abd Allah, Ubayy, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Talha and al-A'mash recited "yaqdi bil-haqq," with the added preposition ba'. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "yaqdi al-haqqa wa huwa khayru al-fasilin."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If indeed what I have were﴾, to the end of the verse. The meaning is: "If the proposed signs were with me, or the punishment, according to the other interpretation, the matter would have been decided." That is, the separation would have taken place and the dispute would have been concluded, because of the manifestation of the proposed sign, or because of the descent of the punishment, according to the two interpretations. Al-Zahrawi reported that the meaning is "the Resurrection would have been established." Al-Naqqash narrated it from 'Ikrima. Some people said: the meaning of "the matter would have been decided" is that death would have been slaughtered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a very weak statement, because its speaker took this meaning from His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And warn them of the Day of regret, when the matter is decided﴾ [Maryam: 39]. The slaughter of death is appropriate here, so he transferred it to this place without any resemblance. Al-Tabari attributed this statement to Ibn Jurayj without restricting it to this surah, and the assumption about Ibn Jurayj is that he was only explaining what is in the Day of regret.

﴿And God knows best the wrongdoers﴾ includes a warning and a threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 59–60:

[p. 377]

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic:

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen. None knows them but He. He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night, and knows what you have earned by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a term appointed may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return. Then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

"Mafatih" is the plural of "miftah" (key), and this is a metaphor (isti'ara) expressing access to the unseen, just as in the visible world a key is used to reach what is hidden from a person. If it were the plural of "miftah," it would have been "mafatih" as well. It is also apparent that "mafatih" is the plural of "maftah," with a fath on the mim, meaning places through which the unseen things are opened. This is supported by the saying of al-Suddi and others: "mafatih al-ghayb" means "khazain al-ghayb" (the treasuries of the unseen). As for "miftah" with a kasra, it means "miftah." Al-Zahrawi said: "maftah" is more eloquent.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: the reference in "mafatih al-ghayb" is to the five things mentioned at the end of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34], up to the end of the verse, because they encompass all things that have not yet come into existence. Then He strengthened the statement with His saying: ﴿and He knows what is on the land and in the sea,﴾ as an alert to the greatest of the created things that are close to humans. His saying: ﴿"min waraqatin"﴾ is in its literal sense, referring to the leaves of plants, and "min" is superfluous. His saying: ﴿"illa ya'lamuha"﴾ means absolutely: before its falling, with it, and after it. His saying: ﴿"wa la habbatin fi zulumati al-ardi"﴾ means in the most hidden state of concealment. All of this, although it is included in His saying ﴿"wa 'indahu mafatih al-ghayb"﴾ according to those who regard the five things and others as its reference, contains clarification, elucidation, and an alert to the places of lessons. That is: "If these insignificant things are known, then other grand matters are more fitting [to be known]."

﴿"wa la ratbin wa la yabisin"﴾ is conjoined to the wording (lafz). Al-Hasan and Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq read: "wa la ratbun wa la yabisun" with a raf' (nominative), conjoining to the position (mawdi') of "waraqatin," because the implied meaning is "wa ma tasqutu waraqatun." As for ﴿"illa fi kitabin mubin"﴾, it was said: it means a literal "kitab" (book). The benefit in this is the testing of what the guardian angels (al-hafaza) write. It is narrated that the guardian angels raise what they have written and compare it with this Book referred to, in order to verify the correctness of what they wrote. It was also said: what is meant by His saying ﴿"illa fi kitab"﴾ is the knowledge of Allah, may He be exalted and majestic, which encompasses everything. Al-Naqqash related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad a saying: "The leaf refers to the miscarried children of the sons of Adam, peace be upon him. The grain refers to the one that does not fall. The moist refers to the living, and the dry refers to the dead." This is a view that proceeds on the method of symbols (rumuz), and it is not authentically transmitted from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him, and it should not be given attention.

His exalted saying ﴿"wa huwa alladhi yatawaffakum bil-layli wa ya'lamu"﴾ and the verse [continues]. In it is an elucidation of the signs set up for reflection, and in it is a coining of a parable for resurrection from the graves: that this also is a kind of death and raising.

Al-tawaffi is the complete receiving of a number. The poet said:

"Indeed the sons of al-Adram are not among anyone,
nor has Quraysh counted them in the tally."

The word has become customary (urf) for death, while in sleep it is used with some figurative extension (tajawwuz).

"Jarahtum" means "kasabtum" (you earned). From it comes "jawarih al-sayd," that is, its hunting animals (kawasib). From it also comes "jawarih al-badan" (the limbs of the body), because they are the earners of the soul. It is possible that "jarahtum" here is from "al-jarh" (wound), as if sin is a wound in religion. The Arabs say: "The wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand." It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, or Salman (Ibn Dinar was uncertain), that he said: "These sins are wounds. Some of them are superficial, and some are fatal. Indeed, associating partners with Allah, the Exalted, is fatal."

"Yab'athukum" means awakening. So the pronoun in "fihi" refers to the day (nahar), as said by Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi. He mentioned sleep with the night and waking with the day, according to what is most common, even though sleep may occur by day and waking by night, which is rare. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to tawaffi, meaning: "He wakes you up during the tawaffi," that is, "within it and in its course." This was said by Abdullah ibn Kathir. It was also said that it refers to the night. This is awkward in wording, though in meaning it is close to the preceding view.

Talha ibn Musarrif and Abu Raja' read: "li-yaqdiya ajalan musamman." What is meant by "ajal" is the terms of the sons of Adam. ﴿"Thumma ilayhi marji'ukum"﴾ means: by the resurrection and the rising. ﴿"Thumma yunabbi'ukum"﴾ means: He will inform you with an informing of establishment (taqwif) and reckoning.

(p. 379) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians, until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail in their duty.﴾ ﴿Then they are returned to God, their true Master. Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of reckoners.﴾

"Al-Qahir" (the Subduer): If it is taken as a descriptive attribute of action, meaning the manifestation of domination through thunderbolts, winds, and punishment, then "fawq" (above) may be construed as a locative adverb of direction, because these things are feared by the servants as coming from above them. If "al-Qahir" is taken as an attribute of essence, meaning power and dominion, then "fawq" cannot be locative; it indicates elevation of rank and status, in the manner of your saying: "The ruby is above the iron."

﴿And He sends over you﴾: its meaning is "He disperses them among you." "Hafazah" (guardians) is the plural of "hafiz," like "katib" and "katabah" (scribe and scribes). What is meant by them are the angels entrusted with recording deeds. It is narrated that they are the angels of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day." This was also said by al-Suddi and Qatada. Some exegetes said: "Guardians who protect the human being from everything until his term comes." The first view is more apparent.

All of them, except Hamza, read "tawaffathu rusuluna" (our messengers take him), with the feminine marker because the collective noun is feminine in form, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Messengers before you were indeed denied﴾ [al-An'am: 34]. Hamza read "tawaffahu rusuluna," and his argument is that the feminine is not real (haqiqi), and the apparent form of the verb is past, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "And women said" (Yusuf: 30). It is also possible that it means "tatawaffahu," in which case the marker is feminine. Hamza applied imalah (vowel inclination) because the Mushaf's orthography is written without an alif, as though it were written with imalah. Al-A'mash read "yatawaffahu rusulunا" with a yа' prefixed and the masculine form.

His saying, Exalted is He, "our messengers" means, according to what Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and all the people of interpretation (ta'wil) have stated, angels who accompany the Angel of Death, assisting him and carrying out his commands.

The majority of people read "la yufarritun" (they do not fail), with shaddah (doubled letter). Al-A'raj read "yufrituna" without shaddah, meaning "they exceed the limit of what they have been commanded." Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: just as the meaning in the common reading "la yuqassirun" (they do not fall short) is that they do not fall short, so too in this reading it means they do not exceed what they have been commanded.

The address in His saying "rudduu" (they are returned) shifts from the second person to the third person. The pronoun in "rudduu" refers to those previously mentioned. It may also refer to the servants, and it then informs of the return of all. The second person "'alaykum" (over you) was used to bring the admonition close to the hearts of the hearers. "Mawlahum" (their Master) is a general term covering the kinds of guardianship that exist between God Exalted and His servants: provision, support, reckoning, ownership, and other things. His saying "al-haqq" (the true) is an adjective (na't) of "mawlahum"; its meaning is that which is not false and not metaphorical. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "al-haqqa" in the accusative, which is in the sense of praise, and it may also be a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him﴾: this is the beginning of a statement that carries the sense of alerting and stirring the listener's soul. "Al-hukm" (judgment), with the definite article, denotes the genus, meaning all kinds of disposal over the servants. ﴿He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾ is understood to mean that God's reckoning of His servants proceeds from His knowledge of them, so He needs no preparation or effort in that, Glorified is He, there is no lord but Him. It was said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "How does God Exalted reckon the servants all at one time?" He said: "As He provides for them all at one time in this world."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 63–64:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say, "Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land and the sea, when you call upon Him humbly and secretly, [saying], 'If He should deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful.'"﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah delivers you from it and from every distress; yet you associate others with Him."﴾

This is a continuation of the rebuke of those who equate idols with Allah the Exalted, and of making them acknowledge the evil of their act in worshipping idols, and their abandonment of Him who delivers from destruction and to whom one turns in times of hardship.

The word "man" (مَن) is an interrogative, in the nominative case by virtue of being the subject (mubtada').

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī recited "man yunajjīkum" (مَن يُنَجِّيكُمْ) and "qul Allāhu yunajjīkum" (قُلِ اللهُ يُنَجِّيكُمْ) with a doubled jīm (tashdīd) and a fatḥa on the nūn. Abū ʿAmr, in the transmission of ʿAlī ibn Naṣr from him, and Ḥumayd ibn Qays and Yaʿqūb recited "yunjīkum" with a single jīm (takhfīf) and a sukūn on the nūn. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with doubling in the first and single in the second, thereby combining the transitivity by means of the alif and the transitivity by means of doubling, as occurs in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 17].

The phrase ﴿ẓulumāti al-barr wa al-baḥr﴾ (ظُلُماتِ البَرِّ والبَحْرِ) is intended to mean its hardships. It is a general term that encompasses hardships that involve actual darkness and those that do not. The Arabs say "a black year" (عامٌ أسْوَدُ), "a dark day" (يَوْمٌ مُظْلِمٌ), and "a day of stars" (يَوْمٌ ذُو كَواكِبَ), and similar expressions, meaning by them severity. Qatādah said: the meaning is "from the distress of land and sea," and al-Zajjāj said the same.

"Tad'ūnahu" (تَدْعُونَهُ) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). "Taḍarru'an" (تَضَرُّعًا) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its governing element is "tad'ūnahu." Taḍarruʿ is an outward quality manifest in a person. "Wa khufyatan" (وَخُفْيَةً) means concealment and secrecy, so the sense of the phrase seems to be: "you call upon Him openly and secretly," a phrase carrying additional meanings.

All the readers, except ʿĀṣim, recited "wa khufyatan" (وَخُفْيَةً) with a ḍamma on the khā'. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr—may Allah be pleased with him—recited "wa khifyatan" (وَخِفْيَةً) with a kasra on the khā'. al-Aʿmash recited "wa khīfatan" (وَخِيفَةً), from "al-khawf" (fear). His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say, "Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land and the sea, when you call upon Him humbly and secretly, [saying], 'If He should deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful.'"﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah delivers you from it and from every distress; yet you associate others with Him."﴾

This is a continuation of the rebuke of those who equate idols with Allah the Exalted, and of making them acknowledge the evil of their act in worshipping idols, and their abandonment of Him who delivers from destruction and to whom one turns in times of hardship.

The word "man" (مَن) is an interrogative, in the nominative case by virtue of being the subject (mubtada').

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī recited "man yunajjīkum" (مَن يُنَجِّيكُمْ) and "qul Allāhu yunajjīkum" (قُلِ اللهُ يُنَجِّيكُمْ) with a doubled jīm (tashdīd) and a fatḥa on the nūn. Abū ʿAmr, in the transmission of ʿAlī ibn Naṣr from him, and Ḥumayd ibn Qays and Yaʿqūb recited "yunjīkum" with a single jīm (takhfīf) and a sukūn on the nūn. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with doubling in the first and single in the second, thereby combining the transitivity by means of the alif and the transitivity by means of doubling, as occurs in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 17].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 65–67:

(p-382) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: He is able to send upon you punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confuse you with sects and make you taste the violence of one another. Observe how We vary the signs that they may understand.﴾ ﴿But your people denied it, while it is the truth. Say: I am not a guardian over you.﴾ ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know.﴾

This is a statement that includes a warning. The more apparent reading from the sequence of the verses is that this address is to the disbelievers mentioned earlier, and this is the view of al-Tabari. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliyah, and a group along with them said: it is addressed to the believers, and they are the intended audience. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: they are four attributes, all of them a punishment, and all of them occurring before the Day of Resurrection. Two of them passed after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by twenty-five years, then they were confused into sects, and some of them were made to taste the violence of others. The other two are certain to occur: the sinking (into the earth) and the stoning. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: some of it is for the disbelievers and some for the believers; the sending of punishment from above and from beneath is for the disbelievers, and the rest is for the believers. This difference is only according to what appears, that the verse encompasses the meanings of both the polytheists and the believers.

It has been narrated from the hadith of Jabir and Khalid al-Khuza'i that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard: ﴿to send upon you punishment from above you﴾, he said: "I seek refuge in Your Face." When (the verse) ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾ was revealed, he said: "I seek refuge in Your Face." When ﴿or to confuse you with sects and make you taste the violence of one another﴾ was revealed, he said: "This is easier," or: "This is lighter." Those who said the verse was revealed concerning the believers relied on this. Al-Tabari said: It is not impossible that the Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge for his community from these things with which the disbelievers were threatened, and he made lighter the third, because in meaning it is what he had supplicated for and was denied, according to the hadith in the Muwatta and elsewhere. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) has said: it is the worst of the three. In my view this is by way of emphasis in admonition; the truth is that it is the lightest of them, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said.

"From above you and from beneath your feet" is a general expression that applies to the human being. Al-Suddi related from Abu Malik: ﴿from above you﴾ is stoning, and ﴿from beneath your feet﴾ is sinking into the earth. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid also said this. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: ﴿from above you﴾ refers to unjust rulers, and ﴿from beneath your feet﴾ refers to the base and evil servants and attendants.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: All of these are examples, not what is meant specifically, since these and others, such as drought and drowning and the like, fall within the generality of the expression.

"Yalbisakum" (to confuse you), according to the reading of the Seven, means "yakhlitakum" (to mix you up). "Shiya'an" (sects) means factions, some of which support one another. "Al-labs" is mixing. The exegetes said it is the divergence of desires and fighting among the community.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Madani read "yulbisakum" with a damma on the yā', from "albasa"; on this reading it is a metaphor taken from "al-libas" (clothing). The meaning is: "or clothe you with strife in sects," and "shiya'an" is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl). The poet has said:

"I wore people, and I wore them out..." (verse incomplete)

This is an expression for mixing with, bearing the hardship of, and being clothed in killing and similar hardships.

"Wa-yudhiqa" (and make taste) is a metaphor, since tasting is one of the most important senses of testing, and it is a metaphor commonly used in much of the speech of the Arabs and in the Qur'an. Al-A'mash read "wa-nudhiqa" with the plural "nun," which is the "nun of majesty" in reference to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. You say: "I made so-and-so taste the bitter aloe," meaning the hatefulness of something you did to him, and the like.

In His saying ﴿Observe how We vary﴾, the verse is a reminder to them; although its wording is that of a wonder addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), its implication is that these signs and proofs are for turning them away from the path of their error. "Al-fiqh" means understanding.

The pronoun in "bihi" (it) refers to the Qur'an in which the varying of the signs came; this was said by al-Suddi, and it is the apparent reading. It was also said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), but this is far-fetched, given the nearness of his address afterward with the kaf in "qawmuka" (your people). It may also be that the pronoun refers to the warning which the verse contains, and al-Tabari inclined to this. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-kadhdhabat bihi qawmuka" with the addition of a tā' (feminine). "Bi-wakil" means: with one entrusted to compel you to faith and guidance. "Al-wakil" means "al-hafiz" (the guardian). This was before the revelation of jihad and the command to fight; then it was abrogated. It was also said: there is no abrogation here, since it is a report.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Abrogation is plausible in it, because what is necessarily implied by the wording is "you are not now"; and there is nothing in it that he will not be in what is to come. His saying ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ means a limit by which its truth is known from its falsehood. ﴿And you will come to know﴾ is pure threat and warning.
