Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 68–69:

The words of Him, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different topic. And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing folk.﴾ ﴿And there is nothing upon those who fear Allah for their account, [of any kind], but it is a reminder, that perhaps they may fear Allah.﴾

The wording of this address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, but its meaning has been disputed. It has been said that the believers are also included in the address along with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the sound view, because the reason for the prohibition, which is hearing vain talk concerning the signs of Allah the Exalted, encompasses them as well as him (ﷺ). It has also been said: rather, the meaning was intended for the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, because his standing up from the polytheists would be hard on them, and his parting from them in displeasure, even if the believers were not in that state with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to confront them by rising from them whenever they mocked and engaged in vain talk, so that they would learn good manners and abandon vain talk and mockery. This interpretation is consistent with the words of Ibn Jarir (may Allah have mercy on him).

The root meaning of khawd (خَوْض, wading, plunging into vain talk) is wading into water; then it is subsequently used for the depths of things that are obscure, by way of comparison with the depths of water.

"Wa-immā" (وَإمّا): a conditional particle, which is usually followed by the heavy nun (the emphatic nun), though it may sometimes not be, as in the saying:

"If an enemy afflicts you in hostility..."

and other examples besides that.

Ibn 'Amir alone read "yunassiyannaka" (يُنَسِّيَنَّكَ) with a shaddah on the sin and a fatha on the nun; the meaning is the same, except that the doubled form is more emphatic.

"Al-dhikrā" (الذِّكْرى) and "al-dhikr" have the same meaning; the feminine form is merely a grammatical (lafzi) feminine. Describing them here as "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is fully apt, because they have placed a thing in other than its proper place. "A'ridh" (أعْرِضْ) in this verse means separation, in the literal sense of turning away and in its most complete aspects; and "fa-la taqʿud" (فَلا تَقْعُدْ) indicates this.

As for the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and there is nothing upon those who fear Allah for their account﴾ ... the verse: the intended "those who" (الَّذِينَ) are the believers, and the pronoun in "hisabihim" (حِسابِهِمْ) refers back to "those who engage in vain talk". Whoever says that the believers are included in His words "turn away" holds that the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in this intent through "those who fear Allah". The meaning according to them, as it has been transmitted, is that when "then do not sit" was revealed, the believers said: "If we do not approach the polytheists or hear their sayings, then we cannot circumambulate or perform worship in the Sacred Precinct." So this was revealed: ﴿and there is nothing upon those who fear Allah﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The permission in this case applies only to the extent that one needs to deal with the polytheists in matters such as worship and the like. Some who hold that "the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in ﴿those who fear Allah﴾, and the believers are included in the first address" said: this last verse is not a permission in any way; rather its meaning is: "Do not sit with them, nor approach them, lest you hear their mockery and their vain talk. Your prohibition from sitting is not because there is anything upon you of their account; rather it is a reminder to you." The meaning may also be understood as: "Perhaps if you keep away from them, they will fear Allah by refraining from mockery."

As for whoever says that the first address is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, because of the difficulty of his parting from them in anger at the disbelievers, he says of this second verse that it is specific to the believers and its meaning is permission. It is as if He said: "So do not sit with them, O Muhammad; as for the believers, there is nothing upon them for their account. If they sit, then let them remind them, perhaps they will fear Allah the Exalted in abandoning what they are engaged in."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This view was indicated by al-Naqqash, but he did not clarify it, and in my opinion there is room for examination in it. The proponent of this view said that this permission for the believers was abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa', His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different topic﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:140]. Likewise, whoever first said that the permission was according to the acts of worship says that this verse in al-Nisa' abrogates that, since it is Madani, and the reference in His words "And it has already been revealed" points to it itself; so consider this carefully, for otherwise the abrogating text must be something other than it. As for "dhikra" (ذِكْرى) on this view, it may be read as "remind them with a reminder," and it may be read as "but turn away whenever you turn away at times other than worship, as a reminder." And "dhikra" on every view may be in the accusative position by an implied verb, or in the nominative by an implied subject.

It befits the believer to follow the ruling of this verse with atheists and with people of argument and vain debate about it. Al-Tabari transmitted from Abu Ja'far that he said: "Do not sit with the people of disputes, for they are the ones who engage in vain talk concerning the signs of Allah the Exalted."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 68–69:

The words of Him, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different topic. And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing folk.﴾ ﴿And there is nothing upon those who fear Allah for their account, [of any kind], but it is a reminder, that perhaps they may fear Allah.﴾

The wording of this address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, but its meaning has been disputed. It has been said that the believers are also included in the address along with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the sound view, because the reason for the prohibition, which is hearing vain talk concerning the signs of Allah the Exalted, encompasses them as well as him (ﷺ). It has also been said: rather, the meaning was intended for the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, because his standing up from the polytheists would be hard on them, and his parting from them in displeasure, even if the believers were not in that state with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to confront them by rising from them whenever they mocked and engaged in vain talk, so that they would learn good manners and abandon vain talk and mockery. This interpretation is consistent with the words of Ibn Jarir (may Allah have mercy on him).

The root meaning of khawd (خَوْض, wading, plunging into vain talk) is wading into water; then it is subsequently used for the depths of things that are obscure, by way of comparison with the depths of water.

"Wa-immā" (وَإمّا): a conditional particle, which is usually followed by the heavy nun (the emphatic nun), though it may sometimes not be, as in the saying:

"If an enemy afflicts you in hostility..."

and other examples besides that.

Ibn 'Amir alone read "yunassiyannaka" (يُنَسِّيَنَّكَ) with a shaddah on the sin and a fatha on the nun; the meaning is the same, except that the doubled form is more emphatic.

"Al-dhikrā" (الذِّكْرى) and "al-dhikr" have the same meaning; the feminine form is merely a grammatical (lafzi) feminine. Describing them here as "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is fully apt, because they have placed a thing in other than its proper place. "A'ridh" (أعْرِضْ) in this verse means separation, in the literal sense of turning away and in its most complete aspects; and "fa-la taqʿud" (فَلا تَقْعُدْ) indicates this.

As for the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and there is nothing upon those who fear Allah for their account﴾ ... the verse: the intended "those who" (الَّذِينَ) are the believers, and the pronoun in "hisabihim" (حِسابِهِمْ) refers back to "those who engage in vain talk". Whoever says that the believers are included in His words "turn away" holds that the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in this intent through "those who fear Allah". The meaning according to them, as it has been transmitted, is that when "then do not sit" was revealed, the believers said: "If we do not approach the polytheists or hear their sayings, then we cannot circumambulate or perform worship in the Sacred Precinct." So this was revealed: ﴿and there is nothing upon those who fear Allah﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The permission in this case applies only to the extent that one needs to deal with the polytheists in matters such as worship and the like. Some who hold that "the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in ﴿those who fear Allah﴾, and the believers are included in the first address" said: this last verse is not a permission in any way; rather its meaning is: "Do not sit with them, nor approach them, lest you hear their mockery and their vain talk. Your prohibition from sitting is not because there is anything upon you of their account; rather it is a reminder to you." The meaning may also be understood as: "Perhaps if you keep away from them, they will fear Allah by refraining from mockery."

As for whoever says that the first address is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, because of the difficulty of his parting from them in anger at the disbelievers, he says of this second verse that it is specific to the believers and its meaning is permission. It is as if He said: "So do not sit with them, O Muhammad; as for the believers, there is nothing upon them for their account. If they sit, then let them remind them, perhaps they will fear Allah the Exalted in abandoning what they are engaged in."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This view was indicated by al-Naqqash, but he did not clarify it, and in my opinion there is room for examination in it. The proponent of this view said that this permission for the believers was abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa', His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different topic﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:140]. Likewise, whoever first said that the permission was according to the acts of worship says that this verse in al-Nisa' abrogates that, since it is Madani, and the reference in His words "And it has already been revealed" points to it itself; so consider this carefully, for otherwise the abrogating text must be something other than it. As for "dhikra" (ذِكْرى) on this view, it may be read as "remind them with a reminder," and it may be read as "but turn away whenever you turn away at times other than worship, as a reminder." And "dhikra" on every view may be in the accusative position by an implied verb, or in the nominative by an implied subject.

It befits the believer to follow the ruling of this verse with atheists and with people of argument and vain debate about it. Al-Tabari transmitted from Abu Ja'far that he said: "Do not sit with the people of disputes, for they are the ones who engage in vain talk concerning the signs of Allah the Exalted."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 70:

(p-387)His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement, and whom the worldly life has deceived. And remind [them] by it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned. It will have, besides Allah, no protector and no intercessor; and if it should offer every compensation, it would not be accepted from it. Those are the ones who have been delivered to destruction for what they earned. For them will be a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

This is a command to abandon [them], and that was according to the small number of the followers of Islam at that time. Qatadah said: Then this was abrogated (naskh) and what resembles it by fighting. Mujahid said: The verse is only for threat and warning, so it is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]; and there is no abrogation in it, because it contains a report, which is the threat. His saying, ﴿as play and amusement﴾, means: since they believe there is no resurrection, they act upon their desires with the conduct of one who plays and is heedless.

﴿And the worldly life has deceived them﴾: that is, it deceived them, from "al-ghurur" (delusion), which is enticing with what is not attained. So they were deceived by the blessings of Allah, His provision, and His respite, and their hope in that regarding what is not attained of His mercy, Exalted is He.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In "gharrathum" here another possibility can be derived, from "al-ghurur" with a fatha on the ghayn, meaning: "I filled their mouths and satisfied them." From it is the saying of the poet:

"When we met at al-Hulaybah, he deceived me with his kindness until I went out, swaying."

And from it: "The bird deceived its young" (gharra al-ta'ir farkhahu). This meaning is not suitable for the explanation of "gharra" in every place.

He attributed the religion to them, in the sense that they made play and amusement their religion. It is possible that the meaning is: "They took their religion, which should have been for them, as play and amusement." The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the religion; it was also said that it refers to the Qur'an.

(p-388)And "an tubsala" is in the position of the object: that is, "lest it be delivered to destruction," or "for fear that it be delivered to destruction." Its meaning is "to be handed over." Al-Hasan and Ikrimah said so. Qatadah said: "to be detained and held as a pledge." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "to be disgraced." Al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd said: "to be recompensed." All these are close in meaning. From it is the saying of al-Shanfara:

"There I do not hope for a life that pleases me, a companion of the nights, delivered up to crimes."

Some people said: it is derived from "al-bas", that is, from "the forbidden" (al-haram), as the poet said:

"She came in the morning blaming you after weakness in the dew; forbidden to you is my blame and my reproach."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is far-fetched.

"Nafs" (soul) indicates the category, and the meaning of the verse is: "Remind by the Qur'an and the religion, and call to it, lest the soul of one who abandons faith be delivered to destruction for what it has earned of disbelief, and preferred it over rejecting Islam."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿besides Allah﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal); "min" is for the beginning of the limit; it is permissible for it to be extra; "dun" is a noun of place, and it is a word used with shared meaning; in this verse it indicates the removal of whatever it is attached to from the descent of the matter, as in the proverb: "Dhamm was ordered to pass beyond 'Ubaydah."

(p-389)The "walī" (protector) and the "shafī'" (intercessor) are the two avenues of protection and aid in all matters. ﴿And if it should offer every compensation﴾: that is, "and if it gives every ransom, however great, making it equivalent for itself, it will not be accepted from it." Al-Tabari related from a speaker that the meaning is: "and if it should equalize" from "al-'adl", the opposite of injustice; and he refuted it, and weakened it by the consensus that the repentance of the disbeliever is accepted.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This refutation is not binding, because the matter is only on the Day of Resurrection, and in it neither repentance nor deed is accepted. The statement is a text from Abu 'Ubaydah. "Al-'idl" in language is the equivalent of a thing from a different kind; it was also said: "al-'idl" with a kasra is "the like," and "al-'adl" with a fatha is "the value." "Ula'ika" is a reference to the category indicated by His saying, "a soul is delivered to destruction." "Ubsilu" means: they were handed over for what they committed of disbelief. "Al-hamim" is hot water, and from it come "al-hammam" (bathhouse) and "al-hammah" (hot spring). From it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"... except the hamim, for it indeed is poured out."

"Alim" is "fa'il" in the sense of "muf'il," that is, "painful."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 71:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Say: "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have enticed away in the earth, bewildered, who has companions calling him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us.' Say: 'Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.'"﴾

The meaning: "Say in your argument: Shall we obey your opinion that we should call upon other than Allah...?" The word "du'a" (calling upon) encompasses worship and other than worship, because whoever makes something the object of his calling, it is that which he worships and upon which he relies.

﴿That which can neither benefit us nor harm us﴾: he means the idols, since they are inanimate objects: stones, wood, and the like. The harm of the idols in religion is not understood by the disbelievers, so He said: ﴿"and neither harm us"﴾; rather, the harm they understand is the coming of worldly hardships.

﴿And be turned back on our heels﴾: this is a metaphor. What is meant by being turned back on the heel is that a person walks forward, which is the good manner of walking, and then he is turned back to walk backwards, which is the base manner of walking. The image was therefore used for one who returns from good to evil, and it occurs in this verse as a depiction of the one who turns back from guidance to the worship of idols. "Guided us" means: directed us. Al-Tabari and others said: turning back on the heels is used of one who hoped for a matter and whose hope was disappointed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an unsound statement.

His exalted saying ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed away﴾, etc.: the kaf is in a position of accusative; it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "a return like the return of the one who..." And "istahwathu" is "istaf'alathu," meaning: "they sought his desire and inclined him." Abu 'Ubayda said: It may be understood as his "hawiyy," which is his earnestness and the riding of his head in yearning toward them. And "al-hawa" (desire), from "hawa, yahwi," is used for falling from a height to a lower place, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"My son fell from the peaks of honour, so his foot and his hand slipped."

This meaning has no place in this verse except that the word be interpreted as: "the devils threw him into a pit." Abu 'Ali went to this, and said: it means "ahwa" (to cause to fall), just as "istazalla" means "azalla" (to cause to slip).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The correct analysis is that the Arabs say: "hawa" and "ahwahu ghayruhu" and "istahwahu," meaning: he asked him to fall himself, or: he asked him to make something fall; "al-hawa" is also used for riding the head in yearning toward a thing, and from it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So make hearts of people incline toward them﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]; and from it is the saying of a jinn poet:

"They incline toward Makkah seeking guidance... no believer among the jinn like their impure ones."

This meaning is the one that suits the verse.

The majority read ﴿istahwathu al-shayatinu﴾ (with the plural "shayatin"); al-Hasan read "istahwathu al-shayatun." Some people said: this is a solecism (laḥn); but it is not so; rather, it is anomalous and ugly, and it is modeled on their saying "sunun" and "ardun," except that these are in the sound plural, whereas "shayatun" is in the broken plural, and this is the point of anomaly. Hamza read "istahwahu al-shayatinu," and he inclined "istahwahu." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-A'mash, and Talha read "istahwihi al-shaytanu" with the yā' and the singular "al-shaytan"; al-Kisa'i mentioned that it is so in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud.

His saying: ﴿"in the earth"﴾ determines that "istahwathu" means only: "sought his hawiyy, which is the earnestness in yearning." "Hayran" is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal); its feminine is "hayra," and it is not declined in definite or indefinite forms. Its meaning is: "astray, bewildered." It is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in "istahwathu," and its governing element is "istahwathu"; it may also be from "kalladhi," with its governing element being the one estimated after the kaf. His saying "istahwathu" implies that he was on a path, and they enticed him away from it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The context of this parable is as if He said: "Is it proper that after guidance we worship idols, so that this would be from us a turning back on the heels, and we would be like a man on a clear path whom the devils enticed away from it, so he left it for their call, and remained bewildered?" His saying ﴿He has companions﴾ may mean: "he has companions on the path from which he went out," and in this case the companions are likened to the believers who call those who have apostatized to return to guidance; this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas. It may also mean: "he has companions, i.e., from the devils who call, or who do not call him to guidance by their claim, but rather deceive him," and in this case the companions are likened to the disbelievers who confirm those who have apostatized from Islam in their apostasy. This interpretation was also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

", 'ti'na'" is from "al-ityan," meaning "al-maji'" (coming). In the codex of 'Abd Allah: "to the guidance, clearly" (bayyinan); this supports the interpretation of those who understood "al-huda" as a factual report from Allah, blessed and exalted. Makki and others related that the intended referent of "like the one" in this verse is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and the companions are his father and his mother, may Allah be pleased with them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, because it is in the Sahih that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, when she heard someone say that the saying of the Exalted ﴿And the one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17] was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "They lied, by Allah; no Qur'an was revealed concerning us except my exoneration."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: My father, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated to me, saying: I heard the jurist and imam Abu 'Abd Allah, known as "al-Nahwi," the resident of Makkah, say: Whoever disputes with any of the atheists should only respond to him and argue with him by the Qur'an and the Hadith; he is like one who calls to guidance by saying "come to us." Whoever argues with them by dialectic and engages them with it is as if he has strayed further from the clear path in order to refute this deviant; he fears for him lest he go astray.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a very good inference.

His exalted saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah﴾, etc.: whoever says that the companions are among the mocking devils, and interprets ﴿to the guidance﴾ as "by their claim," says: "His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance﴾ is a refutation of them according to their claim; so what they claimed is not correct, and it is not guidance; rather it is itself disbelief and misguidance; the guidance is only the guidance of Allah, the Exalted, which is faith." Whoever says that the companions are upon the path to which they call, and that the believers who call the apostates are likened to them, and that the guidance is guidance in its true sense, the verse is understood with His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah﴾ to mean: "The calling of the companions, although it is to guidance, does not by its own nature bring about guidance; rather, one is guided by that calling only if Allah, the Exalted, guides him with His guidance."

﴿And we have been commanded to submit﴾: the lam is the lam of purpose (kay), with "an" implied after it; an object for "umirna" is understood, omitted, its estimate being: "and we have been commanded to sincerity," or "to faith," or something similar; so the estimate of the whole sentence is: "and we have been commanded to sincerity in order that we submit." Sibawayh's view on this is that "li-nuslima" is in the position of the object, and that your saying "umirtu li-aqumа" and "umirtu an aqumа" are equivalent; and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"I wished to forget her, [so it is as if]..."

and other examples. And "li-nuslima" encompasses religion and submission.

"And that you establish prayer and fear Him. And it is He to whom you will be gathered." ﴿And that establish the prayer and fear Him, and it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

"And that establish" (wa-an aqīmū): It is possible that this is by way of interpretation as "wa-iqāmata" (and the establishing of), so that it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the implied object in "wa-umirnā" (and we were commanded). It has also been said that it is rather conjoined to His words "li-nuslima" (that we may submit), its estimated sense being: "that we may submit, and that establish."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: This is the view of al-Zajjāj, but the wording rejects it, because "li-an nuslima" is inflected (muʿrab) and "an aqīmū" is indeclinable (mabnī), and conjoining an indeclinable to an inflected word is not permitted, since conjunction requires sharing the same governing factor (ʿāmil). Unless you make the conjunction only in "an" by itself, and that is strained. Rather, it is to be understood by estimating "wa-an aqīmū" in the sense of "li-nuqīma" (that we may establish), and then it came out in the form of a command, because of the eloquence (jazāla) of the expression. Thus conjunction is permitted, on condition that the grammatical ruling of the wording is disregarded and attention is given to the meaning. This resembles, in respect of what Yūnus narrated from the Arabs, the saying: "udkhulū al-awwalu fal-awwalu" (enter, the first, then the next), with the word "al-awwalu" in the nominative. Its meaning is that "udkhulū" is taken in the sense of "li-yadkhul al-awwalu" (let the first enter); otherwise the only permissible form would be "udkhulū al-awwala fal-awwala" with the accusative.

Al-Zajjāj also said: It is possible that "wa-an aqīmū" is conjoined to "i'tinā" (come to us).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: There is remoteness in this.

The pronoun in His words "wa-ittaqūhu" (and fear Him) refers back to "li-Rabbi al-ʿālamīn" (to the Lord of the worlds). "Wa-huwa" (and He it is) is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar). It is a statement in the form of a report, which contains an admonition (tanbīh) and a warning (takhwīf).

As for His words, exalted is He, "wa-huwa alladhī khalaqa" (and He it is who created) and the rest of the verse: "khalaqa" means He originated (ibtadaʿa) and brought forth from non-existence into existence. "Bil-ḥaqq" (in truth) means: He did not create them in vain, without purpose, but for beneficial purposes and clear realities, among which are what mankind perceives of the inference (istidlāl) by them to the Creator, the descent of provision, and other things. It has also been said that the meaning is: "in that it is right for Him to do so." It has also been said that "bil-ḥaqq" means "by His speech" in His words to the created things, "Be," and in His words: "Come, willingly or unwillingly" [Fuṣṣilat 41:11].

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: The precise statement is that the bringing of created things into existence is by power (qudra), not by speech. The conjunction of "Be" with the moment of the creature's coming into existence has the purpose of showing might and majesty, the execution of commands, and the declaration of intent. An example of this in the observable world is that a person strikes something and breaks it, and says at the moment of breaking, with his tongue, "Break!" That is the execution of resolve and the manifestation of intent. To God belongs the highest likeness: there is no resemblance, no letter, no sound, no change; His command is one, like a glance of the eye. So the meaning of the verse according to this view is: "And He it is who created the heavens and the earth by His word, 'Be,' conjoined with the power by which the creature comes into existence after its non-existence." Thus this is expressed by "al-ḥaqq" (the truth).

"Wa-yawma yaqūlu" (and the day He says): It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and it is connected to the governed element of a verb that is implied, its estimated sense being: "And remember the creation and the return, the day when..." The verse may nevertheless also mean: "And remember the return, the day when God says to the bodies, 'Be,' [so they are] returned." Then it is possible that the speech is complete here, and then it begins with the report that His word, which was in this world, is the truth, as a report about the return. It is also possible that the complete sentence ends at "fa-yakūnu" (and it is), and "qawluhu al-ḥaqq" (His word is the truth) is a new sentence and a predicate. Or, in accordance with the possibility preceding this, "qawluhu" is the subject (fāʿil). Al-Zajjāj said: "Yawma" is conjoined to the pronoun in "wa-ittaqūhu," so the estimated sense here, according to this view, is: "And fear the punishment, or the terrors and hardships, on the day..." It has also been said that the speech is conjoined to His words "khalaqa al-samāwāt" (created the heavens), and the estimated sense according to this is: "And He it is who created the heavens and the earth, and the returning to the gathering on the day..." It is not permissible for these verbs to govern "yawma," whether your estimate is "udhkur" (remember), or "ittaqū" (fear), or "khalaqa" (created), because time nouns, when they are built (mabnī) with verbs, may be put in the accusative only as adverbs of time; and it is not permissible for "wa-yawma" to be connected to "qawluhu al-ḥaqq," because a verbal noun (maṣdar) does not govern what precedes it. Yet some people have stated without restriction that the governing element is "udhkur" or "khalaqa." It is possible that by "yaqūlu" he means the sense of the past, as if he said: "And He it is who created the heavens and the earth in truth on the day He said..." meaning: "He said to them, 'Be.'" Then "wa-yawma" is an adverb of time conjoined to the place (mawḍiʿ) of "al-ḥaqq," since that is in the place of the accusative. The sentence completes at "fa-yakūnu," and "qawluhu al-ḥaqq" comes as a new sentence and a predicate. It is also possible that the sentence completes at "kun" (Be), and it begins with "fa-yakūnu qawluhu al-ḥaqq" (and it is, His word is the truth), with "fa-yakūnu" being a complete verb (tāmma), in the sense of "appears," and "al-ḥaqq" being an attribute (ṣifa) of the speech, and "qawluhu" being the subject.

Al-Ḥasan read "quluhu" with a dammah on the qāf.

"Lahu al-mulk" (His is the dominion) is a subject and predicate. "Yawma yunfakhu fī al-ṣūr" (on the day the Trumpet is blown): "wa-yawma" is a substitute (badal) for the first "yawma," on the basis that "yaqūlu" is in the future and not to be taken in the past sense. It has also been said that it is connected to what the word "al-mulk" contains of the sense of a verb, or to an estimate of "thābit" (established) or "mustaqirr" (fixed) on the day... "Fī al-ṣūr": Abū ʿUbayda said it is the plural of "ṣūra" (form), so the meaning is: "the day the worlds are returned." Al-Jumhūr (the majority) said it is the Trumpet (al-ṣūr), the horn into which, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, it is blown for the swooning (al-ṣaʿq), then for the resurrection. al-Ṭabarī preferred this on the basis of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Isrāfīl has taken the Trumpet into his mouth and bowed his forehead, watching for when he will be commanded, and then he will blow."

Al-Ḥasan read "fī al-ṣuwar" with a fatḥah on the waw, and this supports the first interpretation. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd related it from ʿIyāḍ.

"ʿĀlim" (Knower) is raised by the implied presence of a subject (bi-iḍmār mubtadaʾ); it has also been said that it is an attribute of "alladhī" (He who). Al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read "ʿālimi" in the genitive, as an attribute of the pronoun in "lahu" (His), or as a substitute for it in His words "lahu al-mulk." It has been transmitted from ʿĀṣim. It has also been said that "ʿālimu" is raised by a verb implied from the wording of the passive verb, its estimated sense being: "yanfukhu fīhi ʿālimu" (in it a knower blows), according to what Sībawayh cited:

Let Yazīd weep, a suppliant for a dispute, and another of those whom the calamities have cast down.

The estimate is: "yabkīhi ḍāriʿ" (a suppliant weeps for him). al-Ṭabarī related this interpretation, which resembles "li-yabki Yazīd," from Ibn ʿAbbās. Its parallel in the Qur'an is the reading of one who read "zuyyina li-kathīrin mina al-mushrikīna qatlu awlādihim shurakāʾuhum" (their associates have made to seem attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children), with the zāy vowelled with a dammah and "shurakāʾ" in the nominative. It was related from ʿAbd al-Wārith, from Abū ʿAmr, that he read "yawma nanfukhu fī al-ṣūr" with the first-person plural of majesty.

"Al-ghayb wa-al-shahāda" (the unseen and the witnessed): its meaning is what is absent from us and what is present; this encompasses all existing things.

"And that you establish prayer and fear Him. And it is He to whom you will be gathered." ﴿And that establish the prayer and fear Him, and it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

"And that establish" (wa-an aqīmū): It is possible that this is by way of interpretation as "wa-iqāmata" (and the establishing of), so that it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the implied object in "wa-umirnā" (and we were commanded). It has also been said that it is rather conjoined to His words "li-nuslima" (that we may submit), its estimated sense being: "that we may submit, and that establish."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: This is the view of al-Zajjāj, but the wording rejects it, because "li-an nuslima" is inflected (muʿrab) and "an aqīmū" is indeclinable (mabnī), and conjoining an indeclinable to an inflected word is not permitted, since conjunction requires sharing the same governing factor (ʿāmil). Unless you make the conjunction only in "an" by itself, and that is strained. Rather, it is to be understood by estimating "wa-an aqīmū" in the sense of "li-nuqīma" (that we may establish), and then it came out in the form of a command, because of the eloquence (jazāla) of the expression. Thus conjunction is permitted, on condition that the grammatical ruling of the wording is disregarded and attention is given to the meaning. This resembles, in respect of what Yūnus narrated from the Arabs, the saying: "udkhulū al-awwalu fal-awwalu" (enter, the first, then the next), with the word "al-awwalu" in the nominative. Its meaning is that "udkhulū" is taken in the sense of "li-yadkhul al-awwalu" (let the first enter); otherwise the only permissible form would be "udkhulū al-awwala fal-awwala" with the accusative.

Al-Zajjāj also said: It is possible that "wa-an aqīmū" is conjoined to "i'tinā" (come to us).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: There is remoteness in this.

The pronoun in His words "wa-ittaqūhu" (and fear Him) refers back to "li-Rabbi al-ʿālamīn" (to the Lord of the worlds). "Wa-huwa" (and He it is) is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar). It is a statement in the form of a report, which contains an admonition (tanbīh) and a warning (takhwīf).

As for His words, exalted is He, "wa-huwa alladhī khalaqa" (and He it is who created) and the rest of the verse: "khalaqa" means He originated (ibtadaʿa) and brought forth from non-existence into existence. "Bil-ḥaqq" (in truth) means: He did not create them in vain, without purpose, but for beneficial purposes and clear realities, among which are what mankind perceives of the inference (istidlāl) by them to the Creator, the descent of provision, and other things. It has also been said that the meaning is: "in that it is right for Him to do so." It has also been said that "bil-ḥaqq" means "by His speech" in His words to the created things, "Be," and in His words: "Come, willingly or unwillingly" [Fuṣṣilat 41:11].

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: The precise statement is that the bringing of created things into existence is by power (qudra), not by speech. The conjunction of "Be" with the moment of the creature's coming into existence has the purpose of showing might and majesty, the execution of commands, and the declaration of intent. An example of this in the observable world is that a person strikes something and breaks it, and says at the moment of breaking, with his tongue, "Break!" That is the execution of resolve and the manifestation of intent. To God belongs the highest likeness: there is no resemblance, no letter, no sound, no change; His command is one, like a glance of the eye. So the meaning of the verse according to this view is: "And He it is who created the heavens and the earth by His word, 'Be,' conjoined with the power by which the creature comes into existence after its non-existence." Thus this is expressed by "al-ḥaqq" (the truth).

"Wa-yawma yaqūlu" (and the day He says): It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and it is connected to the governed element of a verb that is implied, its estimated sense being: "And remember the creation and the return, the day when..." The verse may nevertheless also mean: "And remember the return, the day when God says to the bodies, 'Be,' [so they are] returned." Then it is possible that the speech is complete here, and then it begins with the report that His word, which was in this world, is the truth, as a report about the return. It is also possible that the complete sentence ends at "fa-yakūnu" (and it is), and "qawluhu al-ḥaqq" (His word is the truth) is a new sentence and a predicate. Or, in accordance with the possibility preceding this, "qawluhu" is the subject (fāʿil). Al-Zajjāj said: "Yawma" is conjoined to the pronoun in "wa-ittaqūhu," so the estimated sense here, according to this view, is: "And fear the punishment, or the terrors and hardships, on the day..." It has also been said that the speech is conjoined to His words "khalaqa al-samāwāt" (created the heavens), and the estimated sense according to this is: "And He it is who created the heavens and the earth, and the returning to the gathering on the day..." Yet some people have stated without restriction that the governing element is "udhkur" or "khalaqa." It is possible that by "yaqūlu" he means the sense of the past, as if he said: "And He it is who created the heavens and the earth in truth on the day He said..." meaning: "He said to them, 'Be.'" Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 74–75:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error."﴾ ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain.﴾

The governing element of "wa-idh" (and when) is an implied verb, whose estimate is: "Remember" (wa-dhkur), or: "Relate" (quss). Al-Tabari said: God, blessed and exalted is He, alerted Muhammad (ﷺ) to follow the example of Abraham (peace be upon him) in his argument with his people, since they were people of idols, and the people of Muhammad (ﷺ) were people of idols.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This does not necessarily follow from the wording of the verse; yet everything of this kind is open to being taken as an example to follow.

The Seven Readers and the majority of people read "Azar" with a fatha on the hamza that comes before the alif, and a fatha on the zay and the ra'. Al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq and Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: it is the name of Abraham's father.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It has been established that his name was "Tarah." So, according to this view, he has two names, like "Ya'qub" and "Isra'il." In terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis) on this view, it is a badal (apposition) to the ab (father) which is in apposition/annexed position, in the genitive case, and it is a proper noun. Mujahid said: rather, it is the name of an idol, and it is in the accusative position governed by an implied verb, whose estimate is: "Do you take Azar? Do you take idols?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: There is weakness in this.

Some of them said: rather, it is an adjective, and its meaning is: "the crooked one, the one who errs."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is objected to, because "Azar," if it is an adjective, is indefinite, and it is not permissible for a definite noun to be qualified by an indefinite one. This may be justified with some strain by saying that the alif and lam were added to it even though they are not pronounced; and al-Zajjaj pointed to this, since he estimated it thus, saying: "to his father, the erring one." It may also be said that it is a separate (detached) accusative governed by a verb whose estimate is: "I blame the crooked one," or: "the one who errs," and the adjectival quality does not remain in it in this state.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is weak. It was also said: its accusative is by way of the circumstantial (hal), as if he said: "And when Abraham said to his father, while he was in a state of crookedness and error."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and others read it with a damma on the ra', as a vocative (nida'). Even with this, it is valid that "Azar" is the name of Abraham's father (peace be upon him); and it is valid that it means "the crooked one" and "the one who errs." Al-Dahhak said: "Azar" means "thing." With this reading it is not valid for "Azar" to be an adjective.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy, may God be pleased with him, the reading is: "O Azar!" with the vocative particle retained, and "you have taken idols" with the past tense verb. Ibn 'Abbas, also as reported from him, read: "a-izran tattakhidh" with the interrogative alif, a fatha on the hamza of "izran," a sukun on the zay, a fatha on the ra' and tanwin on it, and dropping the interrogative alif from "a-tattakhidh." The meaning of this reading is: "a support, and strength, and backing against God, the Exalted, do you take...?" It is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿Strengthen my back with him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 31]. Abu Isma'il, a man from the people of Sham, read the hamza with a kasra in this arrangement; Abu al-Futuh mentioned it. Its meaning is that it is substituted from a waw, like "wisadah" (cushion) and "isadah." It is as if he said: "a burden and a sin do you take as idols?" Its accusative, on this view, is governed by an implied verb. It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Al-A'mash read: "izran tattakhidh" with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the zay, without the interrogative alif, and "idols, gods" are two objects.

It is mentioned that Azar, the father of Abraham (peace be upon him), was a skilled carpenter and craftsman, and Nimrod was attached to engineering and the stars; so Azar gained favour with him for this reason. He was in charge of the making of idols, which were made by his command and arrangement, and he would stamp the idol with a seal known to him; then that idol would be worshipped. When Abraham (peace be upon him), his son, grew up in the condition that comes later, his father would charge him with selling them. Abraham (peace be upon him) would call out over them: "Who will buy what harms him and does not benefit him?" and he would treat them with contempt, placing them upside down in the water and saying: "Drink!" When his affair became notorious because of this, and he (peace be upon him) began calling to God, the Exalted, he said this statement to his father.

"Araka" (I see you) in this place is shared by sight and the heart, because it is a vision of the heart and its knowledge; and it is built upon a vision of sight. "Mubin" means clear and evident; it comes from "abana al-shay'" (the thing became clear) when it became manifest. It is not the transitive verb derived from "bana, yabin."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is valid that it is the causative form, and the object is implied, its estimate being: "in manifest error, your disbelief."

It was said: Azar was a man from the people of "Kawtha," in the countryside of Kufa. Al-Naqqash said: Abraham (peace be upon him) was born there. It was also said he was from the people of Harran.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The preceding verse necessitates Abraham's (peace be upon him) guidance, and the indication here by "thus" refers to that guidance; that is: "Just as We guided him to call to God, the Exalted, and to reject disbelief, We showed him the dominion of..." The form of "nuri" (We show) is in the future tense, but its meaning is the past. Al-Mahdawi related that the meaning is: "Just as We guided you, O Muhammad, so We showed Abraham..."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is far-fetched, since the wording does not give this meaning. "Nuri" here is transitive to two objects only. It is either from the sight of the eye, or from "ara" which means "to make known." Had it been from "ara" meaning "to inform," and we considered "a'lama" (to inform) derived from "alima," which is transitive to two objects, then "ara" would have to be transitive to three objects; and this is not the case. Nor is it valid to say that the third is omitted, because it is not permissible to omit it, since it is the predicate in the clause which "I know" enters upon in this context. Rather, it is from "alima" meaning "to recognize," then the hamza was added to make it transitive to two objects, and then "ara" was treated in this same way.

As for this vision: it was said to be vision of the eye. It is reported on this that God, the Exalted, opened up the heavens and the earths for Abraham (peace be upon him), until he saw with his eye the highest dominion and the lowest dominion. If this report is sound, then it contains a particularisation of Abraham (peace be upon him) with something that no one before him or after him attained. This is the view of Mujahid, who said: "The heavens and the earths were opened for him, and he saw his place in Paradise." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Salman al-Farisi also held this view. It was also said: it is a vision of sight in the outward dominion, along with which he received consideration and vision of the heart that none of the people of his time, to whom he was sent (peace be upon him), attained. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. In this there is a certain particularisation, in the sense of restriction to the people of his time. It was also said: it is a vision of the heart, by which he saw the dominion of the heavens and the earth through his reflection and contemplation; and this necessarily rests upon his earlier seeing with his eye, and his general perception through his senses.

(p. 400) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: These last two views suit the verse, because the goal for which this was made for him is that he should believe and be among the many certain ones. The indication here is, without doubt, to those prophets and believers before him and after him. Certainty comes to him (peace be upon him) and to others through sight of the outward dominion, and through inferring from it the Maker and the Creator, there is no god but Him.

"Malakut" is an intensive form, like "jabarut," "rahabut" and "rahamut." Ikrima said: it is "malakuthi" in Greek, or in Nabataean. He read "malakuth" with the thaʼ (ث) as a three-dotted letter. Abu al-Sammal read "malkut" with the lam sukun, and this is a dialect form. "Malakut" means "the kingdom," and the Arabs say: "For so-and-so is the malakut of Yemen," meaning his kingdom.

The lam in "wa-li-yakuna" (and that he might be) is connected to a verb placed later, whose estimate is: "and that he might be among the certain, We showed him." "Al-muqin" is one who knows a thing with a knowledge in which no doubt can arise. Al-Dahhak and also Mujahid said: the indication here by "the dominion of the heavens" refers to the stars, the sun and the moon. This returns to and falls within what we have already mentioned, that it is a vision of sight in the outward dominion. It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, in the interpretation of ﴿and that he might be among the certain﴾, that he said: He made clear to him the affairs, their secret and their open aspects, so nothing of the deeds of creatures was hidden from him. When he began cursing the sinners, God, the Exalted, said: "You cannot bear this," so He turned back his sight so that he no longer saw their deeds.

It is mentioned that Azar, the father of Abraham (peace be upon him), was a skilled carpenter and craftsman, and Nimrod was attached to engineering and the stars; so Azar gained favour with him for this reason. He was in charge of the making of idols, which were made by his command and arrangement, and he would stamp the idol with a seal known to him; then that idol would be worshipped. When Abraham (peace be upon him), his son, grew up in the condition that comes later, his father would charge him with selling them. Abraham (peace be upon him) would call out over them: "Who will buy what harms him and does not benefit him?" and he would treat them with contempt, placing them upside down in the water and saying: "Drink!" When his affair became notorious because of this, and he (peace be upon him) began calling to God, the Exalted, he said this statement to his father.

"Araka" (I see you) in this place is shared by sight and the heart, because it is a vision of the heart and its knowledge; and it is built upon a vision of sight. "Mubin" means clear and evident; it comes from "abana al-shay'" (the thing became clear) when it became manifest. It is not the transitive verb derived from "bana, yabin."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is valid that it is the causative form, and the object is implied, its estimate being: "in manifest error, your disbelief."

It was said: Azar was a man from the people of "Kawtha," in the countryside of Kufa. Al-Naqqash said: Abraham (peace be upon him) was born there. It was also said he was from the people of Harran.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The preceding verse necessitates Abraham's (peace be upon him) guidance, and the indication here by "thus" refers to that guidance; that is: "Just as We guided him to call to God, the Exalted, and to reject disbelief, We showed him the dominion of..." The form of "nuri" (We show) is in the future tense, but its meaning is the past. Al-Mahdawi related that the meaning is: "Just as We guided you, O Muhammad, so We showed Abraham..."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is far-fetched, since the wording does not give this meaning. "Nuri" here is transitive to two objects only. It is either from the sight of the eye, or from "ara" which means "to make known." Had it been from "ara" meaning "to inform," and we considered "a'lama" (to inform) derived from "alima," which is transitive to two objects, then "ara" would have to be transitive to three objects; and this is not the case. Nor is it valid to say that the third is omitted, because it is not permissible to omit it, since it is the predicate in the clause which "I know" enters upon in this context. Rather, it is from "alima" meaning "to recognize," then the hamza was added to make it transitive to two objects, and then "ara" was treated in this same way.

As for this vision: it was said to be vision of the eye. It is reported on this that God, the Exalted, opened up the heavens and the earths for Abraham (peace be upon him), until he saw with his eye the highest dominion and the lowest dominion. If this report is sound, then it contains a particularisation of Abraham (peace be upon him) with something that no one before him or after him attained. This is the view of Mujahid, who said: "The heavens and the earths were opened for him, and he saw his place in Paradise." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Salman al-Farisi also held this view. It was also said: it is a vision of sight in the outward dominion, along with which he received consideration and vision of the heart that none of the people of his time, to whom he was sent (peace be upon him), attained. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. In this there is a certain particularisation, in the sense of restriction to the people of his time. It was also said: it is a vision of the heart, by which he saw the dominion of the heavens and the earth through his reflection and contemplation; and this necessarily rests upon his earlier seeing with his eye, and his general perception through his senses.

(p. 400) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: These last two views suit the verse, because the goal for which this was made for him is that he should believe and be among the many certain ones. The indication here is, without doubt, to those prophets and believers before him and after him. Certainty comes to him (peace be upon him) and to others through sight of the outward dominion, and through inferring from it the Maker and the Creator, there is no god but Him.

"Malakut" is an intensive form, like "jabarut," "rahabut" and "rahamut." Ikrima said: it is "malakuthi" in Greek, or in Nabataean. He read "malakuth" with the thaʼ (ث) as a three-dotted letter. Abu al-Sammal read "malkut" with the lam sukun, and this is a dialect form. "Malakut" means "the kingdom," and the Arabs say: "For so-and-so is the malakut of Yemen," meaning his kingdom.

The lam in "wa-li-yakuna" (and that he might be) is connected to a verb placed later, whose estimate is: "and that he might be among the certain, We showed him." "Al-muqin" is one who knows a thing with a knowledge in which no doubt can arise. Al-Dahhak and also Mujahid said: the indication here by "the dominion of the heavens" refers to the stars, the sun and the moon. This returns to and falls within what we have already mentioned, that it is a vision of sight in the outward dominion. It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, in the interpretation of ﴿and that he might be among the certain﴾, that he said: He made clear to him the affairs, their secret and their open aspects, so nothing of the deeds of creatures was hidden from him. When he began cursing the sinners, God, the Exalted, said: "You cannot bear this," so He turned back his sight so that he no longer saw their deeds.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 76–77:**

[p. 401] His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "If my lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾

This *fa'* (then) in His saying "*fa-lamma*" (so when) links what follows it to what precedes it. It indicates that the intended meaning of *malakut* (the dominion of the heavens and the earth) is this detailed account in this verse. "*Janna al-layl*" means the night covered and concealed with its darkness. It is also said "*ajanna*," but the first form is more common. The words *al-jinn* (the jinn), *al-mijann* (shield), *al-jannah* (garden), and *al-janan* (the grave), which means the grave, are likely derived from *janna*, meaning to conceal.

The wording of this story allows that it occurred to him (peace be upon him) during his childhood, before he reached puberty, as Ibn 'Abbas held. He said: "He saw a star and worshipped it." Many people said that the incident occurred before puberty and before being held accountable. It is also allowed that it occurred to him after he reached puberty and became accountable. al-Tabari reported this from a group who said that he asked in the form of a rebuke, without the interrogative particle *alif*. He said: "This is like the saying of the poet:

*They lifted me up and said, "O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed," so I said, while denying their faces: "Are they them?"*

He means: "Are they them?" And like the saying of another:

*By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable: is it Shu'ayth ibn Sahm or Shu'ayth ibn Minqar?*

He means: "Is it Shu'ayth?"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In my view, the first verse is not a proof here.

It has been related that Namrud (Nimrod), the tyrant of that age, had his astrologers observe that a child would be born in a certain year who would bring about the ruin of his kingdom at his hands. So he began to watch pregnant women and assign guards to them. Whichever woman gave birth to a girl was left alone, and whichever gave birth to a boy was brought to the king, who slaughtered him. The mother of Ibrahim became pregnant, and she was a young, strong woman, so she concealed her pregnancy. When her delivery drew near, she sent Tarah, the father of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), on a journey, and she contrived his departure. Then she went out to a cave, where she gave birth to Ibrahim (peace be upon him). She left him in the cave, having prepared provisions for him, and she used to check on him. She would find that he nourished himself by sucking his fingers, from which honey, ghee, and similar things would flow. It is also related: "Rather, an angel nourished him." And it is related: "Rather, she used to bring him the milk of the women whose sons had been slaughtered." Ibrahim (peace be upon him) grew many times faster than others did. Meanwhile, the king sensed his birth and intensified the search for him. He remained in the cave for ten years, and it is said fifteen years. When he first came to understand, he looked out from the cave, saw the star, and the story of the verse took place.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I have related these stories in the most concise wording, and I intended to cover the meanings that pertain to the verse. In my view, it is weak that this story occurred while he was in the cave, because of His saying (peace be upon him) at its end: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you associate [with Allah].﴾ [al-An'am: 78]. These are words that imply an argument and a refutation directed at a people, and his condition in the cave is far from such a thing. Unless it is interpreted that he (peace be upon him) said it to himself, meaning that he said in his own mind the sense of the expression about him: ﴿O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate [with Allah].﴾ [al-An'am: 78]. This is like the saying of the poet:

*Then he turned back and said to himself in reflection: "Indeed, life today is in its returns."*

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Nevertheless, the mode of address (in the verse) makes this unlikely. Had he said, "O my people, indeed I am free of polytheism," this interpretation would be sound and stronger. If we hold that the story occurred to him while he was in the cave, during his youth and before being held accountable, as some exegetes held and as the wording allows, then the matter divides into two aspects. Either his saying "This is my lord" is taken as a firm resolve and belief, and this is false, because firm resolve did not come from the prophets (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all). Or it is taken as a means of prompting reflection and inquiry, as if he said: "Is this shining, radiant one my lord?" if evidence supported it. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is then like what Allah, Exalted, said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7]. That is, unguided in belief.

If we hold that the story occurred to him while he was in unbelief and was accountable, then it is not permissible for him to say "This is my lord" either in firm resolve or as a prompt to reflection, because that would be a level of ignorance or doubt, and he (peace be upon him) is exalted above and protected from all of that. Nothing remains except that he (peace be upon him) said it in the manner of a statement to his people, a rebuke to them, and a establishing of proof against them regarding the worship of idols. It is as if he said to them: "Is this shining one my lord?" or "This is my lord," meaning "according to your claim." Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾ [al-Nahl: 27], and the meaning there is "according to your claim." Then Ibrahim (peace be upon him) pointed out to them, from the star's movement and its setting, a sign of having come into existence, and that it is not fit to be a lord. Then he did the same with something greater and more worthy than it, and then with the sun in the same way. It is as if he said: "If it has become clear that these elevated luminaries are not fit for lordship, then your idols, which are wood and stone, are even more deserving that this be clear about them." In my view, this interpretation (ta'wil) is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you associate [with Allah].﴾ [al-An'am: 78].

He (peace be upon him) gave them these examples because they were people of astrology and of observing the celestial spheres. All of this occurred within a single night. The star, which is Venus according to Qatada, and al-Suddi said it was Jupiter, was inclining toward setting. When it set, the moon rose, meaning it first emerged. Then the night proceeded in full. When the sun rose, the moonlight disappeared before it, due to the spreading of the morning, and its light became faint, and it also drew near its place of setting. This was called *ufool* (setting), because it was close to complete setting, by a figurative usage in naming. Then the sun rose over that. This sequence fits the fifteenth night of the lunar month up to the twentieth, and it does not occur within one single night, as the people of exegesis agreed, except on these nights. By this figurative usage regarding the setting of the moon, *afala* in the language of the Arabs means "to set." It is said: "Where did you vanish from us, so-and-so?" It has also been said that it means "to depart."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a difference only in expression. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Lamps that are not guided by those who lead them, nor are they stars, nor the setting ones that revolve.*

He said "*al-afilin*" (the setting ones), and pluralized it with the *ya'* and *nun* ending, because he intended the lords, and the like. On this basis, His saying about the sun, "This is my lord," is explained: he used the masculine demonstrative when he intended his Lord.

Ibn Kathir and 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read *ra'a* with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and the *hamza*. Nafi' read between *fatha* and *kasra*. 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read both with *kasra*. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and a *kasra* on the *hamza*.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising﴾ and the rest of the verse, "*al-buzoo*" (rising), with regard to these lights, is the first emergence. The discussion of what the wording of the verse implies has already been presented. That this sequence occurred in one night involves a figurative usage regarding the setting of the moon, because if we took its setting to mean its disappearing in the west, that would be after the sunrise. All that we have said is supported by careful reflection.

"*Yahdini*" means "guide me." This wording supports the view of those who said that the incident occurred in childhood. "The misguided people" are the worshippers of created things, such as idols and others. Although misguidance is more general than this, this is what is intended in this context.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 78–80:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, I am free of what you associate [with Allah].﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾ ﴿And his people argued with him. He said, "Do you argue with me concerning Allah while He has guided me? And I do not fear what you associate with Him, except that my Lord should will something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then be reminded?"﴾

When he intended his Lord, he said, "This" (hadha), and he used the demonstrative (dhalika); that is, "this visible thing," or "the shining one," and the like. "But when it set" (afalat), the sun, there remained nothing with which they could be compared, so his proof became manifest, and by this he was strengthened to confront them and to disavow their associating [partners with Allah].

And his saying, ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you associate﴾, supports the view of those who said that the event (of his argument) took place in the state of old age and of being legally responsible. And ﴿I have turned my face﴾, that is: I have directed my intention, my worship, my monotheism, my faith, and other things encompassed by the meaning expressed by "my face." And "fatara" means: he originated (ibtada'a) in bodies. And "hanifan" means: upright (musta'iman). And "al-hanaf" in the language of the Arabs is "inclination" (al-mayl); its original usage is for physical bodies, and in meanings it is used figuratively. So a crooked body is literally "ahnaf" (bow-legged/crooked), that is, inclined; and an upright body is "ahnaf" figuratively, as if it had inclined away from every direction toward uprightness.

"Wa hajjahu" is "fa'alahu" from "al-hujjah" (proof/argument). He said: "Do you dispute with me about the proof concerning the Oneness of Allah, Exalted is He?" A group read "Ata'hajjunani" with both nuns pronounced, which is the original form. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Ata'hajjunnani" with the first nun assimilated into the second. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Ata'hajjunni" with one nun deleted. It was said: the deleted one is the second; and it was said: it is the first. What indicates this is that the remaining one is kasrah-vowelled. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is not permissible to delete the first, because it marks the grammatical case (i'rab); rather, the second was deleted, which serves as a preparatory vowel for the first person pronoun ya', as it is deleted in "layti" and in the saying of the poet:

﴿ ............... ∗∗∗ it harms the costly (things) when it is cut off ﴾

After that, the remaining first one was given kasrah because it is adjacent to the ya'.

"Wa qad hadani" means: He guided me to knowing Him and to His Oneness. Al-Kisa'i inclined "hadani" (imalah, vowel-raising); and the imalah in this is good. And since imalah is permitted in "ghaza" and "da'a," which are of the waw-type roots, it is even more permissible and better in "hadani," which is of the ya'-type root.

It is related that the disbelievers said to Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "Fear lest our gods afflict you with leprosy or some disease, for your harming them and your belittling them." So he, peace be upon him, said to them: "I do not fear what you associate with Him, because it has no power and no ability to benefit." The "ma" in this place has the meaning of "alladhi" (that which). The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to Allah, Exalted and Majestic; in that case, the pronoun in "tushrikun" refers back to "ma," and the sense of the speech is: "And I do not fear the idols that you associate with Allah, Exalted, in lordship." It may also refer back to "ma," needing nothing else; as if the sense were: "what you associate by its cause."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except that my Lord should will something﴾, is an exception that is not from the first (clause); and "shay'an" is in the accusative governed by "yasha'a." Since the force of the speech was that he does not fear harm, he excepted the will of his Lord, Exalted is He, that He should intend harm for him. "'Ilman" is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz); it is a verbal noun with the meaning of the agent, as the Arabs say: "Zayd perspired sweat" (tasabbaba Zayd 'arakan), and the meaning is: "the sweat of Zayd perspired"; likewise the meaning here is: the knowledge of my Lord encompasses all things. ﴿Will you not then be reminded?﴾ is a rebuke, an admonition, and a manifestation of the place of their shortcoming.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 78–80:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 6, verses 81–83**

[p. 406]

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated [with Allah], when you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has not sent down upon you any authority? So which of the two groups has more right to security, if you should know?﴾ ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing [ẓulm] — those will have security, and they are guided.﴾ ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.﴾

This verse, up to "you know," is all part of the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, to his people, and it is his decisive argument against them. The meaning is: "How should I fear the idols, which have no power over anything, being stones and wood, when I have cast them aside and have not venerated them? And you do not fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic, though you have associated with Him in lordship things for which He has not sent down upon you any proof?" Here "al-sulṭān" means proof (ḥujjah).

Then he asked in the form of an affirmation: "So which of the two groups has more right to security?" That is: "The one who does not associate anything with the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, the Exalted, has more right to be secure."

As for His saying, ﴿Those who believed﴾, and the rest of the verse: "alladhīna" is in the nominative case, being the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). "Yalbisū" means "yakhliṭū," i.e., they mix. "Al-ẓulm," in this verse, means shirk (associating others with Allah). Traditions from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, have been transmitted to this effect, and from a group of the Companions, that: "When this verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, became apprehensive and said, 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'That is not what is meant. It is as Luqman said: ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].'"

It is also reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was reading in the codex (muṣḥaf), and when he reached this verse it weighed heavily upon him, so he wrapped his garment around himself and went to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, saying, "O Abu al-Mundhir," and asked him about it. He said to him, "It is shirk, O Commander of the Faithful." So 'Umar's distress was relieved, may Allah be pleased with him. A similar incident occurred between Zayd ibn Ṣūḥān and Salmān, as had happened to 'Umar with Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Mujāhid recited (a variant reading [qira'a]): "walam yalbisū īmānahum bi-shirk," and 'Ikrimah recited "yulbisū" with a damma on the yā'.

"Al-amn" is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is in the prepositional phrase (majrūr) following it. The whole sentence is the predicate of "ūlā'ika," and "wa-hum muhtadūn" means "they are rightly guided" (rāshidūn).

'Alī ibn Abi Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The intended meaning of this verse is Abraham, peace be upon him, specifically." 'Ikrimah said: "It was revealed specifically concerning the emigrants (muhājirūn) among the Companions of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him." A group said: it is from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, to his people, and so it is part of the argument that was given to him. Ibn Jurayj said: it is from the speech of the people of Abraham, peace be upon him, and this also fits as part of the argument, in that they acknowledged the truth while they had been wrongdoers in associating others with Allah. Ibn Ishāq, Ibn Zayd, and others said: rather, that is a statement from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, a beginning of a judgment that has been detailed, general to the time of Abraham's argumentation and to others as well, and to every believer, whether earlier or later.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the clear and eloquent view, to which the meaning of the verse is connected and which gives its arrangement its excellence, and it is a report from Allah, Exalted.

"Tilka" is a demonstrative referring to this previously mentioned argument; it is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and "ḥujjatunā" is its predicate. "Ātaynāhā" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also permissible for "ḥujjatunā" to be an appositive (badal) of "tilka," and "ātaynāhā" to be the predicate of "wa-tilka." "Ibrāhīm" is the direct object of "ātaynā," and the pronoun (the hā') is also a direct object of "ātaynā," placed first. "'Alā" is connected to "ḥujjatunā." In this there is considerable separation (faṣl), and it is also permissible for "'alā" to be connected to "ātaynāhā" according to the meaning, since the sense is: "We made it manifest to Abraham against his people," and similar.

Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, and Ibn 'Āmir recited: "narfa'u darajāti man nashā'" with the word "darajāt" in the genitive construct with "man." 'Āmir, 'Āṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisā'ī recited: "narfa'u darajātin man nashā'."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These are two valid ways of construing the speech, and the meaning intended by both is one. "Darajātin," according to the reading with tanwīn, is in the accusative of place (ẓarfiyyah). "Ḥakīmun 'Alīm" are two attributes that suit this context, since it is a context of will and choice, which requires knowledge and perfection of wisdom. The word "darajāt" originally applies to physical things, and then it is used for ranks and positions in a figurative (ma'nawiyyah) sense.

﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, each of whom We guided; and Noah We guided before them; and among his descendants, David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron.
