The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 87–90:

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And [We guided] some of their forefathers, their offspring and their brothers. We chose them and guided them to a straight path.﴾ ﴿That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been lost to them.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment (al-hukm) and prophethood. If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance. Say: "I do not ask you any wage for it. It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds."﴾

The meaning: "And We guided [some] of their forefathers, their offspring and their brothers, as groups." Here "min" (some of) is partitive (li-l-tab'id). What is intended is "whoever among them believed, whether a prophet or a non-prophet." Jesus, peace be upon him, is included in the words "and of their forefathers," and for this reason Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "The maternal uncle is a father, and the maternal aunt is a mother."

"Wajtabaynahum" means: We chose them, guided them, admitted them into Our special company, guided them to faith and to success in the pleasure of Allah, Exalted. Mujahid said: its meaning is "We made them sincere (akhlasna-hum)."

"Dhurriyyah" means offspring (al-abna'). It may also be applied to all of mankind as "dhurriyyah," because they are the children of [Adam]. Some scholars said: "Dhurriyyah" may also refer to forefathers, based on His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:41], where what is meant is the human species.

As for His saying, ﴿That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides…﴾: "That" refers to the blessing mentioned in His words "and We chose them." Attributing guidance to Allah is an attribution of ownership (idafat milk). "La-habita" means: was lost and gone, due to the evil that overcame them.

"Ula'ika" refers to those previously mentioned. "Al-Kitab" is intended to mean the Mushaf, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. "Al-hukm" is intended to mean intellect (al-lubb), discernment and understanding (al-fiqh) in the religion of Allah, Exalted. "Ha'ula'": refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh who were hostile to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to all disbelievers of that era. This was said by Qatada, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others. "Qawman" is intended to mean the believers of the people of Madinah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and others. Thus, according to this interpretation, although the intention in its revelation was these two categories, the verse encompasses both disbelievers and believers until the Day of Resurrection. Qatada also said, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan: "What is meant by the people (al-qawm) are those previously mentioned among the prophets and believers." Abu Raja' said: "What is meant are the angels." The "ba'" in "bi-ha" is connected to "bi-kafirin," and the "ba'" in "bi-kafirin" is extra, for emphasis.

As for His saying, Exalted, ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided﴾ and the rest of the verse: the apparent reading of the demonstrative "ula'ika" is that it refers to the prophets mentioned before, and those believers who were guided along with them. The meaning of "iqtida'" (following) is to follow the traces in speech, action and conduct. Following all of them is valid only in matters of creed, faith and monotheism, in which there is no disagreement among them. As for the practical rulings of the legal codes (a'mal al-shara'i'), they differ, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law (shir'ah) and a way (minhaj)﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48]. It is also possible that the demonstrative "ula'ika" refers to His saying "qawman."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This follows from some interpretations of what is meant by "qawman," and it disturbs some of them.

The judge Ibn al-Baqillani said: People have differed: was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), before his mission, a worshipper according to the law (shar') of those before him? One group said: he was a worshipper. Then they differed: according to whose law? One group said: according to the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Another group: according to the law of Musa, peace be upon him. Another group: according to the law of 'Isa, peace be upon him. A group suspended judgment on this matter. Another group said: he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was not a worshipper according to the law of those who came before him, and this is the view that is preferred.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The judge's statement should not be understood to mean that he was not a worshipper according to the law of those before him in matters of monotheism or belief, because we find that our law states that the disbelievers who lived before the Prophet, peace be upon him, such as his parents and others, are in the Fire. Allah does not admit anyone into the Fire except for abandoning what he was obligated to do. This is in His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 17:15], and other evidence. The principle of the theologians (mutakallimun) is that reason does not make obligatory and does not impose obligations; rather, the law (shar') makes obligatory. So the correct way to state this is: Adam, peace be upon him, and those after him called to the monotheism of Allah, Exalted, with a general call, and this continued throughout the world. Thus it is obligatory upon every sane adult human to search for the law that commands the monotheism of Allah, Exalted, and to reflect upon the proofs established for it, according to what the law obliges him to reflect upon, and not to worship anything other than Allah, Exalted. As for the one we supposed, who did not find a way to knowledge of a law commanding the monotheism of Allah, Exalted, and who, despite this, did not disbelieve nor worship an idol, but abstained: these are the people of the fatra (the interval between prophets), whom the scholars have declared to be in Paradise, and they are in the position of children and the insane. As for one who fell short in reflection and investigation, and worshipped an idol and disbelieved, he has neglected what was obligatory upon him, and deserves punishment in the Fire. So the Prophet (ﷺ), before his mission, and those who were with him among the people, and before him, were addressed through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, before, regarding the monotheism of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but they were not addressed regarding the subsidiary branches of their legal codes, since these differ, and since no prophet called them to them. As for after the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ): is he and his community addressed by the law of those who came before? One group said: we are not addressed by any of that. Another group said: we are addressed by the law of those before us.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever among this group says that Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his community are addressed by all the laws of those who came before, without qualification, has spoken something impossible, because the rulings of the laws come differently. Rather, they adopt the view of those who said: We are obligated by what has been validly transmitted from the laws of those before us, and which the laws did not differ about, and by the last of what they differed about, since it is the latest abrogating (al-nasikh al-mutaqaddim). Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

Say: "I do not ask you any wage for it. It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds."﴾

The meaning: "And We guided [some] of their forefathers, their offspring and their brothers, as groups." Here "min" (some of) is partitive (li-l-tab'id). What is intended is "whoever among them believed, whether a prophet or a non-prophet." Jesus, peace be upon him, is included in the words "and of their forefathers," and for this reason Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "The maternal uncle is a father, and the maternal aunt is a mother."

"Wajtabaynahum" means: We chose them, guided them, admitted them into Our special company, guided them to faith and to success in the pleasure of Allah, Exalted. Mujahid said: its meaning is "We made them sincere (akhlasna-hum)."

"Dhurriyyah" means offspring (al-abna'). It may also be applied to all of mankind as "dhurriyyah," because they are the children of [Adam]. Some scholars said: "Dhurriyyah" may also refer to forefathers, based on His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:41], where what is meant is the human species.

As for His saying, ﴿That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides…﴾: "That" refers to the blessing mentioned in His words "and We chose them." Attributing guidance to Allah is an attribution of ownership (idafat milk). "La-habita" means: was lost and gone, due to the evil that overcame them.

"Ula'ika" refers to those previously mentioned. "Al-Kitab" is intended to mean the Mushaf, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. "Al-hukm" is intended to mean intellect (al-lubb), discernment and understanding (al-fiqh) in the religion of Allah, Exalted. "Ha'ula'": refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh who were hostile to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to all disbelievers of that era. This was said by Qatada, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others. "Qawman" is intended to mean the believers of the people of Madinah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and others. Thus, according to this interpretation, although the intention in its revelation was these two categories, the verse encompasses both disbelievers and believers until the Day of Resurrection. Following all of them is valid only in matters of creed, faith and monotheism, in which there is no disagreement among them. As for the practical rulings of the legal codes (a'mal al-shara'i'), they differ, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law (shir'ah) and a way (minhaj)﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48]. It is also possible that the demonstrative "ula'ika" refers to His saying "qawman."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This follows from some interpretations of what is meant by "qawman," and it disturbs some of them.

The judge Ibn al-Baqillani said: People have differed: was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), before his mission, a worshipper according to the law (shar') of those before him? One group said: he was a worshipper. Then they differed: according to whose law? One group said: according to the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Another group: according to the law of Musa, peace be upon him. Another group: according to the law of 'Isa, peace be upon him. A group suspended judgment on this matter. Another group said: he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was not a worshipper according to the law of those who came before him, and this is the view that is preferred.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The judge's statement should not be understood to mean that he was not a worshipper according to the law of those before him in matters of monotheism or belief, because we find that our law states that the disbelievers who lived before the Prophet, peace be upon him, such as his parents and others, are in the Fire. Allah does not admit anyone into the Fire except for abandoning what he was obligated to do. This is in His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 17:15], and other evidence. The principle of the theologians (mutakallimun) is that reason does not make obligatory and does not impose obligations; rather, the law (shar') makes obligatory. So the correct way to state this is: Adam, peace be upon him, and those after him called to the monotheism of Allah, Exalted, with a general call, and this continued throughout the world. Thus it is obligatory upon every sane adult human to search for the law that commands the monotheism of Allah, Exalted, and to reflect upon the proofs established for it, according to what the law obliges him to reflect upon, and not to worship anything other than Allah, Exalted. As for the one we supposed, who did not find a way to knowledge of a law commanding the monotheism of Allah, Exalted, and who, despite this, did not disbelieve nor worship an idol, but abstained: these are the people of the fatra (the interval between prophets), whom the scholars have declared to be in Paradise, and they are in the position of children and the insane. As for one who fell short in reflection and investigation, and worshipped an idol and disbelieved, he has neglected what was obligatory upon him, and deserves punishment in the Fire. So the Prophet (ﷺ), before his mission, and those who were with him among the people, and before him, were addressed through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, before, regarding the monotheism of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but they were not addressed regarding the subsidiary branches of their legal codes, since these differ, and since no prophet called them to them. As for after the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ): is he and his community addressed by the law of those who came before? One group said: we are not addressed by any of that. Another group said: we are addressed by the law of those before us.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever among this group says that Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his community are addressed by all the laws of those who came before, without qualification, has spoken something impossible, because the rulings of the laws come differently. Rather, they adopt the view of those who said: We are obligated by what has been validly transmitted from the laws of those before us, and which the laws did not differ about, and by the last of what they differed about, since it is the latest abrogating (al-nasikh al-mutaqaddim). The validity of transmitting this is based on what occurred in the Qur'an and in the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by recounting earlier rulings, such as His saying: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [of grass] and strike with it﴾ [Sad 38:44]; and His saying: "Establish prayer for My remembrance"; and the account of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, marrying his daughter to Musa, peace be upon him; and the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the case of Sulayman, peace be upon him, between the two women regarding the child; and similar examples.

Their view does not necessitate more than the permissibility of being worshipped by that. As for the obligation to be worshipped by it, that is not necessary. And in my view, the closest analogy regarding this is to say: The Prophet (ﷺ) legislated for his community that a person should pray his prayer when he remembers it; then he cited in this regard, not as a form of reasoning (ta'lil), His saying, Mighty and Majestic, to Musa: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:14]. So we transfer this to other incidents and say: Just as the example of forgetting the prayer was legislated for us, so we legislate all these examples.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak analogy. Had the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned His saying, ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:14] as a form of reasoning, the proof from it would be strong. And it is not correct to say that the transmission of what is in the laws from the side of those among them who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others, is valid for us to transmit as valid; and likewise, what the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) legislated: there is no way to establish the validity of the law of 'Isa, peace be upon him, for him.

Ibn Kathir, the people of Makkah, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, the people of Madinah and 'Asim recited "iqtadih" with the pausal ha' (ha' al-sakt, the ha' of pause) maintained both in continuous recitation and at pause. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "iqtadi," saying: with the ha' dropped in continuous recitation and kept when pausing. This is the analogical form, since this ha' resembles the alif of connection (alif al-wasl), which is pronounced when beginning, and is joined when not beginning with it; thus this ha' is kept in pause and dropped in continuous recitation. Ibn 'Amir recited "iqtadihi," with a kasra on the ha', without extending to a ya'. Ibn Mujahid said: This is an error, because it is a ha' of pause, which is not inflected in any state. Abu 'Ali said: The explanation of this is that it may be the pronoun of the verbal noun (masdar), as if he said: "iqtadi al-iqtida'" (follow the following). Ibn Dhakwan recited it in this form, "iqtadihi," extending the vowel of the ya' after the ha'. Another group said: the kasra on the ha' is only on the ha' of pause, just as the ha' of the pronoun is sometimes made quiescent.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, and recitation with extension of the ya' is not permissible on this basis.

As for His saying, Exalted, ﴿Say: "I do not ask you…"﴾ and the rest of the verse: the meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad, to these stubborn disbelievers: I do not ask you, in return for my calling you with the Qur'an to the worship and monotheism of Allah, Exalted, for any reward that I would accumulate or from which I would benefit in this world. The Qur'an is nothing but an admonition, a reminder, and a call for all the worlds."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 91:

His statement, exalted is He:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything to a human being." Say, "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into pages, displaying them while concealing much; and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say, "God." Then leave them in their discourse, playing.﴾

The pronoun in "qadaru" (they measured) and "qalu" (they said): it is said that it refers to the Arabs; this was said by Mujahid and others. It is also said that it refers to the Children of Israel; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is also said that it refers to a specific man among them called Malik ibn al-Sayf; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. And it is said that it refers to Finhas; this was said by al-Suddi.

"Qadaru" is from giving something its due measure and standing, so it is general, encompassing whoever does not know (Allah), whoever does not exalt Him, and other things. However, their argument by saying "God has not sent down anything" necessitates that they were ignorant and did not know God the Exalted with His true knowledge, since they denied that He sends the messengers, peace be upon them. "Haqqa" is in the accusative as an adverbial object of an implied verb. As for the one who says the intended people are the disbelievers of the Arabs, the argument against them comes in His saying: ﴿who sent down the Book which Moses brought﴾, an argument based on a well-known matter, transmitted by a whole community to which the Arabs were not known to be deniers. As for the one who says the intended people are the Children of Israel, the argument against them is sound, because they affirm the validity of the descent of the Book upon Moses, peace be upon him.

It is narrated that Malik ibn al-Sayf was corpulent, so he came disputing with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, according to his claim. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him: "I adjure you by Allah, do you not read in what was sent down to Moses that Allah hates the fat rabbi?" He became angry and said: "By Allah, Allah has not sent down anything to a human being."

The verse, according to the view of the one who says it was revealed about the statement of the Children of Israel, must be Medinan; and al-Naqqash similarly related that it is Medinan. Al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi and others read "wa-ma qaddaru" with a shadda on the dal, and "Allaha haqqa qadrihi" with a fatha on the dal. The majority read the first with a light dal and the second with a sukun on it.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book..."﴾ up to the end of the verse: Allah commanded him to ask in the form of affirmation, directing to the point of proof. The intended "al-Kitab" is the Torah. "Nuran wa-hudan" are two nouns in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "illuminating and guiding." If we make it a circumstantial clause of "al-Kitab," the governing element is "anzala"; if we make it a circumstantial of the pronoun in "bihi," the governing element is "ja'a."

The majority of readers recited "taj'aluna-hu qarati sa tubdunaha wa-tukhfuna" with the ta' from above in the three verbs. Whoever holds that the argument is against the Children of Israel finds this reading sound and consistent with His statement, ﴿and you were taught what you did not know﴾. Whoever holds that the argument is only against the disbelievers of the Arabs is compelled in this reading, since it cannot be read otherwise, to say that it shifted from addressing the Quraysh in their questioning and affirmation to addressing the Children of Israel, rebuking them and rebuking their deeds.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This, despite its remoteness, is easier than rejecting the reading. So it is as if he (on this interpretation) said to the Quraysh: "Who sent down the Book upon Moses?" Then he turned to the Children of Israel and said to them, in the course of speech: "You, O Children of Israel, make it into pages." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "yaj'aluna-hu qarati sa yubdunaha wa-yukhfuna kathiran" with the ya' in the three verbs. Whoever sees the argument as directed at the Quraysh sees it as a report from Allah, exalted and majestic, about what the Jews did with the Book. It is possible that the report is addressed to the Quraysh, or to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, alone; and what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was informed of in the Qur'an, his community receives.

"Qaratis" is the plural of "qirtas," meaning sheets and leaves; the meaning is that they make it into something with sheets, in which it is written. Their rebuke for "displaying" and "concealing" is for their concealing of the signs of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the report of his prophethood, and everything in it that constitutes proof against them.

His statement: ﴿and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew﴾. Mujahid and others said: it is addressed to the Arabs. The meaning, according to this, is to mention Allah's favour upon them in this: "You, O company of Arabs, were taught guidance, monotheism, and direction to the truth, which you did not know, nor did your fathers."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and you were taught what you did not know﴾, on this meaning, is suitable for addressing both those who benefited from the teaching and those who did not benefit from it; and it is valid to bestow favour through the teaching of both groups. It is not a requirement that the one who is taught must teach in turn; but the complete teaching is that with which learning occurs.

A group said: rather, it is addressed to the Children of Israel, and the meaning on this view branches into two aspects. One is that it is intended as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, that they were taught the religion of Allah, exalted, and its guidance, which they had not known, because the fathers of the addressed Children of Israel had also been taught, and some of them had known; this is not the case with the fathers of the Arabs. The other aspect is that the intention is to blame them, i.e., "You and your fathers were taught what you did not know after the teaching, and you did not benefit from it, because of your aversion and your misguidance."

Then Allah, exalted, commanded him to hasten to the point of proof, i.e., "Say to them: Allah, exalted is He, is the One who sent down the Book upon Moses." It is possible that the meaning is: "If they are ignorant, or perplexed, or ask, or the like, then say: Allah." Then He commanded him to leave whoever disbelieved and turned away.

This verse is abrogated by the verse of fighting, if it is interpreted as a treaty of truce; and it is possible that abrogation does not enter it if it is taken to contain pure threat and warning, free of any truce.

"Al-khawd" is going into what its realities cannot be probed; its origin is in water, and then it is used for problematic, ambiguous meanings. "Yal'abun" is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 92:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed, confirming that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of the Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayer ever attentive.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, "And this": it refers to the Qur'an. "Blessed" is an attribute of it. "Confirming" [is an attribute] likewise. The nunation was dropped from "muṣaddiq" because of the construct (iḍāfa), and it is a non-definitive (ghayr maḥḍa) construct, by which "muṣaddiq" does not become definite; for this reason it is permissible for it to be an attribute of an indefinite noun. "Alladhī" is in the position of the object, and its governing element is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is not suitable that "muṣaddiq", even with the nunation dropped from it, should govern "alladhī", and that the dropping of the nunation be attributed to the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn); rather, that occurred as an anomaly in poetry, in his saying:

"I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering God except a little."

It is not to be analogized upon. "Between his hands" (bayna yadayhi) refers to the Torah and the Gospel, because what came before is between the hands of what came after. A group said: "What is between his hands" is the Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is not correct, because the Qur'an is itself between the hands of the Resurrection.

The majority read "wa-litundhira Umma al-Qura", meaning: "you, O Muhammad". Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, related from 'Asim: "wa-liyundhira", meaning the Qur'an, with its admonitions and its commands. The lām in "wa-litundhira" is connected to a verb that comes later, its estimated form being: "We sent it down that you may warn the Mother of the Cities and those around it."

The Mother of the Cities is Makkah. It was so named for four reasons: among them, that it is the origin of the religion and the Law; among them, what is related that the earth was spread out from it; among them, that it is the middle of the earth; and among them, what has reached us concerning the Law, that it is the qibla of every town. So it is, for all of this, a mother, and the rest of the towns are daughters. The estimated form of the verse is: "to warn the people of the Mother of the Cities", and "and those around it" intends the people of the rest of the earth. "Around it" is an adverbial of place, whose governing element is an implied verb, its estimated form being: "and whoever dwells around it."

Then, Blessed and Exalted is He began to praise a people, describing them and informing that they believe in the Hereafter, the Resurrection and the Gathering, and that they believe in the Qur'an and affirm its truth. Then, Blessed and Exalted is He strengthened their praise by [stating] that they are attentive to their prayer (ṣalāt), which is the foundation of the acts of worship and the mother of the acts of obedience.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, and Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, related from 'Asim: "ṣalawātihim" in the plural. Whoever reads it in the singular, it is a singular noun that indicates the plural. When ṣalāt is attached to a pronoun, it is written only with an alif, and it is not written in the muṣḥaf with a waw except when it is not attached to a pronoun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 93:

(p-419) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down"? If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels extend their hands, saying, "Discharge your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant towards His signs."﴾

These are general expressions. Whoever commits any of the things that fall under these expressions is included in the wrongdoing which Allah, exalted is He, has magnified by His saying "And who is more unjust", meaning: "No one is more unjust..." Qatadah and others said: what is meant by these verses is Musaylimah and al-Aswad al-'Ansi, and they mentioned the Prophet's (ﷺ) vision of the two bracelets (al-suwarayn). As-Suddi said: what is meant by them is 'Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh al-'Amiri, who used to write down the revelation for the Prophet (ﷺ), and who was the foster brother of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him). When the verses ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] ﴿then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a firm lodging﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13] ﴿then We made the sperm-drop into a clot, then We made the clot into a lump, then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] were revealed, 'Abdullah ibn Sa'd said, of his own accord: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Write it down, for it was thus revealed." 'Abdullah became suspicious, apostatised, joined Makkah, and said: "I send down the like of what Allah has sent down." It is also reported from him that "the Prophet (ﷺ) sometimes dictated to him: 'And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful', and he changed it himself to: 'And Allah is Hearing, Knowing'. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Both are the same.'" And similar to this.

(p-420) 'Ikrimah said: the first of them concerns Musaylimah, and the last concerns 'Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. Az-Zahrawi and al-Mahdawi mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning an-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he opposed the Qur'an with his saying: "By those who scatter in scattering, and those who bake bread, baking" and other such frivolities.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The commentators restricted the mention of these verses to a group of people who may have been the occasions of their revelation; but they apply, until the Day of Resurrection, to whoever engages in any of their meanings, such as Tulayhah al-Asadi, al-Mukhtar ibn Abi 'Ubayd, and others. Al-Jumhur recited ﴿sa-unzilu mithla ma anzala﴾ with a light (single-consonant) pronunciation of the nun (i.e., sa-unzilu, from anzala). Abu Haywah recited "sa-unazzilu", with a fatha on the nun and a shaddah on the zay.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers﴾, etc. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted; its estimate is: "you would see a marvel," or "a terror," or the like. Omitting this answer is more eloquent than stating it, because when the answer is not stated for the listener, it is left to his utmost imagination. "The wrongdoers" is a general term for whoever commits what has been mentioned before, and other kinds of wrongdoing which amount to disbelief. "Al-ghamarat" is the plural of "ghamrah", which is an ambiguous, bewildering calamity; it is likened to the surging of water (ghamrat al-ma'), and from it is the saying of the poet:

Nothing saves from the surges (al-ghamarat) except
the bara'ka of battle or flight

"And the angels" are the angels of taking the soul. ﴿Extending their hands﴾ is a metaphor for stretching them out with harm, as Exalted is He has said, relating the story of the two sons of Adam: ﴿If you stretch out your hand towards me to kill me﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 28]. This harm is, without doubt, the beginnings of punishment and its signs. Ibn 'Abbas said: they strike their faces and their backs. As for extending the hands merely for the taking of the soul, this is shared by the righteous and the disbelievers. It was also said: what is meant is the extending of hands in Hell, and the surges likewise, but they will not be given a decree that would cause them to die.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Discharge your souls﴾, is a report of what the angels say; the estimate is: "They say, discharge your souls." The angels' saying may mean: "So discharge your souls from these calamities and trials, and free them, if what you claimed in the world was true." In this there is rebuke and reminder of their past vile deeds. Al-Hasan said: this rebuke, in this sense, is in Hell. It may also be that it is meant in the sense of reproach and humiliation, as a man says to one whom he overpowers by himself regarding some matter: "Do such-and-such", for that matter which he himself is taking up from him in a manner of humiliation and instilling terror in him.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, etc.: this is a report of the angels' saying to the disbelievers at the taking of their souls. "Al-Hun" is al-hawan (humiliation), and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Isba':

"Away from me! My mother is no shepherdess
grazing the she-camels, nor do I acquiesce in humiliation (al-hun)."

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and 'Ikrimah recited "'adhab al-hawan" with an alif.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You used to say about Allah other than the truth﴾: this is a comprehensive expression for every kind of disbelief; but it becomes evident from it, and from His saying ﴿and for being arrogant towards His signs﴾, that the rebuke is directed at those mentioned just before, who claimed revelation and that they would send down the like of what Allah, Exalted is He, has sent down. For these are acts in which there is clearly the saying of what is other than the truth about Allah, Exalted is He, and in which arrogance is clearly evident.

[p. 422]

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verse 94**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you behind your backs. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners among you. Your ties have certainly been severed between you, and what you used to claim has strayed from you.﴾

This is a report of what will be said to them after their souls are taken, either at the moment their souls leave their bodies or on the Day of Resurrection. Both possibilities are valid.

"Furada" means one by one, individually. The alif at its end is the alif of feminine form. From this is the saying of the poet:

*You see the blue spear-points beneath his chest, singly and in pairs, his neighings have weakened them.*

[p. 422] Abu Haywa recited "furadan" with tanwin, on the pattern of "fu'alan." This is the dialect of Tamim. As for "furada," it is said to be the plural of "fardun" with a fatha on the ra', and it is also said to be the plural of "fardun" with a sukun on the ra'. The purpose of the verse is to confront the disbelievers with their isolation, their lack of helpers, and their need for God, Mighty and Majestic, now that their servants and intercessors are absent. Thus His saying ﴿as We created you the first time﴾ is a comparison with the first state of being alone at the time of creation. Another meaning may also be drawn: that His saying ﴿as We created you﴾ includes additional meanings beyond being alone, as if He said: "And you have certainly come to Us alone, and in such and such states." According to this view, the reference in His saying "as" is to what the Prophet (ﷺ) said about those who will be gathered: that they will be gathered barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised.

"Khawwalnakum" means "We gave you." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used to recite the verse of Zuhayr:

*There, if they are entrusted with wealth, they bestow it; if they are asked, they give; and if they become prosperous, they are lavish.*

"Behind your backs" is an allusion to the worldly life, because they leave those things behind as existing.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors﴾ and the rest of the verse, is a confrontation with their error in worshipping idols and venerating them. Al-Tabari said: It is related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he said: "Al-Lat and al-'Uzza will intercede for me."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Whoever among the Arabs believed that they intercede and bring one closer to God, Exalted, and considered them partners in this sense, then the address of the verse applies to them firmly, and this was the case for most of them. But whoever among them did not acknowledge any god other than them is not included in this verse.

[p. 423] Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read "baynukum" with a damma (raf'). Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "baynakum" with a fatha (nasb). As for the raf', it has several aspects. The first is that the zarf (adverbial noun of place or time) is used as a noun, and the verb is attributed to it, just as they used it as a noun in His saying ﴿a barrier between us and you﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and as in what Sibawayh related of their saying: "red between the eyes." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred this view. The second aspect is that some exegetes, among them al-Zahrawi, al-Mahdawi, Abu al-Fath and others, related that "al-bayn" in the language is used to mean separation and also to mean connection, so it is as if He said: "Your connection has certainly been severed."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: In my view there is an objection to this, because it has not been transmitted from the Arabs as heard usage; rather it was derived from the verse, and the verse is open to multiple meanings. Al-Khalil said in *al-'Ayn*: "Al-bayn means connection, based on His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Your ties have certainly been severed between you﴾." Here he justified the use of the word by the verse, and the verse is open to other interpretations. Abu al-Fath did strengthen the view that al-bayn means connection, and said: "Some scholars perfected this with the saying: 'The separation has been fair to the separation.'" The third aspect of the raf' is that "al-bayn" retains its original meaning of separation, from "baana, yabeenu," meaning it became distant. The verb "taqatta'a" in His saying is then used figuratively, similar to what is said of a distant matter in terms of distance: "The roads were cut off between such-and-such and such-and-such," as an expression for the great distance. The intended meaning is: "The distance has certainly been cut off between you because of its length." So the word "bayn," which means separation, is used to express that.

As for the reading with nasb, it is that the word is a zarf, and the verb is attributed to a deleted subject. Its estimate is: "The connection, or the bond, has certainly been severed between you," or something similar.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a clear aspect, and the people interpreted it accordingly: Mujahid, al-Suddi and others. Another aspect, which Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash held, is that the verb is attributed to the zarf, while the zarf remains in its accusative form, though in intention it is nominative. Similar to this in his view is His saying ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾ [al-Jinn: 11].

Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and al-A'mash read "taqatta'a ma baynakum," with the addition of "ma." "Dalla" means perished and departed. And ﴿what you used to claim﴾ refers to their claim that they intercede and share in divinity with God, Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 95–96:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ ﴿He is the Cleaver of the daybreak, and He made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

This is the beginning of an admonition to take heed and to reflect. The meaning connects with what precedes it, because the intent is "Indeed, Allah..." and not these idols. Mujahid and Abu Malik said: this refers to the split in the grain of wheat and the date-stone.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On this view, the lesson is restricted to some grains and some date-stones, and there is no basis for that. Al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others said: this refers to the action of Allah, the Exalted, in splitting every grain into the plant that comes from it, and splitting every date-stone into the trees that arise from it.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the apparent meaning, which gives the complete lesson. Glory be to the Creator, the All-Knowing.

Al-Dahhak said: "Faliq" means "Khaliq" (Creator). Al-Suddi and Abu Malik said: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ refers to the bringing forth of green plants and green trees from the dry grain and the dry date-stone; it is as though He made greenness and freshness life, and dryness death. ﴿And brings the dead out of the living﴾ refers to the bringing forth of dry plant matter and trees.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: rather, all of that refers to the bringing forth of a living human from a dead drop of semen, and the bringing forth of a dead drop of semen from a living human; and likewise all animals, birds, from eggs, fish, and all living creatures.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is more preferable. The proponents of the first view were drawn to the suitability of their interpretation with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾. On this preferred interpretation, the two are distinct meanings, each of which is valid. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: the believer brings out of the disbeliever, and the disbeliever out of the believer.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿That is Allah﴾: a subject and predicate, containing admonition. ﴿So how are you deluded?﴾ means: how are you turned away and diverted?

And ﴿Faliq al-Isbah﴾ means: its splitter and its revealer. Al-Falaq means the dawn (al-subh). The majority read "Faliq al-Isbah" with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu Raja' read "Faliq al-Asbah" with a fatha on the hamza, as the plural of "subh". A group read "Faliq al-Isbaha" with the tanwin dropped from "Faliq" because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters, and with "al-Isbah" in the accusative governed by "Faliq", as though he intended "Faliqun al-Isbaha" with tanwin on the qaf. This is an anomalous reading. Sibawayh permitted something like this only in poetry, and cited as evidence:

"Then I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering Allah except a little."

Al-Nahhas related from al-Mubarrad that this is permissible in ordinary speech. Abu Haywa, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Waththab read "Faliqa al-Isbah" as a past-tense verb. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' , Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "wa Ja'ilu al-layl" (and the Maker of the night); 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa ja'ala al-layl" (and He made the night). Since "Faliq" carries the sense of the past tense, it is as though the wording were "Faliqa al-Isbah wa ja'ala". The accusative of "al-shams wa al-qamar" supports this. The majority read "sakanan" (as rest); it is reported from Ya'qub as "sakinan", but Abu 'Amr al-Dani said that this is not sound from him. Its accusative, when we read "wa ja'ilu", is governed by an implied verb, since the participle has the sense of the past; the implied verb is taken as "wa ja'ilu al-layl yaj'aluhu sakanan" (and the Maker of the night makes it a rest). This is like your saying, "This is the giver of Zayd a dirham yesterday." What Abu 'Ali related on this is that it is governed by what is in the sentence of the meaning of "giver". Abu Haywa read "wa al-shamsi wa al-qamari" in the genitive, as a conjunction with the wording "al-layl".

"Husbanan" is the plural of "hisab", like "shuhban" is the plural of "shihab"; that is, they run by reckoning. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Qatadah and Mujahid. Mujahid said, in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: the meaning is a reckoning like the reckoning of the millstone, which is the wheel and the axle around which its turning revolves.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 97–98:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And it is He who has placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾ ﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul, and [for you there is] a place of lodging and a place of storing. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾

This address encompasses both believers and disbelievers; so the proof through it is established against the disbelievers, and the lesson through it is possible and open to the believers. "Ja'ala" (placed/made) here means "khalaqa" (created), because it takes a single object. It is also possible that it means "sayyara" (made/rendered), and the second object is understood in "li-tahtadu" (that you may be guided), since it can be read as: "And it is He who placed for you the stars as guidance." "Fi zulumat" (in the darknesses) here is in its literal sense: in the darkness of the night, by the indication of "the stars," which exist only at night. It is also valid that "the darknesses" here mean hardships, in the situations in which one happens to be guided by the sun.

Allah Most High mentions the stars for three benefits, and these are His saying: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]; His saying Most High: ﴿and We made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]; and His saying Most High: ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea.﴾ Therefore it is obligatory to believe that whatever is beyond these aspects, from the saying of the people of astrological influence, is false, a fabrication against Allah Most High, and disbelief in Him.

"Fassalna" (We have detailed) means: "We made clear and divided." "Al-ayat" (the signs) means: the proofs. And ﴿for a people who know﴾ is a specification of them by mention, and an alert from Him to their obtaining the detailed signs that have been set forth; as for others, the signs pass by them while they turn away from them.

His saying Most High: ﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul, and [for you there is] a place of lodging and a place of storing﴾, etc. "Al-insha'" (producing) is the doing of a thing. And ﴿from a single soul﴾ means Adam, peace be upon him.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fa-mustaqarr" with a fatha on the qaf, meaning a place of settling. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "fa-mustaqirr" with a kasra on the qaf, meaning an active participle. They all agreed on the fatha on the dal in "mustawda'" as a place of depositing, and it may also be taken as a passive/noun of place. This is not valid for "mustaqarr," because "istaqarra" is intransitive, so a noun of place cannot be formed from it as an object. As for Harun al-A'war's narration from Abu 'Amr: "wa-mustawdi'" with a kasra on the dal; whoever reads "fa-mustaqarr wa-mustawda'" (taking both as places of settling and depositing) attaches them to a prepositional phrase, its estimate being: "for you there is a place of settling and a place of depositing." Whoever reads "fa-mustaqirr wa-mustawda'" (with the active participle in "mustaqirr" and the passive participle in "mustawda'") attaches them to a prepositional phrase, its estimate being: "so from you there is one who settles and one who is deposited."

The interpreters differed on the meaning of this settling and depositing. The majority said: "The settled one is in the womb, and the deposited one is in the loins of the fathers, until Allah Most High decrees their emergence." Ibn 'Awn said: "I walked to the house of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i while he was ill, and they said: he has died. Then one of them informed me that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad asked him about 'mustaqarr wa-mustawda',' and he said: 'The settled one is in the womb, and the deposited one is in the spine.'" al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "The settled one is in the graves, and the deposited one is in the world." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The mustaqarr is the earth, and the mustawda' is with the womb." Ibn Jubayr said: "The mustawda' is in the loins, and the mustaqarr is in the Hereafter." What reflection requires is that the son of Adam is deposited in his father's back, and is not settled in it in an absolute sense, because he inevitably moves: he moves to the womb, then moves to the world, then moves to the grave, then moves to the place of gathering, then moves to Paradise or the Fire, where he settles in one of them in an absolute settlement, and there is no depositing in it, because he has no further movement. And he, in every intermediate station between these two states, is settled in relation to the one before it and deposited in relation to the one after it, because the word "wadi'ah" (deposit) necessarily implies a transfer.

And "yafqahun" means: they understand. The explanation of the like of this has already preceded shortly.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 99:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and by it We brought forth the vegetation of every thing, then We brought forth from it green growth, from which We bring forth grain piled up; and from the palm tree, from its spathe, are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapes, and the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar. Look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripening. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾

"Al-sama'" (the sky) in this place means the cloud; and everything that shades you is a sama' (sky). And "ma'" (water): its origin is "mawah." The waw moved and the letter before it was opened, so it became "mah," and the ha' was replaced with the hamza, for the sake of the hamza's firmness, because the alif and the ha' are weak and whispered sounds.

His saying: ﴿nabat kulli shay'﴾ (the vegetation of every thing). Some of the exegetes said: that is, of what grows. The general application of "every thing" is apt, because the mention of vegetation before it has restricted the intended meaning. But al-Tabari said: what is meant by "every thing" is what grows from all animals, plants, minerals and other things, because all of that is nourished and grows by the descent of water from the sky. The pronoun in "minhu" (from it) refers to the vegetation; in the second instance it refers to the green growth. "Khadiran" (green) carries the meaning of "akhdar" (green), and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The world is green and sweet," meaning: "green (khadra')."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems that "khadiran" always comes to signify freshness, and color has no place in it; "akhdar" is firmly about color, while in freshness it is a metaphorical usage.

His saying: ﴿grain piled up﴾ (habban mutarakiban) encompasses all ears of grain and what resembles them, such as the pine nut, the pomegranate, and other plants of every kind.

His exalted saying: ﴿And from the palm tree﴾: its implied sense is "and We bring forth from the palm tree." ﴿From its spathe, clusters﴾ is a nominal clause; its predicate is placed first, and the clause is in the position of the object of "We bring forth." "Al-tal'" is the first thing that emerges from the palm tree in its sheaths. "Qinwan" is the plural of "qinw," which is the "idhq" (cluster), with a kasra on the 'ayn, and it is the bunch. "Al-'urjun" is its stalk which holds the dates.

Al-A'raj read "qanwan" with a fatha on the qaf. Abu al-Fath said: it should be a noun of collective form that is not a broken plural, because "fa'lan" is not among the patterns of the plural. Al-Mahdawi said: it is also related from al-A'raj that he read with a damma on the qaf, because it is the plural of "qunw" with a damma on the qaf. Al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Qays and the people of the Hijaz, while the kasra is more famous among the Arabs. "Qinw" in the dual becomes "qinwan," with the nun being declinable. "Daniyah" means: near to the reach of the hand; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and al-Dahhak. It was also said: close to one another.

The majority read "wa-jannatin" with the accusative ending on "wa-jannatin," as a conjunction to His saying "nabat" (vegetation). Al-A'mash, Muhammad ibn Abi Layla, and what was transmitted from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) on the authority of 'Asim read "wa-jannatun" with the nominative, on the assumption of "and for you are gardens" or something similar. Al-Tabari said: it is conjoined to "qinwan."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: His saying is weak.

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate﴾ is in the accusative by consensus, as a conjunction to His saying "habban" (grain). And ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾: Qatadah said: its meaning is that they resemble one another in color and differ in fruit. Al-Tabari said: it is permissible that they resemble one another in fruit and differ in taste, and it is possible that he means: they resemble one another in taste and differ in appearance. These conditions are found, when considered, among the kinds of fruits.

His exalted saying ﴿"Look"﴾ is a sight of the eye that is followed by reflection of the heart. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read ﴿"ila thamarihi"﴾ (at its fruit) with a fatha on the tha' and the mim, and it is the plural of "thamarah," like "baqarah" and "baqar," and "shajarah" and "shajar." Yahya ibn Wathhab and Mujahid read "thumurihi," and they said: it means the kinds of property. (p-430)

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems that the meaning is: "Look at the wealth that is obtained from it." This is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Abu 'Ali said: The best view regarding it is that it is the plural of "thamarah," like "khashabah" and "khushub," and "akamah" and "ukam," and from it is the saying of the poet:

...... ∗∗∗ you see the hills in it prostrating to the hooves

Its counterpart in the defective (weak-letter) class is "labah" and "lub," "naqah" and "nuq," "sahah" and "suh." It is also permissible that it be the plural of a plural, so you say: "thamarah," "thimar," and "thumur," like "himar" and "humur." A group read "ila thumrihi" with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim, as though they sought lightness by making the mim quiescent. "Al-thamar" in the language is the fruit of trees and what emerges; and if trees are called "thimar," it is a figurative usage.

The majority of people read "wa-yan'ihi" with a fatha on the ya', and it is the verbal noun of "yana'a; yayna'u," when it ripens. It is said: "yana'a" and "ayna'a." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) explained this verse as ripening, and from it is the saying of al-Hajjaj: "Indeed I see heads that have ripened." "Yana'a" is also used to mean: "it stood out and became bright green." From it is the saying of the poet:

...... in domes around a mansion, around which the olive trees have ripened

It was also said regarding "yan'ihi" that it is the plural of "yani'," like "tajir" and "tajr," and "rakib" and "rakb." Al-Tabari mentioned this.

Ibn Muhaysin, Qatadah and al-Dahhak read "wa-yunihi" with a damma on the ya', meaning: its ripeness. Ibn Abi 'Ablah and al-Yamani read "wa-yani'ihi."

His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ is an emphatic statement of admonition and reminder, and the explanation of the like of it has preceded.

[p. 431]

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic:

﴿They ascribed to God partners, the jinn, though He created them, and they falsely attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glory be to Him, exalted above what they describe.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 103–105:

(p-433) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives [all] vision; and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.﴾ ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidences (basa'ir) from your Lord. So whoever sees, it is for his own benefit, and whoever is blind, it is to his own detriment. And I am not a guardian over you.﴾ ﴿Thus do We vary the verses, so that they may say, "You have studied [them]," and that We may make it clear to a people who know.﴾

The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) have agreed that Allah, blessed and exalted, will be seen on the Day of Resurrection; the believers will see Him. This was also related by Ibn Wahb from Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. The method is to demonstrate that such vision is rationally possible, and then to rely on the revealed text (al-sam') for the occurrence of that possible matter. A concise demonstration of this is drawn from our knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted: since it is possible for us to know Him without being in a place, nor being spatially confined, nor being opposite (to something), and since our knowledge is not attached to more than existence, it is possible that we see Him without being opposite, nor enclosed, nor in a modality, nor bounded. The Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Nahwi used to say: "The question of knowledge (of Allah) has shaved the beards of the Mu'tazilah; then the Law came with this," and that is His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking at their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] The transitivity of "naẓar" with "ilā" in the speech of the Arabs only signifies the meaning of sight (ru'yah), not the meaning of waiting (intizar), as the Mu'tazilah claimed. This position was attributed to Malik, and he said: "Where then are they from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, indeed they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15]?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He argued by the indication of the discourse (dalil al-khitab), mentioned by al-Naqqash. And from it is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in what is authentically and widely reported and transmitted abundantly: "Indeed you will see your Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as you see the moon on the night of the full moon," and similar hadiths, with variation in the wording.

(p-434) The Mu'tazilah went to prohibit the possibility of seeing Allah, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and to deem it impossible, relying on mere opinions. They held fast to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No vision can perceive Him.﴾ The People of the Sunnah answered their argument by saying that the verse is specific to this world, while the vision in the Hereafter is established by reports about it.

Another answer is to distinguish between the meaning of "idrak" (perception) and the meaning of "ru'yah" (seeing). We say: He, mighty and majestic, is seen by the eyes but not perceived by them. Perception (idrak) includes encompassing a thing, reaching its depths, and surrounding it from all its directions, and all of that is impossible with respect to the attributes of Allah, mighty and majestic. Seeing does not require that the seer encompass the seen and reach its limit. On this interpretation, the converse is consequently implied in His saying: ﴿and He perceives [all] vision,﴾ and its meaning is made beautiful. Something similar was related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, who distinguished between seeing and perception. As for al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, he also distinguished between seeing and perception, and argued by the saying of the Children of Israel: "Indeed we are overtaken (lamudrakun)," and said: they saw them but did not perceive them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All of this is erroneous, because this perception is not the perception of sight; rather it is borrowed from it, or it is a homonym (bi-ishtirak). He said: Some of them said: the believers see Allah, the Exalted, by a sixth sense that will be created on the Day of Resurrection, and this verse remains, in its prohibition of perception by eyes in general, unimpaired. He said: Some of them said: this verse is specific to the disbelievers, meaning: "Their eyes will not perceive Him, because they are veiled from Him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All these opinions are weak, claims that are not supported by any Qur'an or hadith.

"Al-Latif" means the one who is gentle (mutalattif) in His creation, His origination, His perfecting, and in His dealings with His creatures and servants. "Al-Khabir" means the one who tests (al-mukhtabir) the inner matters of people and their outer ones.

"Al-basa'ir" is the plural of "basirah," which is what results from the intellect's attainment of things considered through reflection. It is as if He said: "There has come to you in the Qur'an and the verses the paths of seeing the truth and what helps toward it."

(p-435) And "basirah" for the heart is borrowed from the sight of the eye. "Basirah" is also the established belief, in the saying of the poet:

"They went, their insights upon their shoulders, and my insight runs with it, a swift and sturdy steed."

Some people said regarding this line: "basirah" means the trail of blood; the poet describes a group who set out in pursuit of blood, then slackened, and placed the matter behind their backs.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"whoever sees"﴾ and ﴿"whoever is blind"﴾ are metaphorical expressions for whoever is guided and whoever goes astray. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾ was at the beginning of the matter, before Islam became dominant; then after that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became a guardian over the world, taking them to Islam by the sword.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"Thus do We vary the verses, so that they may say, 'You have studied [them]'"﴾, to the end of the verse: the kaf in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿"Thus"﴾ is in a position of accusative governed by "nuṣarrifu" (We vary). That is: just as We have made the insights clear and other things, We vary the verses, i.e., We repeat them and clarify them. A group read: "wa-liyaqūlū darasta" with the lam sukun, in the form of a command, which carries the meaning of rebuke and threat. The majority read: "wa-liyaqūlū" with the lam kasra, taking it as the lam of "kay" (purpose); and it is, on this reading, the lam of ṣayrūrah (consequence), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]; that is: "when their affair came to that." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 103–105:

(p-433) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives [all] vision; and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.﴾ ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidences (basa'ir) from your Lord. So whoever sees, it is for his own benefit, and whoever is blind, it is to his own detriment. And I am not a guardian over you.﴾ ﴿Thus do We vary the verses, so that they may say, "You have studied [them]," and that We may make it clear to a people who know.﴾

The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) have agreed that Allah, blessed and exalted, will be seen on the Day of Resurrection; the believers will see Him. This was also related by Ibn Wahb from Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. The method is to demonstrate that such vision is rationally possible, and then to rely on the revealed text (al-sam') for the occurrence of that possible matter. A concise demonstration of this is drawn from our knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted: since it is possible for us to know Him without being in a place, nor being spatially confined, nor being opposite (to something), and since our knowledge is not attached to more than existence, it is possible that we see Him without being opposite, nor enclosed, nor in a modality, nor bounded. The Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Nahwi used to say: "The question of knowledge (of Allah) has shaved the beards of the Mu'tazilah; then the Law came with this," and that is His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking at their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] The transitivity of "naẓar" with "ilā" in the speech of the Arabs only signifies the meaning of sight (ru'yah), not the meaning of waiting (intizar), as the Mu'tazilah claimed. This position was attributed to Malik, and he said: "Where then are they from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, indeed they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15]?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He argued by the indication of the discourse (dalil al-khitab), mentioned by al-Naqqash. And from it is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in what is authentically and widely reported and transmitted abundantly: "Indeed you will see your Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as you see the moon on the night of the full moon," and similar hadiths, with variation in the wording.

(p-434) The Mu'tazilah went to prohibit the possibility of seeing Allah, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and to deem it impossible, relying on mere opinions. They held fast to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No vision can perceive Him.﴾ The People of the Sunnah answered their argument by saying that the verse is specific to this world, while the vision in the Hereafter is established by reports about it.

Another answer is to distinguish between the meaning of "idrak" (perception) and the meaning of "ru'yah" (seeing). We say: He, mighty and majestic, is seen by the eyes but not perceived by them. Perception (idrak) includes encompassing a thing, reaching its depths, and surrounding it from all its directions, and all of that is impossible with respect to the attributes of Allah, mighty and majestic. Seeing does not require that the seer encompass the seen and reach its limit. He said: Some of them said: the believers see Allah, the Exalted, by a sixth sense that will be created on the Day of Resurrection, and this verse remains, in its prohibition of perception by eyes in general, unimpaired. **Ibn 'Atiyya:** His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord. There is no god but Him. And turn away from the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated others with Him. We have not made you a guardian over them, nor are you a custodian over them.﴾ ﴿Do not revile those who call upon other than God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge. These are two commands to the Prophet (ﷺ). Their content is limiting himself to following the revelation and maintaining a truce with the disbelievers. This was at the beginning of Islam. Then turning away from them was abrogated (naskh) by fighting them and driving them to the religion, willingly or unwillingly.

This implies that their polytheism and everything else depends on the will of God, may He be exalted and glorified.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿We have not made you a guardian over them﴾: this was at the beginning of Islam, and likewise ﴿nor are you a custodian over them﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The reason for it was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said to Abu Talib: 'Either Muhammad and his companions stop reviling our gods and disparaging them, or we will revile his God and satirize him.' So the verse was revealed." Its ruling remains in the community in every circumstance. Whenever the disbeliever is in a position of strength, and it is feared that he might revile Islam, or the Prophet (ﷺ), or God, may He be exalted, then it is not permissible for a Muslim to revile their religion or their crosses, nor to expose himself to anything that would lead to that or something similar. He referred to the idols, which do not understand, with the word "those who" (alladhina), in accordance with the belief of the disbelievers concerning them. In this verse there is a kind of truce.

The majority of readers read ﴿'adwan﴾ (عَدْوًا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a sukun on the dal. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), from "transgression" (al-i'tida'). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu Rija', Qatada, Ya'qub, Salam, and 'Abdullah ibn Zayd read ﴿'udwan﴾ (عُدُوًّا) with a damma on the ʿayn and the dal, and a shadda on the waw. This is also in the accusative as a verbal noun, from the same root. Some Kufan readers read ﴿'aduwwan﴾ (عَدُوًّا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a damma on the dal. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning "in a state of enmity toward God, may He be exalted." It is a singular word that indicates the plural.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿without knowledge﴾: this is an explanation of the meaning of the transgression mentioned earlier.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community﴾: this refers to what God, may He be exalted, made attractive to these idol-worshippers, namely clinging to the idols and defending them. God's making the deeds of nations attractive is what He creates and invents in souls of love for good or evil, and following its paths. The devil's making things attractive is by what he casts into souls of whisperings and evil suggestions.

His words: ﴿Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them﴾: this contains a beautiful promise for the good-doers and a severe threat for the evildoers.
