(p-438) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And they swore by God their most solemn oaths that if a sign should come to them, they would surely believe in it. Say: "Signs are only with God." And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾ ﴿And We turn about their hearts and their sight, just as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"and they swore"﴾, refers back to the polytheists mentioned earlier. "Jahd" (solemnly, with utmost effort) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its governing element is ﴿"and they swore"﴾ according to the school of Sibawayh, since it carries the same meaning; according to the school of Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad, it is a verb from the same root. The lam in His saying ﴿"la-in"﴾ is the lam preceding the oath (lam al-muwaṭṭi'a, the "preparatory lam"), signalling the oath. As for the lam that follows the oath, it is in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿"la-yu'minunna"﴾. "Āya" here means a sign (ʿalāma).

It is related that when the verse ﴿"If We wish, We shall send down upon them a sign from the heaven, so their necks would remain humbly bowed before it"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4] was revealed, the unbelievers swore at that time that if it were sent down they would believe; so this verse was revealed. It is also related that they proposed that al-Safa be turned into gold, and swore to that effect. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up supplicating about this, and Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him and said: "If you wish, it will become gold; but if they do not believe, they will be destroyed entirely at once, as was done to the nations when they did not believe in the proposed signs. And if you wish, they will be delayed until whoever among them repents." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, until whoever among them repents." Then this verse was revealed. Ibn Muṣarrif recited ﴿"la-yu'manna"﴾ with a fatḥa on the mīm and nūn, and with the light nūn.

Then He said: "Say to them, O Muhammad, by way of rebuttal and correction: Signs are only in the hand of God, Exalted is He, and with Him; they are not with me, so that they may be demanded of me." Then He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿"And what will make you aware"﴾. The commentators differed about who is addressed by His saying ﴿"And what will make you aware"﴾, and who is the questioner in the word ﴿"what" (mā)﴾, to which the pronoun, the subject in ﴿"yush'irukum"﴾, refers? Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: the addressees are the unbelievers. al-Farra' and others said: the addressees are the believers; ﴿"wa-mā yush'irukum"﴾ means ﴿"wa-mā yu'limukum?"﴾ and ﴿"wa-mā yudrikum?"﴾. Some read ﴿"yush'irkum"﴾ with a sukūn on the rā', which is a lightening; and what makes it preferable is that the movement goes from a kasra to a ḍamma.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim, in the narration of Dawud al-Iyadi, read ﴿"innaha"﴾ with a kasra on the alif, as a resumption (qaṭ') and a fresh statement. Whoever reads ﴿"tu'minun"﴾ with the tā' (this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Hamza) keeps the address to the unbelievers consistent at the beginning and the end. Whoever reads ﴿"yu'minun"﴾ with the yā' (this is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i) may be understood to address the believers at the beginning and end; or it may be understood that the address in ﴿"wa-mā yush'irukum"﴾ is to the unbelievers, and then the statement about them is resumed for the believers. The second object of ﴿"yush'irukum"﴾ is omitted, and its estimation varies according to each interpretation.

Nafi', 'Asim in the narration of Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿"anna-ha"﴾ with a fatḥa on the alif. Some of them took it as ﴿"anna"﴾ which enters upon sentences and comes after verbs such as "I knew" and "I thought," and ﴿"yush'irukum"﴾ governs it. Some held that the ﴿"lā"﴾ in His saying ﴿"lā yu'minun"﴾ is superfluous, and that the meaning of the speech is: "And what will make you aware that when they come they will believe?" or "they will believe," so ﴿"lā"﴾ was added, as it was added in His saying ﴿"And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 95], because the meaning is: "And the return of the destroyed town is forbidden." It also occurs in the verse of the poet:

Ābā jūduhu lā al-bukhla wa-stajalat bihi / "naʿam" min fatan lā yamna'u al-jūda qātilah

Al-Zajjaj said: he meant "his generosity refused stinginess," just as it occurs as superfluous in the verse of the poet:

Afa-minka lā barqun ka-anna wamīḍahu / ghābun tasannamahu ḍirāmun muthaqqab

Maintaining this view was motivated by preserving the meaning, for if it were not superfluous the speech would become an excuse for the unbelievers and the intended sense of the verse would be corrupted. Al-Zajjaj and others weakened the notion that ﴿"lā"﴾ is superfluous, and said: this is an error. Some took ﴿"anna-ha"﴾ to mean ﴿"la'alla-ha"﴾ ("perhaps"), and Sibawayh related this from al-Khalil; it is an interpretation which does not require positing a superfluous ﴿"lā"﴾. Al-Kisa'i related that it is so in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: ﴿"wa-mā adrākum la'allaha idhā jā'at lā yu'minun"﴾. From this sense is the verse of the poet:

Qultu li-Shaybān udnu min liqā'ihi / anna tughaddhī al-qawma min shiwā'ihi

All of these carry the meaning of "perhaps." Abu 'Ali weakened this, on the grounds that the expectation it contains does not suit the verse that follows, which rules that they will not believe. In his view the more preferred reading is that ﴿"anna"﴾ retains its own function, and that the meaning is: "Say: signs are only with God, because when they come they will not believe"; that is, He does not bring them, because of their persistence in their disbelief. The verse then resembles His saying ﴿"And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them"﴾ [al-Isra': 59], i.e., "the proposed signs." Abu 'Ali also held that ﴿"lā"﴾ is superfluous, and expanded on his evidence for this.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, says: It follows from this interpretation that ﴿"wa-mā"﴾ would be negative; Abu 'Ali mentioned this, so consider it. Some exegetes related that at the end of the verse there is an omission which dispenses with positing a superfluous ﴿"lā"﴾ or interpreting it as "perhaps"; its estimation according to them is: "that when they come, they will not believe, or they will believe."

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, says: This view is weak; the wording of the verse does not support it nor require it. The verse may bear the sense that it includes information that they will not believe, and it is said to them: "What will make you aware of this reality?" That is: there is no way for you to become aware of it; it is true in itself, and they would not believe even if it came. On this interpretation, ﴿"wa-mā"﴾ is interrogative. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿"wa-mā yush'irukum idhā jā'at lā yu'minun"﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"And We turn about their hearts and their sight, just as they did not believe in it"﴾. The meaning, according to one group, is: "And We turn about their hearts and their sight in the Fire and in its blaze in the Hereafter, because they did not believe in this world." Then, on this reading, He resumes: ﴿"and We leave them"﴾ in this world, ﴿"in their transgression, wandering blindly."﴾

Another group said: the turning about (taqlib) means only a diversion from the truth and guidance, and leaving them in misguidance and disbelief. The meaning of the verse is: "These people who swore that they would believe if a sign came—We turn about their hearts and their sight, so that if it came they would not believe in it, just as they did not believe the first time, in what they were called to of worshipping God, Exalted is He." Thus God, on this interpretation, informs about the manner of His action toward them.

Abu Raja' read ﴿"yadharuhum"﴾ with a yā'; it is also transmitted from 'Asim. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read ﴿"wa-yuqallibu"﴾ and ﴿"wa-yadharuhum"﴾ with a yā' in both, as a reference to God, Blessed and Exalted is He. He also read, as related from him by Mughira: ﴿"wa-taqallaba"﴾ with a fatḥa on the tā' and lām, meaning "their hearts and their sights turn about," with a ḍamma on both; ﴿"wa-yadharhum"﴾ with a yā' and a jazm on the rā'.

Another group said: the word ﴿"kamā"﴾ in this verse is in fact in the sense of recompense (mujāzāh), i.e., "because they did not believe the first time, We will repay them by turning their hearts away from guidance and sealing upon their hearts." It is as though He, Glorified is He, said: "And We turn about their hearts and their sight as recompense, because they did not believe the first time, in what they were called to of the Law."

The pronoun in ﴿"bihi"﴾ may refer to God, Majestic and Exalted is He, or to the Qur'an, or to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿"Wa-nadharuhum"﴾ means: we leave them. Al-A'mash and al-Hamadhani read ﴿"wa-yadharhum"﴾ with a yā' and a jazm on the rā', as a lightened form.

"Al-ṭughyān" is excessive floundering in evil and overindulgence in what a person seizes upon; "al-ʿamā" is hesitation and bewilderment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 111–112:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them and We gathered against them all things before them, they would not have believed unless Allah willed; but most of them are ignorant.﴾ ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy – devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with embellished speech as deception. And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they invent.﴾

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informs in this verse that even if He brought about everything they proposed – the sending down of angels, the reviving of their forebears, such as what some of them proposed, that Qusayy and others be resurrected so that they would testify to the truthfulness of Muhammad, or that every thing that could be conceived of being gathered before them be assembled – they would not believe, except by the will and the subtle grace which the Exalted creates and brings into being in the soul of whomever He wills, there being no lord besides Him. This implies a refutation of the Mu'tazilah in their claim regarding signs that compel the disbelievers to faith. Ibn Juraij said: this verse was revealed concerning those who mocked. The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is not established except by a chain of transmission.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, and others, read "qibalan" (قِبَلًا) with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning "confrontation and direct witnessing." This is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Al-Mubarrad said the meaning is "a direction (nāḥiyah)," as one says, "I have a debt in the presence of so-and-so" (lī qibala fulānin dayn).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: its accusative, according to this, is as an adverb of place (ẓarf).

'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and others read "qubulan" (قُبُلًا) with a damma on the qaf and the ba'. Likewise Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it here. And one reading has "al-'adhāba qibalan" (الْعَذَابَ قِبَلًا) with a kasra on the qaf, and its meaning has been disputed. 'Abdullah ibn Zayd, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "qubul" is the plural of "qabil," meaning category upon category and kind upon kind, just as "qadib" is pluralized as "qudub." Others said it is the plural of "qabil," which means "guarantor (kafil)," that is: "and We gather against them every thing as guarantors of the truthfulness of Muhammad, Allah bless him and give him peace." Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said this. Al-Farisi mentioned it and declared it weak. Some said: "qubul," with a damma, has the same meaning as "qibal," with a kasra, that is "confrontation," as one says "qubula" and "dubura," and from it is the saying of the Exalted, ﴿torn from the front [qubul]﴾ [Yusuf: 26]. And from it is the reading of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "li-qubuli 'iddatihinna" (لِقُبُلِ عِدَّتِهِنَّ), meaning "for facing their waiting period" and confronting it in time. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Abu Haywah read "qubulan" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', by way of lightening. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "qabalan" with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ba'. Ubayy and al-A'mash read "qabilan" with a fatha on the qaf, a kasra on the ba', and an added ya'. As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿but most of them are ignorant﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers mentioned earlier, and the meaning is: "they are ignorant that the verse necessitates their faith, without fail." The wording thus implies that the minority are not ignorant; there were among them those who believed that even if the signs came, they would not believe unless Allah, Exalted is He, willed that for them.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet﴾ and what follows: it contains consolation for the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, and presents to him a model. That is: "What you have been tested with, O Muhammad, of enemies, other prophets have been tested with too, so that Allah, Exalted is He, may try the resolute ones among them (ulu al-'azm)." "Enemy" ('aduwwan) is singular in meaning plural; it is in the accusative as the first object of "ja'alna" (We made), and the second object is in His saying, "for every prophet." "Shayatin" (devils) is an apposition to His saying, Glorified is He, "enemy." It is also permissible for "shayatin" to be the first object and "enemy" the second. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾, by it is meant the rebellious of both kinds, who possess the traits of evil, like the devils. This is the view of a group of exegetes, and it is supported by the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he once prayed and the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, said to him: "Seek refuge, O Abu Dharr, from the devils of jinn and mankind." He said: "Are there devils among mankind?" He said: "Yes." Al-Suddi and 'Ikrimah said: the devils are those assigned to mankind, and the devils assigned to the believing jinn. They claimed that the jinn have devils assigned to misguiding them, and that they inspire the devils of mankind with evil and whispering, learning it from one another. They said: there are no devils among mankind.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is a view that rests neither on a report nor on reasoning.

"Yuhi" (inspires) means he casts it covertly, so it is like secret conversation and whispering. "Zukhruf al-qawl" (embellished speech) means: adorning it and decorating it with falsehoods, said 'Ikrimah and Mujahid. Ornamentation is mostly used for evil and falsehood. "Ghurur" (deception) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and its meaning is that they incite the misguided with it and make them imagine that they are upon something when the matter is otherwise. The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, "fa'aluhu" (they did it), refers to their conviction of enmity, and it may refer to the inspiring implied by "yuhi."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so leave them and what they invent﴾: this is an expression containing a command to tolerance, abrogated by the verses of fighting. Qatadah said: every "dhar" in the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, is abrogated by fighting. "Yaftaruna" means "they differ and fabricate," and it derives from "al-fira," by analogy with tearing a hide (fary al-adim).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 113–114:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may commit what they are committing.﴾ ﴿Shall I seek other than Allah as a judge, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book, detailed? And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth, so do not be of the doubters.﴾

﴿Wa-li-taṣgha ilayhi﴾ (and that it may incline to it): its meaning is "li-tamīla" (that it may incline). One says ṣagha, yaṣghā; its原 form is yuṣghī (with a kasra on the ghayn), but the guttural letter has been restored to a fatha. It is also said ṣagha, yaṣghū; aṣgha, yuṣghī; and ṣaghiya, yaṣghā.

"Afʾidah" (hearts) is the plural of "fu'ād" (heart). "Yaqtarifūn" means "yuwāqi'ūn" (they commit) and "yajtariḥūn" (they perpetrate). It is used mostly for evil, sins and the like.

The readers recite the lam in the three verbs with a kasra, as the lam of "kay" (purpose). Either it is coordinated with "ghurūran" (as deception), or it is connected to a delayed verb whose implied sense is "they did that" or "We made that happen," in which case it is the lam of result (ṣayrūrah). This is what al-Zajjāj said. It is not possible that these lams, on this reading, are the lam of command with the sense of threat; and it remains in "wa-li-taṣgha," in the manner of what came in that regard in the verse of the poet: "Did there not come to you..." (verse cited), and other readings recited with it. Abu al-Fath said: al-Hasan recited them with sukūn in all three, and it is the lam of purpose, coordinated with His saying "ghurūran," the sense being: "for the sake of deception; and that it may incline..." The sukūn of this lam is rare in usage but strong in analogy.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It appears that al-Hasan's reading, with sukūn on the three lams, should be taken as the lam of command implying warning and threat. The written form on this reading is "wa-l-tasgha." Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that his sukūn was in all three lams, and so did Abu al-Fath; and he mentioned that al-Hasan only made the second and third lams sukūn.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That contradicts the written form of the Mushaf in "wa-li-taṣgha."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It results that the lam in "wa-li-taṣgha" may be made sukūn, according to what we mentioned in the reading of the majority. Abu 'Amr said: al-Hasan's reading is only "li-taṣghiya" with a kasra on the ghayn; and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i's reading is "li-tuṣghiya" with a damma on the taʾ and a kasra on the ghayn, from "aṣgha, yuṣghī"; and al-Jarrah ibn 'Abd Allah also recited thus.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Afa-ghayra": it is in the accusative governed by "abtaghī." "Ḥakaman" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) or explanation (bayān). "Mufaṣṣalan" means: the ambiguity is removed; its verses have been made distinct. Although the meaning of this verse is general, in that Allah Exalted is not to be sought as a judge other than Him in every matter and every case, we need, in describing the speech and the coherence of the meanings, to look to a matter preceding it which serves as the cause of His saying, ﴿Shall I seek other than Allah as a judge?﴾. It is, Allah knows best, His judgment against them that they do not believe, even if He sent them every sign; and His judgment in making enemies for the prophets among the jinn and humankind. And "ḥakaman" is more emphatic than "ḥākiman," since it is a form denoting justice from among judges; whereas "al-ḥākim" follows the verb, so it may be said of one who is unjust. "Ḥakaman" is in the accusative as a specification or a circumstantial state.

With this verse the Kharijites disputed with 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding his declaring them unbelievers over the arbitration. But they have no proof, because Allah Exalted has Himself made judgment in the matter of game and between the spouses; so the arbitration of the believers is part of His judgment, Exalted is He.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾: it includes calling upon their believers as witnesses, and a rebuke and admonition regarding their polytheists and envious ones.

Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim recited "munazzalun" with tashdid; the rest with takhfif. "Al-kitāb" the first time is the Qur'an; the second time it is a generic noun: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scriptures. Describing the People of the Book as having knowledge is a general statement with the meaning of the specific; it refers only to their scholars and rabbis.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not be of the doubters﴾: it is a affirmation, an emphasis, and a rebuke of the doubters.

(p-447) ﴿"Wa-tammat"﴾ here means "continued, and was established from eternity as truthful and just." It does not mean "completed" in the sense of lacking something. A similar usage occurs in the Sira in the saying "wa-tamma Hamzah 'ala Islamih" ("Hamzah persisted in his Islam"), in the hadith concerning Abu Jahl.

"Al-kalimat" refers to what was revealed to His servants. ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kalimat" in the singular here, in Yunus in both places, and in Ha Mim al-Mu'min. Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read all of these in the plural, "kalimat." Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read the plural only in this place. Al-Tabari held that it means the Qur'an, as one says "kalimat fulan" for a poem or an eloquent sermon.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "In my view this is far-fetched and open to objection. The intended meaning is rather an expression of the binding force of His words, 'sidqan' (in truth) regarding what they contain of information, and 'adlan' (in justice) regarding what they contain of rulings. Both are verbal nouns in the position of the circumstantial accusative (hal). Al-Tabari said they are in the accusative of specification (tamyiz), but this is not correct." The phrase ﴿lā mubaddila li-kalimatihi﴾ ("none can alter His words") means: in their meanings, such that someone would show that His information is contrary to what He reported, or show that His command is not enforced. An example of this is that Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿"If Allah returns you to a group of them, and they ask your permission to go out"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83], up to ﴿"the ones who stay behind"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83]. Then the hypocrites said after that to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers: ﴿"Leave us, that we may follow you"﴾ [al-Fath: 15]. Then Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿"They want to change the word of Allah. Say: You will not follow us; thus has Allah said before"﴾ [al-Fath: 15]. Or it refers to His saying ﴿"Say: You will never go out with me, ever"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83], because its content is a report that they will not be permitted to go out. As for the wording, the Children of Israel did alter and change it. This is the view of a group of scholars. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they altered it only through interpretation (ta'wil). The first view is more likely correct. In the codex (harf) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb the reading is: "lā mubaddila li-kalimati Allah."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"If you obey most of those on earth"﴾, and the rest of the verse: the meaning is, "Proceed, O Muhammad, with what you have been commanded, and carry out your message, for if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray." He, glorified is He, said "most" (akthar) because the people of the earth at that time were mostly disbelievers, and the believers were only a small number.

(p-448) Ibn ʿAbbas said: "'Al-ard' (the earth) here means the world (al-dunya)." It is related that the cause of this verse was that the polytheists disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning slaughtered animals, saying: "You eat what you kill, and you leave what Allah has killed?" So the verse was revealed. He, Exalted is He, described them as following their own assumptions and pursuing their guesswork. "Al-kharṣ" (guesswork) means estimation (al-hazr) and conjecture (al-zann).

Most readers read ﴿"yaḍill"﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "yuḍill" with a damma on the ya'. Ahmad ibn Abi Shurayh transmitted this from al-Kisa'i. The "man" in His saying ﴿"man yaḍill"﴾ is in the accusative position by a hidden verb, its estimated form being "yaʿlamu man" ("He knows who"). It was also said to be in the nominative position, as if he said, "Whoever (ayy) strays from His path." Abu al-Fath mentioned this, and Abu ʿAli considered it weak. **Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-An'am, verses 118–119**

(p. 449) Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to? Indeed, many [people] lead [others] astray by their desires without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾

The purpose of this verse is the prohibition of what is slaughtered for idols (nusub) and other than Allah, and of carrion (maytah) and its kinds. The wording comes as a command to do the opposite of what is prohibited. The verse does not intend the case of a believer who forgets to say the basmalah (tasmiyah), or who deliberately omits it. 'Ata' said: this verse is a command to mention the name of Allah, the Exalted, over drink, food, slaughter, and everything that is eaten. The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿if you are believers in His signs﴾ mean: "if you are taking up His rulings and His commands." Belief in them entails and requires acting upon them and submitting to them.

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat﴾, and the rest of the verse: "wa-ma" here is an interrogative (istifham) that carries the sense of affirmation (taqrir). The construction of this sentence is: "And what is it for you in not eating?" The phrase "an" (that) is in the genitive position, with the preposition (harf al-jarr) understood. It may also be in the accusative position, if no preposition is understood, and the governing element is the sense of the verb in the words of Allah, ﴿"And what is [the matter] with you"﴾; its implied sense is: "What prevents you, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden?" That is, the forbidden has already been made clear to you from the permitted, and doubt and confusion have been removed from you.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿وَقَدْ فُصِّلَ لَكُمْ مَا حُرِّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (wa-qad fussila lakum ma hurrima 'alaykum) with the verbs in the passive voice in both places. Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿وَقَدْ فَصَّلَ﴾ (wa-qad fassala) with the verb in the active voice in both places. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), from 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿وَقَدْ فَصَّلَ﴾ with the verb in the active voice, and ﴿لَكُمْ مَا حُرِّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ with the verb in the passive voice. 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi read ﴿وَقَدْ فَصَلَ﴾ with the verb in the active voice and the sad vowelled with a fatha and lightened (fasala, without doubling), and ﴿مَا حُرِّمَ﴾ in the passive voice. The meaning is: He has distinguished the forbidden from the permitted and separated it out by clarification.

The "ma" in the words of Allah, ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾, is intended to mean: from all that has been forbidden, such as carrion and others. It is in the accusative position as an exception, and the exception is disjunctive (istithna' munqati', an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it).

As for the words of Allah, ﴿"And indeed, many"﴾, they refer to the disbelieving opponents who dispute about foods, by what we have mentioned of their saying: "You eat what you slaughter, and you do not eat what Allah has slaughtered?" Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿لَيَضِلُّونَ﴾ (layadilluna) with a fatha on the ya', meaning that the misguidance is attributed to them themselves. This is the case in this surah; and in Yunus: ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead astray﴾ [Yunus 10:88]; in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿rivals, that they may lead astray﴾ [Ibrahim 14:30]; in al-Hajj: ﴿turning aside his side, to lead astray﴾ [al-Hajj 22:9]; in Luqman: ﴿to lead astray from the way of Allah without knowledge﴾ [Luqman 31:6]; and in al-Zumar: ﴿rivals, to lead astray﴾ [al-Zumar 39:8]. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read likewise in this verse and in Yunus, and in the four that follow it they vowel the ya' with a damma, meaning that the misguidance of others is attributed to them. This is more forceful in censuring them, because every one who misguides is himself astray, but not every one who is astray misguides others. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i, in the six places, read ﴿لَيُضِلُّونَ﴾ with a damma on the ya', meaning that the misguidance of others is attributed to them.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, explained that their misguidance is of the most reprehensible kind, that it is by desire and not by reflection and consideration. The phrase ﴿without knowledge﴾ means: without reflection. Whoever goes astray through reflection has some excuse, but that does not benefit one in claiming that he exerted effort (ijtihad).

(p. 450) Then He threatened them, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾

(p. 450) Then He threatened them, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾

"The Exalted, the Majestic, said:

﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾

This is a prohibition general from both its ends, because sin (al-ithm) encompasses the rulings and the attributes attached to the disobedient regarding all acts of disobedience; and the outward (al-zahir) and the inward (al-batin) together cover all acts of disobedience. However, those who interpret the verse have held that it is among those general statements that are specified (mukhassas). So al-Suddi said: its outward is the well-known fornication that the Arabs used to practise, and its inward is taking secret lovers (ittikhadh al-akhdan). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the outward is what Allah the Exalted has explicitly forbidden of women, by His saying ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa: 23], and the verse continues; and His saying ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾ [al-Nisa: 22], and the verse continues; and the inward is fornication.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: he means the nakedness that the Arabs used to practise during their circumambulation (tawaf). Some people said: the outward is the actions, and the inward is the belief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: and this is good, because it is general.

Then the Exalted threatened those who earn sin with requital for what they have acquired of that, and who bear its burden. And "al-iqtiraf" means al-iktisab (acquiring/earning).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 121:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is defiance. And indeed, the devils inspire to their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, indeed you would be associates [of Allah].﴾

The purpose of this verse is the prohibition of carrion (maytah), since it is a reply to the saying of the polytheists: "You eat what you kill yourselves, but not what Allah kills?" The verse also prohibits what is slaughtered for idols (al-ansab). Nevertheless, its wording is general and includes animals over which the tasmiyah (invoking the name of Allah) was omitted from the slaughter of Muslims. Muhammad ibn Sirin, 'Abdullah ibn 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Nafi', 'Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Khatmi, al-Sha'bi, and others held to this generality. Thus, whatever over which the tasmiyah was omitted, whether through forgetfulness or deliberately, is not to be eaten. A great group of the scholars said: what is slaughtered and over which the tasmiyah was not said through forgetfulness may be eaten, and what over which it was not said deliberately may not be eaten. This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). Al-Zahrawi related from Malik ibn Anas that he said: the slaughtered animal over which the tasmiyah was omitted, whether deliberately or through forgetfulness, may be eaten. This is also related from Rabi'ah. 'Abd al-Wahhab said: the tasmiyah is a sunnah (recommended practice). If the slaughterer omits it through forgetfulness, the animal may be eaten, according to the view of Malik and his companions. If he omits it deliberately, Malik said: it may not be eaten. Some of his companions understood his saying "it may not be eaten" as meaning prohibition (tahrim), while others understood it as disapproval (karahah). Ashhab said: the slaughter of one who deliberately omits the tasmiyah may be eaten, unless he is one who treats it lightly. Al-Tabari said something similar.

According to the majority of scholars, the slaughter of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) falls under the ruling of what has had the name of Allah Most High mentioned over it, inasmuch as they have a religion and a law. Some people said that the slaughter of the People of the Book was abrogated (nusikha) from this verse; this was said by Ikrimah and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan.

The pronoun in "wa-innahu" (﴿and indeed it﴾) in ﴿and indeed it is defiance﴾ refers to the eating (al-akl) contained in the verb in His saying ﴿and do not eat﴾. It is also possible that it refers to "non-mention" (tark al-dhikr), which is contained in His saying "over which the name has not been mentioned" (lam yudhkar). "Fisq" (defiance) means going out of obedience; this is its usage in the Law (shar').

As for His saying ﴿And indeed, the devils﴾ and the rest of the verse: Ikrimah said that by "the devils" in this verse is meant the rebellious humans (maradat al-ins) among the Magians (majus) of Persia, because they used to side with the Quraysh in their enmity towards the Prophet (ﷺ). They addressed them, drawing attention to the argument we mentioned concerning slaughter, by their saying: "You eat what you kill, but you do not eat what Allah kills?" That address of theirs is the "inspiration" (wahy) meant, the "allies" are associates, and "dispute" is that argument. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and 'Abdullah ibn Kathir said: rather, the devils are the jinn, and the word is to be taken in its literal sense. The unbelieving jinn are allies of the unbelieving Quraysh, and their inspiration to them was by whispering, until they inspired them with that argument, or through the tongues of soothsayers (kuhhan). Abu Zumayl said: I was with Ibn 'Abbas when a man came to him and said: "Abu Ishaq (meaning al-Mukhtar) claims that revelation came to him last night." Ibn 'Abbas said: "He spoke the truth." So I recoiled, and Ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿"And indeed, the devils inspire to their allies."﴾

Then Allah Most High forbade obeying them, in wording that contains a threat, and presented the most severe example, in that He likened a believer to a polytheist. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) an opinion that those who disputed with that argument were a people from among the Jews.

The Qadi Abu Sa'id (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak, because the Jews do not eat carrion. However, it is conceivable that they did this from them by way of sophistry, as if they were arguing on behalf of the Arabs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 122–123:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, from which he cannot emerge? Thus has what they used to do been made attractive to the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And thus We have placed in every town its greatest criminals so they may plot therein. But they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾

In the preceding verse there was mention of a group of believers who were commanded to abandon outward and inward sin, and other matters, and mention of a group of disbelievers who go astray by their desires, and other matters. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave an example for both groups: He likened those who believed after their disbelief to dead people who were brought to life. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and Mujahid and others. And He likened the disbelievers and the bewilderment of their ignorance to people in darkness who wander therein and cannot leave it, so that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, might make clear the distinction between the two groups and the gulf between the two states.

The majority of readers recited "أوَمَن" (a'a-man) with a fatha on the waw, so the first is the interrogative alif (hamzat al-istifham) entering upon the conjunctive waw that links one sentence to another, and "مَن" is in the sense of "الَّذِي" (alladhi, "the one who"). Talha ibn Musarrif recited "أفَمَن" (afa-man) with a fa', and the meaning is close to that of the waw. The fa' in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"فَأحْيَيْناهُ"﴾ is conjunctive. As for ﴿"نُورًا"﴾ (light), the most apt interpretation of it is faith (al-iman). As for ﴿"يَمْشِي بِهِ"﴾ (walks by it), it is intended to mean the entire conduct in deeds and words. Abu 'Ali said: It is also possible that what is intended is the light that the believers will be given on the Day of Resurrection. As for ﴿"فِي الناسِ"﴾ (among the people), it is connected to "يَمْشِي" (walks), and it is valid for it to be connected to "كانَ مَيْتًا" (was dead). His saying, Exalted is He, (p-453) ﴿"كَمَن مَثَلُهُ"﴾ (like one whose likeness is), is in the sense of "كَمَن هُوَ" (like one who is). The kaf in His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ زُيِّنَ﴾ (thus has ... been made attractive) is connected to a deleted element that the apparent wording of the speech indicates; its estimated form is: "Just as We gave life to the believers and made for them a light, thus has it been made attractive to the disbelievers..." It is also possible that it is connected to His saying, Exalted is He, "كَمَن مَثَلُهُ" (like one whose likeness is), i.e., "in the manner of this state is the making-attractive."

Nafi' alone recited "مَيِّتًا" (mayyitan) with a kasra on the ya' and its doubling, while the rest recited "مَيْتًا" (maytan) with a sukun on the ya'. Abu 'Ali said: the light form is like the heavy form, and the deleted ya' is the second one, which was converted from a waw; it was elided by deletion just as it was elided by conversion.

A group said: although these expressions that are used as examples apply to every believer and every disbeliever, they were revealed concerning specific persons. Al-Dahhak said: the believer who was dead and then was given life is 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Mahdawi related from some of them that it is Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him. 'Ikrima said: it is 'Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Zajjaj said: it has come in the tafsir that it refers to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: They agreed that the one who is in darkness is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and the indication and the comparison refer to his state and the states of his likes, by His saying, ﴿And thus We have placed in every town﴾. This verse contains a warning of the corruption of the state of the disbelievers mentioned earlier, because it is the requirement of the state of those who preceded them of their counterparts. 'Ikrima said: this verse was revealed concerning those who mocked.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He means that the comparison is for them, and "جَعَلْنا" (We placed) in this verse is in the sense of "صَيَّرْنا" (We made), so it transitively takes two objects. The first object is ﴿"مُجْرِمِيها"﴾ (its criminals), and the second is "أكابِرَ" (greatest). In the speech, according to this, there is an inversion: its estimated form is "And thus We have placed in every town its criminals as greatest," and the more important is placed first, since it is because of their greatness that they committed crimes. It is also valid that the first object is "أكابِرَ" (greatest) and "مُجْرِمِيها" (its criminals) is an annexed construction, and the second object is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿فِي كُلِّ قَرْيَةٍ﴾ (in every town); and "لِيَمْكُرُوا" (so they may plot) is in the accusative by the lam of becoming (lam al-sayrura).

"الأكابِرُ" (al-akabir) is the plural of "أكْبَرُ" (akbar), as "الْأفاضِلُ" (al-afadil) is the plural of "أفْضَلُ" (afdal). It is also said "أكابِرَةٌ" (akabira), as "أحْمَرُ" (ahmar) has "أحامِرَةٌ" (ahamira). From this is the saying of the poet: (p-454)

؎ Indeed the three "reddish ones" have destroyed my wealth, and I was formerly devoted to them.

He means: wine, meat, and saffron. "اَلْمَكْرُ" (al-makr) is devising by falsehood, deception, and the like. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿وَما يَمْكُرُونَ إلا بِأنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (but they plot only against themselves), means: because the consequence of that returns upon them. "وَما يَشْعُرُونَ" (and they do not perceive), i.e., they do not know. It is a word derived from "الشِعار" (al-shi'ar), which is the garment that touches the body; so it is as if one who does not perceive has been denied knowing by sensory knowledge. In this there is an emphasis on the description of their ignorance, since animals know sensory knowledge. As for this verse, perception is negated in it concerning a specific event.

**Verses 124–125**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿When a sign comes to them, they say, "We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah." Allah knows best where to place His message. Those who committed crimes will be struck with humiliation before Allah and a severe punishment for what they used to scheme.﴾ ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe.﴾

This verse is a censure of the disbelievers and a warning to them. It means: when a sign and proof of the soundness of the Law comes to them, they overstep the bounds, shrink back, and say, "Only let the sea be split for us, only let the dead be brought to life for us," and similar things. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answers them with His saying, ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾, meaning: among those whom He chooses and selects, not among those who disbelieve. They keep overstepping against Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Zajjaj said: Some of them said, "The most eloquent proof of the truthfulness of the messengers is that before their mission they were not obeyed among their people." The word "a'lam" (knows best) is a suspended verb, and the governing verb of "ḥaythu" (where) is a verb whose implied form is: "He knows where..."

Then Allah, Exalted is He, threatens that these great criminals will be struck, in this world, with humiliation and abasement before Allah, Exalted is He. "Before Allah" is connected to "will strike." It is also permissible for it to be connected to "ṣaghār" (humiliation), because it is a verbal noun. Al-Zajjaj said: The implied meaning is: humiliation is established before Allah, Exalted is He. Abu 'Ali said: It is connected to "ṣaghār" alone, without an implied "is established" or anything else.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾, and the rest of the verse: "man" (whoever) is a conditional particle, and "yashraḥ" (He expands) is the answer of the condition. The verse is explicit that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills the guidance of the believer and the misguidance of the disbeliever. According to all the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the adherents of the prophetic way), this is by the eternal will, which is one of the attributes of His essence, blessed and exalted is He.

"Guidance" (al-hudā) in this verse is the creation of faith in the heart and its origination. Expanding the breast is the facilitation of faith, making it beloved, and preparing the heart to accept it and attain it. The word "hudā" is a shared term (lafẓa mushtaraka): it comes with the meaning of "invitation," as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]; and it comes with the meaning of guiding the believers to the paths of the gardens and to the ways and deeds that lead to them, as in His saying: ﴿He will not let their deeds be lost﴾ [Muhammad: 4] ﴿He will guide them and set their affairs right﴾ [Muhammad: 5], and other instances. However, in this verse, and in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the guided one, and whomever He leaves astray, they are the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 178], and in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56], and similar verses, it is not appropriate to interpret it except as the creation of faith and its origination, since the other senses of guidance are rejected by the context of the speech before and after it.

His saying, ﴿He expands his breast﴾: these are borrowed expressions here. "Sharḥ" (expansion) originally means widening and spreading in bodies. When a body is expanded and widened, it is prepared to be dwelt in. So the making ready and illumination of the heart, and its preparation to accept, is compared to expansion and widening, and its acceptance and attainment of faith is compared to dwelling in an expanded body. "Ṣadr" (breast) is an expression for the heart, and this is what is intended, since faith is among its qualities. Likewise, "Islam" here is an expression for faith, since Islam is more general than it; what is intended here is faith alone, as shown by the context of the expansion and guidance. But it was expressed by "Islam" because it is more general. The lowest level of guidance is the love of deeds and the carrying out of acts of worship. In "yashraḥ" there is a pronoun referring back to "guidance." He said: Its referring back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is clearer.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The view that the pronoun refers to the one guided is a view upon which the doctrine of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree over human acts) is built concerning the creation of actions. It should be held to be weak. The pronoun refers to the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since this is supported by both the wording and the meaning. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when this verse was revealed, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is the breast expanded?" He said: "When light enters the heart, the breast expands and becomes spacious." They said: "Is there a sign of that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes: turning toward the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it comes."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And whomever He wills to leave astray﴾, the discussion is like the discussion of His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide﴾. His saying, ﴿He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾, are borrowed expressions opposite to the expansion of the breast for Islam. "Yajʿal" (He makes) here means "He judges him by this judgment," as you say: "This makes Basra a city (miṣr)," meaning: it judges it by its judgment.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning is close to "ṣayyara" (He makes/turns into). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi related it and also said: It is permissible for "ja'ala" to mean "sammā" (He names), as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], meaning "they named them." He said: This verse may bear this meaning.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is weak in this verse.

The majority of people, and the Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers), except Ibn Kathir, read "ḍayyiqan" with a kasra on the ya and its shadda (doubling). Ibn Kathir read "ḍayqan" with a sukun on the ya, and he read the same in al-Furqan. Abu 'Ali said: They are equivalent to "al-mayyit" and "al-mayt" (the dead). Al-Tabari said: They are equivalent to "al-hayyin" and "al-layyin" and "al-hayn" and "al-layn." He said: It is also possible that "al-ḍayq" is a verbal noun from your saying: "The matter became tight (ḍāqa al-amr, yaḍīqu, ḍayqan, wa ḍīqan)." It is reported from al-Kisa'i that he said: "al-ḍīq" with a doubled and kasra-ed ḍād is used for physical bodies and livelihood, and "al-ḍayq" with a fatha on the ḍād is used for affairs and meanings.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ḥarajan" with a fatha on the ra. Nafi' and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, read "ḥarijan" with a kasra. Abu 'Ali said: Whoever reads the ra with a fatha, it is a descriptive of the verbal noun, as you say: "a man who is fit (qamanun) for such-and-such," "ḥaraysh for such-and-such," and "danafun." Whoever reads the ra with a kasra, it is like "danifun," "qamin," and "farigh." It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, once read it with a fatha on the ra, and one of the Companions recited it to him with a kasra on the ra. He said: "Bring me a man from Kinana, and let him be a shepherd from the Banu Mudlij." When he came, he said to him: "O young man, what is the ḥarajah among you?" He said: "It is the tree that grows among other trees, which neither a shepherd nor a wild animal can reach." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Likewise is the heart of the hypocrite; nothing of good reaches it."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿as if he were climbing into the sky﴾: that is, as if this one with the constricted breast is trying to ascend into the sky whenever he tries to believe or reflects upon it, and finds its difficulty upon him like the difficulty of climbing into the sky. Ibn Jurayj, 'Ata' al-Khurasani and al-Suddi said this interpretation. Ibn Jubayr said: The meaning is: he finds no path except one that is steep, from the severity of his constriction.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yaṣṣaʿʿadu," with the ta assimilated into the ṣād, from "yatasaʿʿadu" (yataṣaʿʿadu). 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, read "yaṣṣāʿadu," with the ta assimilated, from "yatasāʿadu fi al-samā'." Ibn Kathir alone read "yaṣʿadu." Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash and Ibn Musarrif read "yataṣaʿʿadu," with an added ta.

"Fī al-samā'" (into the sky) means: from below to above in the air. Abu 'Ali said: It does not refer to the very canopy of the sky; rather, as Sibawayh said: "al-qaydud" is "the tall one in other than a sky," meaning, in other than an elevation, "ṣaʿadan" (steeply). He said: From this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ [al-Baqara: 144], meaning, in the directions of the atmosphere.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is according to those who do not interpret "the turning of the face" as supplication to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for guidance to a qibla. For with supplication it is proper that one turns his face toward the canopied sky, according to the habit of supplicators, since they are accustomed to blessings and bounties coming from that direction. The verse may also mean that the comparison is to one who climbs a steep ascent, as if he were climbing with it into the air. "Yaṣʿadu" means "he rises," and "yaṣṣaʿʿadu" means "he burdens himself with what is hard for him." From this is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "Nothing has burdened me as much as the proposal of marriage (khuṭbat al-nikāḥ) has burdened me." There are other examples. "Yaṣṣāʿadu" in meaning is like "yaṣṣaʿʿadu."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Thus does Allah place defilement﴾: that is, just as all of this, guidance and misguidance, happened by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His decree, so does Allah place the rijs (defilement). The lexicographers said: "Rijs" comes with the meaning of punishment, and it comes with the meaning of impurity (najas). Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he said: "Rijs" is everything that has no good in it. Some of the Kufans said: "Rijs" and "najas" are two dialects with the same meaning. "Yajʿal" here may well mean "yulqī" (He casts), as you say: "I placed your goods one upon another (ja'altu matā'aka ba'ḍahu 'alā ba'ḍ)," and as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And He puts the wicked one upon another﴾ [al-Anfal: 37].

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning for "ja'ala" was related by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. It is also good that "yajʿal" in this verse means "yuṣayyir" (He makes), and that the second object is implied in "upon those who do not believe," as if He said, glorified is He: "a companion of those who..." or "one bound to those who..." and similar.

Expanding the breast is the facilitation of faith, making it beloved, and preparing the heart to accept it and attain it. The word "hudā" is a shared term (lafẓa mushtaraka): it comes with the meaning of "invitation," as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]; and it comes with the meaning of guiding the believers to the paths of the gardens and to the ways and deeds that lead to them, as in His saying: ﴿He will not let their deeds be lost﴾ [Muhammad: 4] ﴿He will guide them and set their affairs right﴾ [Muhammad: 5], and other instances. However, in this verse, and in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the guided one, and whomever He leaves astray, they are the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 178], and in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56], and similar verses, it is not appropriate to interpret it except as the creation of faith and its origination, since the other senses of guidance are rejected by the context of the speech before and after it.

His saying, ﴿He expands his breast﴾: these are borrowed expressions here. "Sharḥ" (expansion) originally means widening and spreading in bodies. When a body is expanded and widened, it is prepared to be dwelt in. So the making ready and illumination of the heart, and its preparation to accept, is compared to expansion and widening, and its acceptance and attainment of faith is compared to dwelling in an expanded body. "Ṣadr" (breast) is an expression for the heart, and this is what is intended, since faith is among its qualities. Likewise, "Islam" here is an expression for faith, since Islam is more general than it; what is intended here is faith alone, as shown by the context of the expansion and guidance. But it was expressed by "Islam" because it is more general. The lowest level of guidance is the love of deeds and the carrying out of acts of worship. In "yashraḥ" there is a pronoun referring back to "guidance." He said: Its referring back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is clearer.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The view that the pronoun refers to the one guided is a view upon which the doctrine of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree over human acts) is built concerning the creation of actions. It should be held to be weak. The pronoun refers to the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since this is supported by both the wording and the meaning. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when this verse was revealed, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is the breast expanded?" He said: "When light enters the heart, the breast expands and becomes spacious." They said: "Is there a sign of that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes: turning toward the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it comes."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And whomever He wills to leave astray﴾, the discussion is like the discussion of His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide﴾. His saying, ﴿He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾, are borrowed expressions opposite to the expansion of the breast for Islam. "Yajʿal" (He makes) here means "He judges him by this judgment," as you say: "This makes Basra a city (miṣr)," meaning: it judges it by its judgment.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning is close to "ṣayyara" (He makes/turns into). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi related it and also said: It is permissible for "ja'ala" to mean "sammā" (He names), as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], meaning "they named them." He said: This verse may bear this meaning.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is weak in this verse.

The majority of people, and the Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers), except Ibn Kathir, read "ḍayyiqan" with a kasra on the ya and its shadda (doubling). Ibn Kathir read "ḍayqan" with a sukun on the ya, and he read the same in al-Furqan. Abu 'Ali said: They are equivalent to "al-mayyit" and "al-mayt" (the dead). Al-Tabari said: They are equivalent to "al-hayyin" and "al-layyin" and "al-hayn" and "al-layn." He said: It is also possible that "al-ḍayq" is a verbal noun from your saying: "The matter became tight (ḍāqa al-amr, yaḍīqu, ḍayqan, wa ḍīqan)." It is reported from al-Kisa'i that he said: "al-ḍīq" with a doubled and kasra-ed ḍād is used for physical bodies and livelihood, and "al-ḍayq" with a fatha on the ḍād is used for affairs and meanings.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ḥarajan" with a fatha on the ra. Nafi' and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, read "ḥarijan" with a kasra. Abu 'Ali said: Whoever reads the ra with a fatha, it is a descriptive of the verbal noun, as you say: "a man who is fit (qamanun) for such-and-such," "ḥaraysh for such-and-such," and "danafun." Whoever reads the ra with a kasra, it is like "danifun," "qamin," and "farigh." It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, once read it with a fatha on the ra, and one of the Companions recited it to him with a kasra on the ra. He said: "Bring me a man from Kinana, and let him be a shepherd from the Banu Mudlij." When he came, he said to him: "O young man, what is the ḥarajah among you?" He said: "It is the tree that grows among other trees, which neither a shepherd nor a wild animal can reach." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Likewise is the heart of the hypocrite; nothing of good reaches it."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿as if he were climbing into the sky﴾: that is, as if this one with the constricted breast is trying to ascend into the sky whenever he tries to believe or reflects upon it, and finds its difficulty upon him like the difficulty of climbing into the sky. Ibn Jurayj, 'Ata' al-Khurasani and al-Suddi said this interpretation. Ibn Jubayr said: The meaning is: he finds no path except one that is steep, from the severity of his constriction.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yaṣṣaʿʿadu," with the ta assimilated into the ṣād, from "yatasaʿʿadu" (yataṣaʿʿadu). 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, read "yaṣṣāʿadu," with the ta assimilated, from "yatasāʿadu fi al-samā'." Ibn Kathir alone read "yaṣʿadu." Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash and Ibn Musarrif read "yataṣaʿʿadu," with an added ta.

"Fī al-samā'" (into the sky) means: from below to above in the air. Abu 'Ali said: It does not refer to the very canopy of the sky; rather, as Sibawayh said: "al-qaydud" is "the tall one in other than a sky," meaning, in other than an elevation, "ṣaʿadan" (steeply). He said: From this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ [al-Baqara: 144], meaning, in the directions of the atmosphere.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is according to those who do not interpret "the turning of the face" as supplication to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for guidance to a qibla. For with supplication it is proper that one turns his face toward the canopied sky, according to the habit of supplicators, since they are accustomed to blessings and bounties coming from that direction. The verse may also mean that the comparison is to one who climbs a steep ascent, as if he were climbing with it into the air. "Yaṣʿadu" means "he rises," and "yaṣṣaʿʿadu" means "he burdens himself with what is hard for him." From this is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "Nothing has burdened me as much as the proposal of marriage (khuṭbat al-nikāḥ) has burdened me." There are other examples. "Yaṣṣāʿadu" in meaning is like "yaṣṣaʿʿadu."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Thus does Allah place defilement﴾: that is, just as all of this, guidance and misguidance, happened by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His decree, so does Allah place the rijs (defilement). The lexicographers said: "Rijs" comes with the meaning of punishment, and it comes with the meaning of impurity (najas). Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he said: "Rijs" is everything that has no good in it. Some of the Kufans said: "Rijs" and "najas" are two dialects with the same meaning. "Yajʿal" here may well mean "yulqī" (He casts), as you say: "I placed your goods one upon another (ja'altu matā'aka ba'ḍahu 'alā ba'ḍ)," and as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And He puts the wicked one upon another﴾ [al-Anfal: 37].

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning for "ja'ala" was related by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. It is also good that "yajʿal" in this verse means "yuṣayyir" (He makes), and that the second object is implied in "upon those who do not believe," as if He said, glorified is He: "a companion of those who..." or "one bound to those who..." and similar.

"Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:"

﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight. We have detailed the signs for a people who remember.﴾ ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace (dar al-salam) with their Lord, and He is their Protector (waliyyuhum) because of what they used to do.﴾

"Wa hadha" (and this): a reference to the Qur'an and to the law (al-shar') that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. "Al-sirat" (the path): the road. The attribution of the path to the Lord (idafat al-sirat ila al-Rabb) is in the sense that it comes from Him, the Exalted, and by His command. "Mustaqiman" (straight): a emphatic circumstantial qualifier (hal mu'akkidah). It is not like the circumstantial qualifier in your saying, "Zayd came riding" (ja'a Zaydun rakiban); rather, this emphatic qualifier contains the intended meaning.

"Fassalna" (We have detailed): its meaning is: We made clear and explained. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿for a people who remember﴾: that is, for the believers who prepare themselves for reflection and take the way of guidance. The pronoun in His saying, the Exalted, "lahum" (for them), refers back to the people who remember. As for "al-Salam" (the Peace), two meanings are possible. The first is that "al-Salam" is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, so the Abode is attributed to Him, since it is His possession and His creation. The second is that it is the verbal noun (masdar) meaning "al-salamah" (safety), as you say, "al-salamu 'alayka" (peace be upon you), and as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their greeting therein will be peace﴾ [Ibrahim: 23], meaning in the Hereafter, after the Gathering. "Waliyyuhum" (their Protector): that is, the Protector of the favour bestowed upon them. And ﴿because of what they used to do﴾: that is, because of what they used to put forward of good and to perform of obedience and righteousness.

(p-460) "Wa-yawma" (And [mention] the Day): it is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb, whose assumed sense is "And mention the Day of..." It is also possible that the governing word is "waliyyuhum" (their allies), with the phrase being coordinated with the position of "bima kanu" (for what they used to do). The pronoun in "yahshuruhum" (He will gather them) refers to the two groups upon whom Allah places the abomination: all the disbelievers, jinn and humans, and those for whom is the Abode of Peace, jinn and humans. The general emphasis expressed by the words "jami'an" (all of them) indicates this.

Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "yahshuruhum" with the letter ya (yahshuru); the rest read it with the letter nun (nahshuru). Both are valid.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic is He, mentioned what will be said to the disbelieving jinn. There is an implied verb in the speech, indicated by the apparent meaning of the speech; its assumed sense is "We will say, O assembly of jinn..." The words of Allah, "qad istakthartum" (you have acquired a great deal), mean "you have been excessive" (or "you have gone too far"). "Min al-ins" (from among humans) means "in their misguidance and leading them astray," as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. The disbelievers among humans, who are the allies of the reproached jinn, said by way of excusing the jinn: ﴿Our Lord, some of us have enjoyed others﴾, that is, benefited.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This happens in many ways. Al-Tabari and others related that humans used to seek refuge with the jinn in valleys and places of fear, and the jinn would become exalted over humans and dominate them, just as the Arab does with the soothsayer, and the protector with the one seeking protection. When an Arab descended into a valley he would call out, "O Lord of the valley, I seek refuge with You this night," and then he would consider that his safety came only through the protection of the jinn of that valley. This is the enjoyment of some of them by others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is an example of enjoyment, and if it were investigated, other aspects would become clear, all of them worldly.

As for "the reaching of the appointed term," al-Suddi said: It is death, to which all of them have arrived. It was also said: it is the gathering (resurrection). And it was said: it is the end to which all of them have arrived of the enjoyment, as if they were indicating that this is by Your decree and Your judgment, since every matter has its appointed term. Al-Hasan read "wa-ballighna ajalana" with a kasra on the lam, doubled.

(p-461) The words of Allah, ﴿He will say, "The Fire is your abode, abiding therein forever, except what Allah wills"﴾ and so on, are a report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of what He will say to them on the Day of Resurrection, following their earlier speech. The verb came in the past tense, though in reality it refers to the future, because its occurrence is certain. This is common in the Qur'an and in eloquent speech. "Mathwakum" means the place of your reward, like your station (muqamukum), which is the place of dwelling. This is the statement of al-Zajjaj and others. Abu 'Ali said in "al-Ighfal": "al-mathwa," in my view, is a verbal noun with no place of its own, because it governs the state in which "khalidin" (abiding) is, whereas a place has no sense of a verb, so it could not govern; and the assumed sense is "the Fire is the possessor of your abiding."

As for the exception in the words of Allah, ﴿except what Allah wills﴾, one group said: "ma" here means "man" (whoever), so the intended meaning is: "except those whom Allah wills, from among those who believed in this world after having disbelieved, from among these disbelievers."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Since these are a category, the use of "ma" for them is acceptable. Al-Farra' said: "illa" means "siwa" (other than), and the intended meaning is "other than what He wills of increase in punishment." Al-Zajjaj inclined to this view. Al-Tabari said: the excepted part is the period between their gathering and their entry into the Fire.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is acceptable on the basis of the expression in the words of Allah, ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾, which by its form does not restrict itself to the future tense to the exclusion of other tenses. Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he understood this exception as the final state of these people in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. It is then attributed to him that he said: this verse is one that no one should use to judge Allah concerning His creation, [claiming] that He will not cause them to enter Paradise or the Fire.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: There is consensus on the eternal abiding of the disbelievers, and this report from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) is not authentic.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In my view, the more probable interpretation of this exception is that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, and it is not something said on the Day of Resurrection. The excepted party are those among the disbelievers who, in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, would believe on that day. It is as if, when He informed them (p-462) that He said to the disbelievers, ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾, He made an exception for them of those among them who could possibly believe.

And ﴿Wise, All-Knowing﴾ are two attributes appropriate to this verse, because the eternal abiding of these disbelievers in the Fire is an act issuing from wisdom and knowledge of the proper placement of things.

The words of Allah, ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾: Qatada said: "nuwalli" means "We make some of them allies of others in disbelief and wrongdoing."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This interpretation is supported by what preceded concerning the jinn and humans and the enjoyment of some of them by others. Qatada also said: the meaning of "nuwalli" is "We cause some of them to follow others into entering the Fire," that is, "We make some of them follow others." Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "We empower some of the wrongdoers over others, and make them agents of retribution against them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This interpretation is not supported by the wording of the preceding verse. However, it is preserved in the usage of the Companions and the Successors. Among that is what is reported: when 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) was informed that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan had killed 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq, he ascended the pulpit and said: "Indeed, the mouth of the fly has killed the spoiled child of Satan." And ﴿Thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others for what they used to earn﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 130–132:

His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He:

﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?” They will say, “We bear witness against ourselves.” And the worldly life had deluded them, and they will bear witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers.﴾ ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people are unaware.﴾ ﴿And for each are degrees from what they have done. And your Lord is not unaware of what they do.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾: it is included in the address on the Day of Gathering. The pronoun in (p-463) "minkum" (from among you): Ibn Jurayj said: the two groups are included by its apparent meaning, and what is meant is one of them, by way of metonymy (tajawwuz). This is found in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is His saying, ﴿From both of them come out the pearl and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas it only comes out of the salt water (ujaj). Al-Dahhak said: the pronoun refers to both groups, and among the jinn there are messengers from among them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 133–135:**

Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿Your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and replace you with whomever He wills after you, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.﴾ ﴿What you are promised is certainly coming, and you cannot escape.﴾ ﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your position, and I am acting. Soon you will know to whom the final home belongs. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾

"Al-Ghaniyy" (the Self-Sufficient) is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*) of Allah, the Exalted, because He, Blessed and Exalted, has no need of anything from any direction. Then this attribute was followed by His words, "the Possessor of mercy." So He joined self-sufficiency to bounty, and this is the most beautiful harmony. Then He followed these words, which contain a threat, that warn against the seizure of Allah, the Exalted, whether this comes swiftly or after a respite and the passing of two generations. This is Allah's customary way with creation. As for "replacement" (*al-istikhlaf*), just as Allah brought this human world into existence by producing it from the descendants of a earlier people, whose origin was Adam, peace be upon him.

The majority (*al-jama'ah*) read "*dhurriyyati*" with a *dammah* on the *dhal* and a shaddah on the *ra'* with a kasrah. Zayd ibn Thabit read it with a kasrah on the *dhal*, and likewise in the surah of Al 'Imran. Abu Hatim reported from Aban ibn 'Uthman that he read "*dharriyyati*" with a fatha on the *dhal* and a light (unstressed) *ra'* with a kasrah. Abu al-Zinad reported from him that he recited on the pulpit "*dharyati*," with a fatha on the *dhal* and a sukun on the *ra'*, on the pattern of *fa'lah*. He said: "I asked him, and he said: Zayd ibn Thabit taught it to me."

The *min* in Allah's words "*min dhurriyyati*" is partitive (*li al-tab'id*). Al-Tabari held that it has the meaning of your saying: "I took a dinar from my garment," in the sense of "from it, and in its place." "*Tu'adun*" (what you are promised) is derived from "*al-wa'id*" (threat), as indicated by the context: "and you cannot escape." The reference is specifically to the threat mentioned above. As for taking it as a general statement without restriction, that would imply the carrying out of every threat, and the principles of belief reject this. "*Bi-mu'jizin*" means "escaping by fleeing," that is, they cannot exhaust (*yu'jizuna*) the one pursuing them.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to threaten them with His words "*i'malu*" (act), meaning: "You will soon see the outcome of your corrupt deeds." The form "*if'al*" here carries the meaning of warning and menace. "*'Ala makanatikum*" means "according to your state and your way." Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, read from 'Asim "*'ala makanatikum*" in the plural form of *makanah* throughout the Qur'an, while all the other readers read the singular throughout the Qur'an. "*Man*" may be understood as having the meaning of "*alladhi*" (the one who), in which case it is in the accusative position as the object of "*ta'lamun*" (you will know). It may also be understood as an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (*bi-al-ibtida'*), with the predicate being Allah's words "*takunu lahu*" (belongs to him). "*'Aqibatu al-dar*" means the ultimate outcome of the Hereafter. It is also possible that it means the ultimate outcome in this world, in terms of victory and dominance. Thus the verse contains information about the unseen (*i'lam bi-ghayb*).

Then He affirmed the judgment decisively: "*Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed*," meaning their efforts will not prosper. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "*man yakunu*" with the *ya'* here and in surah al-Qasas, treating the word "*al-'aqibah*" as masculine in meaning.
