(p-466)

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has created of the tilth and the cattle, and they say, "This is for God," so they claim, and "This is for our associates." But what is for their associates does not reach God, while what is for God reaches their associates. Evil is what they judge.﴾

The pronoun in "wa-ja'alū" (and they assigned) refers to the Arab unbelievers who took idols as equals to their Lord, those who were already refuted from the beginning of the surah.

And "dhara'a" means "created, brought into being, and scattered on the earth." It is said: "God Most High dhara'a the creation (yadhra'uhum, dharan, and dhurū'an)," i.e., "He created them." His words, Most High, "and they assigned a share (from such and such)," imply that another share remains that is not included in the ruling of the first; so He clarified it with His words, "and they say, 'This is for God,' so they claim, and 'This is for our associates.'" Then He interrupted their speech by stating that this is a claim and a fabrication. And "al-za'm" (claim), in much of the speech of the Arabs, is closer to what is not certain or true. It is said "za'm" with a fatḥa on the zay, and this is how the majority recited it; "zu'm" with a ḍamma on it, and [with it] al-Kisā'ī alone recited it in this verse; and "zi'm" with a kasra on the zay, and I do not know of anyone who recited it that way.

And "al-ḥarth" (tilth) in this verse means the crops, the trees, and what comes from the land. His words, Most High, "for our associates," mean the idols and images. They called them "associates" according to their belief about them, that they share with them in good and evil and bring it about for them.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the Arabs used to set aside from their produce, their crops, their fruits, and their cattle a portion they called for God, Most High, and a portion they called for their idols. Their custom was to show more care and concern for the share of the idols than for the share of God, Most High, since they believed the idols were in need, and God, Most High, is not. So when they gathered the crop and the wind blew and carried some of what was for God to what was for their associates, they left it; and if it carried some of what was for their associates to what was for God, they returned it. If what was set aside for God was irrigated from the water meant for their associates' share, they left it; and if it was the reverse, they blocked it. And if they did not obtain anything in the share of their associates, they said, "The gods must have expenses," and so they would assign God's share to that. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others said this meaning: they did this and similar actions, and likewise with the cattle; and when a year of drought struck them, they would eat God's share and avoid their associates' share.

(p-467)As for His words, Most High, "So what is for their associates does not reach God," etc.: the majority of interpreters said that what is meant by His words "does not reach" and His words, glorified be He, "reaches" is what we previously mentioned of their protecting the share of their gods when the wind blew and other such things. Ibn Zayd said: it is only that when they slaughtered for God, Most High, they mentioned their gods over that slaughter; and when they slaughtered for their gods, they did not mention God, Most High. So it is as if He said: "what is for them does not reach the mention of God, Most High," and He said: "what is for God reaches the mention of their associates."

And "mā" (what) is in the nominative position; it is as if He said: "Evil is that which they judge." In my view, it is not appropriate here to treat "sā'a" (evil) in the manner of "ni'ma" and "bi'sa," because the explained element here is implicit, and it must be made explicit by agreement of the grammarians. It is appropriate to treat it in the manner of "bi'sa" only in His words, Most High, "Evil is the example of the people" [al-A'raf: 177], because the explained element is apparent in the speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 137:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And thus have their partners made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children, to bring them to ruin and to confuse them regarding their religion. And had Allah willed, they would not have done so. So leave them and what they fabricate.﴾

"Many" (al-kathir) in this verse is intended to refer to those among the polytheists of the Arabs who used to bury their daughters alive (wa'd). "Partners" (al-shuraka') here are the devils who command this and make it attractive, and also those among the children of Adam who encourage it and transmit it from generation to generation, since they all share in the ugliness of this act and its consequences in the Hereafter. The purpose of this verse is the censure of wa'd (burying daughters alive) and the condemnation of committing it.

The reading differs. The community of readers, except Ibn 'Amir, recited: "wa-kadhalika zayyana" with a fatha on the zay; "qatla" in the accusative; "awladihim" with a kasra on the dal; "shurakauhum." This is the clearest reading. Sibawayh reports that a group recited: "wa-kadhalika zuyyina" with a damma on the zay; "qatlu" in the nominative; "awladihim" with a kasra on the dal; "shurakauhum" in the nominative.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the reading of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Abd al-Malik, judge of the army, companion of Ibn 'Amir. It is as if he said: "zayyanahu shurakauhum" (their partners made it attractive). Sibawayh said: This is like the saying of the poet:

"Let Yazid be wept for by one humbled by a dispute, and one bewildered by what the calamities command."

It is as if he said: "one humbled by a dispute weeps for him."

Qutrub permitted that the partners in this reading are the subject, raised by the killing, as if the verbal noun had been put in apposition to the object, and then the agent was mentioned after it, as if he said: "that their partners killed their children," just as you say: "Zayd made riding the horse beloved to me," meaning, "that Zayd rode the horse."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sound view is that when a verbal noun is annexed to an object, the agent is not mentioned. Moreover, the majority in this verse hold that the partners are the ones who make it attractive, not the killers. The interpretation Sibawayh mentioned is the sound one. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, according to the reading of one who recited: "yusabbaha lahu fiha bil-ghuduwwi wal-asali rijal" with a fatha on the doubled ba', meaning "yusabbihu rijal" (men glorify Him).

Ibn 'Amir recited: "wa-kadhalika zuyyina" with a damma on the zay; "qatlu" in the nominative; "awladahum" with a fatha on the dal; "shurakaihim" with the shurakai in the genitive. This is a weak reading in the usage of the Arabs; the leading grammarians do not permit separating in this manner with adverbial phrases except in poetry, as in his saying:

"As the writing is inscribed by the hand of a Jew, one day approaching or removing..."

(p-469) How then with the object in the most eloquent speech? Yet its justification, despite its weakness, is that it came as an anomaly in a verse recited by Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, which is:

"So I made her smooth with a smoothing-stone, as the she-camel of Abu Mazada is smoothed."

And in the verse of al-Tirimmah, which is his saying:

"They circle around the pastures of Hawzi, not frightened in its valley by the clatter of the bows and quivers."

The partners, according to this reading, are those who interpret the burying of others' daughters; so they are the killers. The sound meaning, however, is that they are the ones who make it attractive, not the killers, and this is implied by the reading of the community.

Some people of Syria, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Amir, recited: "zinna" with a kasra on the zay and a sukun on the ya', according to the advanced order, from the separation by the object. Al-Zahrawi reported that a group of the people of Syria recited: "wa-kadhalika zuyyina" with a damma on the zay; "qatlu" in the nominative; "awladihim" with a kasra on the dal; "shurakaihim" in the genitive. The partners, according to this reading, are the children who were buried alive, because they are partners in lineage (p-470) and inheritance; and describing them as partners implies a sanctity for them, and in it is a clarification of the corruption of the act, since it is the killing of one who has a sanctity.

"Li-yurdujum" means: that they might destroy them, from al-radan (ruin). "Wa-liyalbisu" means: that they might mix (confuse); the community reads it with a kasra on the ba'. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "wa-liyalbasu" with a fatha on the ba'. Abu al-Fath said: it is a metaphor from al-libas (clothing), an expression for intense mixing. These two verbs support the first reading in our order, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus made attractive﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And had Allah willed, they would not have done so﴾, requires that nothing happens except by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and in it is a refutation of those who say that a person creates his own actions.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So leave them﴾, is a pure threat; and ﴿what they fabricate﴾ means: what they invent of lies in legislating this for themselves and believing that these are permitted to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 138:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And they say, "These are cattle and crops set apart; none may eat of them except whom we will," by their claim; and [there are] cattle whose backs have been forbidden, and cattle over which they do not mention the name of Allah, fabricating against Him. He will recompense them for what they used to invent.﴾

This verse includes an enumeration of what they legislated for themselves, and bound themselves to as a form of devotion, lying about Allah the Exalted and fabricating against Him. He, the Exalted, described that they deliberately singled out some of their cattle, namely the camels, the cows, and the sheep; or the camels alone, since other animals, when taken singly, are not called "an'am" (cattle). And [they singled out] some of their crops and fruits, and this was called "harth" (tilth), since it comes from tilling. They said, "These are ḥijr," i.e., forbidden. The majority of readers recited "ḥijr" with a kasra on the ḥa' and a sukun on the jim. Qatada, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj recited "ḥujr" with a ḍamma on the ḥa' and a sukun on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-A'mash, Ikrima, and 'Amr ibn Dinar recited "ḥirj" with a kasra on the ḥa', the ra' placed before the jim, and a sukun on it. The first and second readings both carry the meaning of "al-tahjir" (restriction), which is prohibition and forbidding, while the last is from "al-ḥirj," which is constriction and prohibition.

These cattle were, according to Ibn Zayd, permitted for men and forbidden for women. It was also said that they were an endowment for the sustenance of the custodians (sadana) of the idol-houses and their attendants; this was related by al-Mahdawi. That is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, "except whom we will."

His saying, the Exalted, "by their claim" means: by their assertion, which is closer to falsehood than to truth. Their claim here is in their saying "ḥijr," and their prohibition thereby of what Allah the Exalted did not prohibit. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "bi-za'amihim" with a fatḥa on the zay and the 'ayn, and likewise in the one mentioned previously.

﴿And cattle whose backs have been forbidden﴾: the Arabs had customs: when a she-camel did such-and-such, out of abundance of offspring, or the joining of females together, and the like, her back was forbidden, so she was not ridden; and when a stallion did such-and-such, his back was forbidden. Allah the Exalted enumerated this by way of refuting them, since they legislated it by their own opinion and their lying.

﴿And cattle over which they do not mention the name of Allah﴾: it was said that they had a custom regarding certain cattle that no pilgrimage would be performed upon them; so they were ridden in every manner except for the pilgrimage. This is His saying, the Exalted, "over which they do not mention the name of Allah." This is the view of a group of exegetes, and it is related from Abu Wa'il. Another group said: rather, this refers to slaughtering; meaning that they set aside a portion of them for their gods, not mentioning the name of Allah the Exalted over their slaughter. His saying, the Exalted, "fabricating" (iftira'an) is a verbal noun put in the accusative as an object of purpose, or by supposing an implied verb, its estimate being: "they fabricate that." And "He will recompense them" is a warning of retribution in the Hereafter. The pronoun in "against Him" refers to the name of Allah the Exalted. And "they used to invent" [al-An'am: 137], i.e., they lie and fabricate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 139:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And they say: "What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives; but if it is stillborn, then they are partners in it. He will repay them for their description. Indeed, He is Wise, All-Knowing."﴾

This verse includes an enumeration of their corrupt doctrines. Their custom regarding some of the cattle was that they would forbid what was born of them to their women, and reserve it for their men. The ha' in "khālisatun" (exclusively): it has been said that it is for emphasis (mubālaghah), as in "rāwiyah" (transmitter of much poetry) and others, and this is like when you say, "So-and-so is my exclusive (khāliṣatī)." Although the rule of the ha' of emphasis is that it attaches to a form of intensification such as "'allāmah" (very learned), "nassābah" (very knowledgeable in genealogy), "baṣīrah" (very perceptive), and the like. It has also been said that it is for the feminine gender of the cattle, since what is in their wombs is also cattle. It has also been said that it is according to the feminine form of the word "mā," because "mā" in this place occupies the position of your saying "jamā'atan" (as a group) and "jumlatan" (entirely).

The majority of reciters and people read "khāliṣatun" with a nominative ending (raf'). ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, and al-Aʿmash read "khāliṣun" without a ha'. The nominative of these two readings is as the predicate of the inchoative (khabar al-ibtidā'). Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), with a variant report, al-Aʿraj, Qatādah, and Sufyān ibn Ḥusayn read "khāliṣatan" with an accusative ending (naṣb). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, as Abū al-Fatḥ reported, read "khāliṣan." The accusative of these two readings is because it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, "fī buṭūni" (in the wombs). That is because the sense of the sentence is: "And they say: what is settled in the wombs of these cattle..." The verb was deleted and the prepositional phrase bore the pronoun. The circumstantial state is from the pronoun, and its governing element is the sense of settledness (al-istiqrār). Abū al-Fatḥ said: It is also valid for it to be a state from "mā," according to the view of Abū al-Ḥasan in his permission of placing the state before its governing element.

Ibn ʿAbbās also read, as did Abū Ḥaywah and al-Zuhrī, "khāliṣuhu," with "khāliṣ" in construct with a pronoun referring to "mā"; its meaning is "what is pure and comes out alive." The predicate, according to the reading of the one who read "khāliṣatan," is in His saying, Glorified is He, "li-dhukūrinā" (for our males). The meaning intended by "mā" in His saying, "mā fī buṭūni" (what is in the wombs), al-Suddī said: it is the fetuses. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and al-Shaʿbī said: it is the milk. Al-Ṭabarī said: the wording encompasses both.

His saying, "wa-muḥarramun" (and forbidden), indicates that the ha' in "khāliṣatun" is for emphasis; for had it been for feminine gender, He would have said "wa-muḥarramatun." And "azwājinā" (our wives) refers to the group of women who are prepared to be wives; this was said by Mujāhid. al-Ṭabarī related from Ibn Zayd that what is meant by "azwājinā" is the daughters.

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is far from the meaning's linkage. His saying, "wa-in yakun maytatan" (but if it is stillborn): it was among their custom that what came out of the fetuses dead from those dedicated cattle is lawful for men and women alike; and likewise what died of the dedicated cattle themselves.

Ibn Kathīr read "wa-in yakun" with a yāʾ and "maytatun" with a nominative ending, so he did not attach a feminine marker to the verb, since the feminine of the subject it is attributed to is not real feminine. The meaning: "if there occurs a dead [thing] or a dead [event] occurs." Ibn ʿĀmir read "wa-in takun" with a tā', and "maytatun" with a nominative ending, so he attached the feminine marker to the verb, since the subject was grammatically feminine, and he attributed the verb to "maytah," as Ibn Kathīr did. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), read "takun" with a tā' and "maytatan" with an accusative ending, so he made it feminine, although the preceding noun is masculine, because he took it according to the sense.

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: So the estimate is: "and if the soul (nasamah) — or the like — is a dead one." Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafs, read "yakun" with a yāʾ and "maytatan" with an accusative ending, so they made the verb masculine, because they attributed it to the pronoun referring to what preceded in His saying, "mā fī buṭūni hādhihi al-anʿām" (what is in the wombs of these cattle), which is masculine. The "maytatan" is in the accusative as a predicate. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: This reading is strengthened by His saying, "fa-hum fīhi" (then they are partners in it), and He did not say "fīhā" (in it, feminine). Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ read "wa-in takun mayyitatan" with a shaddah. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd read: "fa-hum fīhi sawāʾ" (then they are equal partners in it).

Then Exalted is He followed with their threat, for what they described as drawing near to Allah Exalted, and legislated from falsehood and fabrication. "Innahu ḥakīm" (indeed He is Wise): that is, "in His punishment of them for that"; "ʿalīm" (All-Knowing): of the few and the many of what they fabricated concerning that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 140–141:

(p-474) His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Certainly lost are those who have killed their children in foolishness, without knowledge, and have forbidden what Allah has provided for them, fabricating [lies] against Allah. They have certainly gone astray and were not [rightly] guided.﴾ ﴿And it is He who produces gardens, both trellised and untrellised, and date palms and crops of varying [kinds of] food, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due [zakah] on the day of its harvest. And do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who commit excess.﴾

This wording contains a reprimand for the ugliness of their deed and a wonder at the wretchedness of their state, regarding their burying of daughters alive, their prohibition of cattle and tilled crops. 'Ikrimah said: burying [daughters alive] was practised among Rabi'ah and Mudar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The majority of the Arabs did not do this. Then among its perpetrators were some who did it out of fear of poverty and destitution, and some of them did it out of jealousy, fearing captivity. Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir read "qattalū" with a doubled tā' for emphasis (intensification), while the rest read "qatalū" with a single tā'.

And "what Allah has provided for them" refers to those cattle and the crops which they reserved without any legal basis and without any reward in the afterlife, rather by fabricating against Allah, Exalted is He, and by lying. "They have certainly gone astray" is a report about them of their bewilderment, and it is in the sense of the wonder expressed by His saying, Exalted is He, "Certainly lost..." "And were not" means: "in this deed." It may also mean: "and were not, before their error, guided by this deed," but they increased in error by this deed.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "And it is He who produces gardens, both trellised..." to the end of the verse: this is an alert to the places of reflection. "Produces" means: created and originated. "Jannah" (garden) is derived from "janna," meaning to conceal. "Trellised" (ma'rushat): Ibn 'Abbas said: this refers to grape vines; some of them are trellised and raised, and some are not trellised. Al-Suddi said: "al-ma'rushat" are what is trellised, like the vine and others, the orchards. It was said: "al-ma'rush" is what the children of Adam trellis of the kinds of trees, and "ghayr al-ma'rush" is what grows on mountains, deserts and the like. It was said: "al-ma'rush" is what is hung on a wall, and "ghayr al-ma'rush" is what is not hung. "Mukhtalifan" (varying) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), with the sense of the variation in its fruit occurring, since at the time of its production there is no fruit on it; so it is a prospective circumstance, coming after the production. (p-475) "Mutashabihan" (similar) means in appearance, and "ghayr mutashabih" (dissimilar) means in taste; so said Ibn Jurayj and others.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Eat of its fruit": this is the very permission, and it implies an indication to the blessing in that. It is also read "min thumurihi" with a damma on the thā', and this has been mentioned before. "And give its due on the day of its harvest": a group of the people of knowledge said: it refers to the obligatory zakah, among them Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Tawus, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son; and Malik ibn Anas said it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is objected to on the ground that the surah is Meccan, and this verse, according to the majority view, is not excepted; al-Zajjaj related that it was said concerning this verse that it was revealed in Medina; and it is also objected to on the ground that there is no zakah on what is mentioned of pomegranates and everything in its meaning.

Ibn al-Hanafiyyah also said, as did 'Ata', Mujahid, and others among the people of knowledge: rather, His saying, Exalted is He, "and give its due" is a recommendation to give rights from the wealth other than zakah; the sunnah is that a man gives from his crop at the harvest, at the winnowing, and at the stacking in the threshing floor; then when it is cleaned and measured, he takes out the zakah from it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: its due is the permission to gather the ears of grain that fall. A group said: this was the ruling on the charity of the Muslims until the obligatory zakah was revealed and abrogated it; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ibrahim, and al-Hasan. Al-Suddi said concerning this surah that it is Meccan and was abrogated by zakah; Sufyan said to him: "From whom?" He said: "From the scholars."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Abrogation does not properly apply to this verse, because this verse and the verse of zakah do not conflict; rather, this one is based on recommendation and that one on obligation.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "hisadihi" with a kasra on the ha'; 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "hasadihi" with a fatha on the ha'; both are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun.

His saying, Exalted is He, "And do not be excessive": this verse, whoever says it concerns obligatory zakah, makes this prohibition of excess either addressed to people against withholding its payment, since that is excess in action; this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib; or addressed to rulers against overburdening people and harming them, since that is excess in action; this was said by Ibn Zayd. And whoever takes the verse as a recommendation to rights other than zakah, the prohibition of excess in those rights is consequently applicable, because of the harm to wealth and its waste in that.

It is related that the verse was revealed because Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas harvested his crop and said: "By Allah, no one will come to me today except that I will feed him." Then he evening came and he had no produce left, so this verse was revealed. Abu al-'Aliyah said: they used to give something at the harvest, then they competed and became excessive, so the verse was revealed. Whoever says it is abrogated, the prohibition applies to the time of the verse's ruling.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 142–143:

(p-477) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And of the cattle, some for burden and some for carpeting. Eat of what God has provided for you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a manifest enemy.﴾ ﴿Eight pairs: of sheep two, and of goats two. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾

"Hamulatan" (for burden) is coordinated with ﴿gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [al-An'am: 141]; the implied sense is: "And He produced from the cattle that which is for burden." The ḥamūlah (burden-bearing animal) is that which carries loads, of camels and cattle, according to whoever customarily rides them. The "ha'" in ḥamūlah is for emphasis (mubālagha). Al-Ṭabarī said: it is a collective noun (ism jam') that has no singular from its own form. The farsh (carpet-type animal) is that which does not carry a heavy load, such as sheep and young cattle and camels. This is what is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and others. It is called farsh and farīsh. Some people held that it is called "farsh" only because of its softness, and that it is among what is handled and walked upon and over which one has free disposal, since its body is close to the ground.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: the ḥamūlah is the camel, the horse, the mule and the donkey; al-Ṭabarī mentioned it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is from him an explanation of the word itself, not in terms of its application in this verse; and it does not enter the verse for other than the cattle. It was specifically mentioned only because of what the Arabs prescribed regarding them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿provided by God﴾ is an explicit permission and the removal of what the disbelievers had instituted concerning the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah and other things. Then He followed the prohibition of those customs with His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. "Khutuwāt" is the plural of "khuṭwah" (step), i.e., "do not walk in his misguiding paths." The difference among the readers regarding "khuṭuwāt" has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. Among its irregular readings is the reading of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: "khuṭu'āt" with a ḍamma on the kha' and the ṭa' and with a hamza. Abu al-Fath said: this is the plural of "khaṭ'ah," from "al-khaṭa'" (error). Among the irregular readings is the reading of Abu al-Samal: "khaṭawāt," with a waw without a hamza, which is the plural of "khaṭwah," the measure of the distance between the two feet of one walking. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition of that by establishing the enmity of Satan toward the son of Adam.

His saying, Exalted is He, "thamāniyata" (eight): its case-ending (naṣb) has been disputed. Al-Akhfash 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is governed by a hidden verb, its implied sense being: "Eat the flesh of eight pairs..." So the verb was omitted, and the noun was omitted, and the genitive that follows was placed in its position. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "mā" in His saying, ﴿Eat of what God has provided﴾. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl). And it was said: it is in the accusative as a substitute for His saying, ﴿burden and carpeting﴾; and this is the most correct of the opinions and the most consistent with the meaning of the verse. Al-Kisa'i said: "anshaʾa" (He produced) governs it. "Al-zawj" (pair) is the male, and "al-zawj" is the female; each of the two is the mate of the other; and they are four kinds, so they come to eight pairs.

"Al-ḍaʾn" is the plural of "ḍāʾinah" and "ḍāʾin." Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Hasan read: "min al-ḍa'n," with a fatḥa on the hamza. Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "wa-min al-ma'z," with a sukun on the 'ayn. It is the plural of "mā'iz" and "mā'izah." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read: "wa-min al-ma'az," with a fatḥa on the 'ayn. So "ḍa'n" and "ma'z" are like "rākib" and "rakb," "tājir" and "tajr," and "ḍa'n" and "ma'az" like "khādim" and "khadam," and the like. Aban ibn 'Uthman read: "min al-ḍa'ni ithnān," as a beginning and a fronted predicate. It is said of the plural of "mā'iz": "ma'z," "ma'az," "ma'iz," "mi'zā," and "am'ūz."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males..."﴾: this is a division addressed to the disbelievers, until their lying against God, Exalted is He, becomes evident; i.e., "It must be that He has forbidden the two males; then it would follow that you forbid all males; or the two females, then it would follow that you forbid all females; or that which the wombs of the two females contain, then it would follow that you forbid all of them; and you have not committed yourselves to anything that this division requires." In these questions there is both confirmation and rebuke.

Then He followed their confirmation and their rebuke with His saying, Exalted is He, "Inform me" (nabbi'ūnī), i.e., tell me, "with knowledge," i.e., from a source of revelation, or a book from the books of God, Exalted is He; ﴿if you are truthful﴾. "In" is a conditional particle, and its answer is in "nabbi'ūnī." It is permissible to front the answer of this conditional, since "in" shows no governing effect on the past tense; had it shown a manifest governing effect, the fronting of the answer would not have been permissible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 142–143:

(p-477) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And of the cattle, some for burden and some for carpeting. Eat of what God has provided for you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a manifest enemy.﴾ ﴿Eight pairs: of sheep two, and of goats two. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 144:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And of camels two, and of cattle two. Say: Has He forbidden the two males, or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? Who then is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to lead people astray without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

The discussion of this verse, regarding its meaning and the order of the division, is like the discussion of the previous statement of Him, glorified is He: ﴿And of sheep two, and of goats two﴾ [al-An'am: 143]. It is as if He said: "Are you the ones who claim that Allah has forbidden certain kinds of these livestock? Then its prohibition must be either in the two males, or in what the wombs of the two females contain. But He has not forbidden this, nor that. So nothing remains except that no prohibition has occurred."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you?﴾ up to the end of the verse, is an interrogative in the form of rebuke, since there is no longer any possibility for them to claim the impossible, namely that they witnessed Allah's command to them concerning this.

"Shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of "shahid" (witness). Then His saying, Exalted is He, "Who then is more unjust," includes a mention of the state of the one who fabricates a lie against Allah, Exalted is He, and an affirmation of the extreme degree of his wrongdoing. As-Suddi said: Those who released (camels as sawaib) and split the ears (of camels as bahira) used to say: "Allah has commanded us to do this." Then Exalted is He clarified the evil of their intention in fabricating, for if anyone fabricated a falsehood against Allah without any purpose, it would be a great wrong; how much more so if he intended by it to lead a community astray? It is also possible that the lam in "li-yudilla" (to lead astray) is the lam of consequence (lam al-sayrurah).

Then He definitively decided the ruling, there is no lord besides Him, that He does not guide the wrongdoing people; that is, "He does not direct them." This is apparently general, but its specification has been made clear by what the Shari'ah requires, namely that Allah, Exalted is He, guides many wrongdoers through repentance.

(p-480) This is a command from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to convey the law to all people and to explain on Allah's behalf what has been revealed to him. This verse was revealed in Makkah, and at that time there was nothing forbidden in the Shari'ah apart from these things. Then the surah "al-Ma'idah" was revealed in Madinah, and additional prohibitions were added, such as the strangled animal (al-munkhaniqah), the animal killed by a blow (al-mawqudhah), the animal that falls from a height (al-mutaraddiyah), and the animal gored by another (al-natihah). Although these are in the ruling of carrion (maytah), there was a possibility in one's consideration that they might be placed with the slaughtered animals (al-mudhakkayat), because they die through causes and not by natural death. When the text made clear that they are assimilated to carrion, they became an addition to the prohibitions. Then the text was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the prohibition of wine, by a revelation that was not miraculous, and concerning the prohibition of every animal with fangs among the predatory beasts. All of these are additions to the prohibitions. The word "tahrim" (prohibition), when it comes from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is suitable to bring the thing mentioned to the furthest limit of prohibition and forbiddance. It is also suitable, according to the language, to stop short of that limit within the sphere of disliking (karahiyah) and the like. Whatever is accompanied by an indicator of full acceptance (tasjim) from the Companions who interpreted, and upon which all of them agreed, and whose wording in the hadiths did not vary, and which people have maintained in its original form, it is necessary by the Shari'ah that its prohibition has reached the furthest limit of forbidding and prohibition, and it is joined to the swine and to carrion. This is the nature of the prohibition of wine. Whatever is accompanied by an indicator in the wording of the hadith, and over which the community has differed despite their knowledge of the hadiths, such as his (ﷺ) saying: "Every animal with fangs among the beasts of prey is forbidden," and it has been related that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs among the beasts of prey." Then the Companions and those after them differed concerning the prohibition of this. Therefore, for these reasons, it is permissible for the one who considers the matter to take the word "tahrim" as a general prohibition meaning disliking and the like. Likewise is what is accompanied by an indicator of interpretation (ta'wil), such as his (ﷺ) prohibition of the flesh of domestic donkeys (al-humur al-insiyyah). (p-481) Some of the Companions present interpreted that it was because they are impure (najas), some interpreted that it was so that the people's beasts of burden would not perish, and some interpreted it as a definite prohibition. The disagreement in the community concerning the prohibition of their flesh is established. Therefore, it is permissible for the scholar who considers the matter to take the word "tahrim," according to his effort (ijtihad) and analogical reasoning (qiyas), to mean disliking or the like.

It is related from Ibn 'Amir that he read "fima uhiya ilayya" with a fatha on the hamzah and the ha'. The majority of people read "yat'amuhu." Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali read "yattami'uhu" with a shaddah on the ta' and a kasrah on the 'ayn. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and the companions of 'Abdullah read "ta'imahu," with a past-tense verb. Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read "illa an yakuna" with the ya', on the assumption of "illa an yakuna al-matu'mu..." (unless the thing eaten is...). Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, and also Abu 'Amr read "illa an takuna" with the ta' from above, "maytatan," on the assumption of "illa an takuna al-matu'matu..." (unless the thing eaten is...). Ibn 'Amir alone, and Makki mentioned it from Abu Ja'far, read "illa an takuna" with the ta', "maytatun" with the raf', taking "takuna" in the sense of "taqa'" (to occur). On this reading it is necessary to make "daman" (blood) conjoined to the place of "an takuna," because it is in the accusative position by way of exception. "Al-masfuh" means that which flows, which runs. Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, made this a distinction between a little and a lot. "Al-masfuh" means blood that is flowing and similar. From it is the saying of the poet, who is Tarafah:

"When women visit him from among us, while he is ill, they pour forth tears after the crying."

And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"My cure is a tear, if I pour it out, and is there any benefit at the traces of a deserted abode from wailing?"

Thus, blood mixed with the flesh, and blood that flows out of the broth of the meat, and what resembles these, are lawful. The blood that is not flowing is this, and it is pardoned. It was said to Abu Mijlaz, concerning a pot over which there was redness from blood, that he said: "Allah only prohibited flowing blood." 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) and others said similarly, and the scholars are in consensus upon it. It was also said: "Blood is forbidden, because when it separates it has flowed out."

(p-482) "Al-rijs" means filth, and the forbidden. Bodies and meanings are described by it, as he (ﷺ) said: "Leave them, for they are foul-smelling," and the hadith continues. Likewise it was said concerning the arrows (al-azlam) that they are "rijs." "Al-rijs" also means punishment, linguistically in the sense of "al-rijz." The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿or a transgression (fisqan)﴾ mean the sacrifices that they dedicate to their idols.

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Then whoever is compelled﴾ (the verse), Allah, the Exalted, permitted in it, in the case of necessity, the committing of what is forbidden, without transgression. People differed regarding the conditions: one group said, provided that the person does not transgress in his eating, so that he eats more than what keeps him alive, and reaches the limit of satiety or beyond. Another group said: rather, provided that he does not transgress by having his journey be one of highway robbery or killing a soul, or his conduct be in disobedience, for such a person has no concession. As for one who is not in these circumstances and is compelled, he may eat to satiety and take provision. This is the well-known opinion of Malik ibn Anas (may Allah have mercy on him). And the one who held the first view, that of restricting oneself to sustaining life, was 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him).

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ are a permission which the strength of the wording gives.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 146:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We prohibited to them their fat, except what their backs carry, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone. That was Our recompense to them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful.﴾

(p-483) When Allah, Exalted and Majestic, mentioned what He prohibited to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), He followed it with mention of what He prohibited to the Jews, because in that is a refutation of their claim: "Allah, Exalted is He, has not prohibited anything to us; rather, we have prohibited to ourselves what Israel (Isra'il) prohibited for himself."

The discussion of the word "Jews" (hadu) has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, along with the meaning of their being named "Jews" (yahud).

As for ﴿every animal with claws﴾, it refers to camels, ostriches, geese, and similar animals that do not have separated toes and that have a claw (zufur). Abu Zayd said: "What is meant is camels specifically," but this specification is weak. An-Naqqash reported from Tha'lab that everything that does not hunt is zu zufur (having claws), and what hunts is zu mikhlab (having talons).

The noble Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not consistent, because the lion has claws.

The majority of readers recited zufur with a ḍammah on the ẓā' and the fā'. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj recited zufr with the fā' sukun. Abu as-Sammal and Qa'nab recited zifr with a kasrah on the ẓā' and sukun on the fā'.

Allah, Exalted and Majestic, informed us in this verse of the prohibition of fats upon the Children of Israel; these are: ath-thurub, the kidneys, and any pure fat, excluded from the exception stated in the verse.

The scholars differed regarding the prohibition of this for Muslims concerning Jewish slaughter. Ibn al-Mundhir in al-Ashraf reported from Malik and others that eating fat from Jewish slaughter is forbidden, and this is the apparent position of al-Mudawwana.

The noble Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is based on the view concerning Allah's saying, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And the food of those given the Book is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], that it refers to what is eaten from their slaughter; as for what is not lawful for them, no dhakah (ritual slaughter) applies to it, rather it is like blood in the slaughter of Muslims. And according to this view, Malik's position in al-Mudawwana comes into line: regarding what a Jew slaughters that is not lawful for them, such as a camel or a hare, it is not eaten.

(p-484) It is narrated from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, that he disliked fat from the slaughter of the People of the Book without declaring it prohibited. Some people permitted fat from the slaughter of the People of the Book, and their slaughtering what is forbidden to them, if a Muslim instructs them to do so.

The noble Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is on the basis that Allah's saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the food of those given the Book is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], means the slaughtered animals; so whenever slaughter occurs in its described manner, permission is established. This is a weak view, because it strips the word "food" (ta'am) of the meaning of being something eaten by the People of the Book, and restricts it to the meaning of slaughter; and that is an untenable strain.

As for the tendon (at-tarid), some prohibited it, some disliked it, some permitted it, and Malik permitted it in al-Mudawwana, then retracted to forbidding it. Ibn Habib said: what was prohibited to them, and we know that from our Book, it is not lawful for us from their slaughter.

Allah's saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except what their backs carry﴾, intends what is mixed with the flesh on the back, the flanks, and similar; as-Suddi and Abu Salih said: al-alaya (the rump fat) is among what their backs carry. "Or the entrails" (al-hawaya): it said: it is the plural of hawiyyah, on the pattern fa'ilah, so the pattern of hawaya on this view is fa'a'il, like safinah and safa'in; it was also said: it is the plural of hawiyah, on the pattern fa'ilah, so hawaya on this view is fawa'il, like daribah and dawarib; and it was said: it is the plural of hawiya', so its pattern on this view too is fawa'il, like qasi'a' and qawasi'. As for hawaya on the first pattern, its origin is hawa'i, the final ya' became alif, so the hamza was opened for that, then it was changed to ya'. As for the last two patterns, the origin of hawaya is hawawi, and the second waw was changed to hamza. Al-hawiyyah is what coils in the belly and curls around; it is the intestines, the viscera, and similar things. Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, as-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: al-hawaya (p-485) are the intestines (al-mabi'ir); some said: they are the membranes in which the bowels lie, and they are the "daughters of milk."

Allah's saying, Exalted is He, ﴿or what is mixed with bone﴾, intends throughout the whole body.

"Al-hawaya" is conjoined to "ma" in Allah's saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except what they carry﴾; so it is in the accusative position, conjoined to what is accusative by the exception. Al-Kisa'i said: "al-hawaya" is conjoined to "az-zuhur" (the backs), as if he said: "except what their backs carry, or what the entrails carry." Some people said: "al-hawaya" is conjoined to "ash-shuhum" (the fats).

The noble Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On this view, al-hawaya would enter into the prohibition; but this view is supported neither by the wording nor by the meaning; rather both reject it.

Allah's saying, Exalted is He, ﴿That is Our recompense to them for their rebellion﴾: "dhalika" is in the nominative position; and "We recompensed them for their rebellion" requires that this prohibition was only a punishment for them for their sins, their rebellion, and their disobedience toward the prophets. Allah's saying, Exalted is He, "and indeed We are truthful," is a statement that implies a rebuke of their lie in their saying: "Allah did not prohibit anything to us; rather, we followed Israel in what he prohibited for himself"; and it implies a refutation and rejection of their claim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 147–148:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy, and His might is not turned away from the guilty people." ﴾ ﴿The idolaters will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Likewise did those before them deny, until they tasted Our might. Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you could bring forth to us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess."﴾

He means: "If they deny you regarding what you have reported, that God the Exalted has forbidden these things to them, and they say: 'God the Exalted has forbidden us nothing; we only forbade what Israel forbade for himself'" - al-Suddi said: "This was their statement" - "then say (p-486), O Muhammad, in a manner of wonder at their state and magnifying their slander in denying you, while knowing the reality of what you said: 'Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy,' since He does not hasten punishment upon you despite the severity of your sin."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is like your saying, when you see a disobedience or a wrongful matter: "How forbearing God is!" while you mean: "For His granting respite to the like of that." So in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy﴾, there is an intensification of describing them with utmost transgression and severe rebellion.

Then He followed this statement with a threat, in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and His might is not turned away from the guilty people﴾. It is as if He said: "Do not also be deceived by the breadth of God the Exalted's mercy; for He has a might that is not turned away from the guilty, either in this world or in the Hereafter." This verse, and what resembles it from the Meccan verses, has a ruling that was superseded by fighting. God the Exalted informed His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, that the polytheists would argue for the correctness of what they were upon, of their polytheism and their religiosity in forbidding those things, by God's granting them respite and His leaving their state as it is, and that had He willed otherwise He would not have left them in that state.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is clear that the polytheists have no proof in what they mentioned, because we say: "God the Exalted, had He willed, they would not have associated"; but He, Exalted and Majestic, willed their association, and enabled them to acquire association, sins, love of it, and occupation with it; then He attached punishment and reward to those things and acquisitions. This is what the apparent meanings of the Qur'an require, in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿as a recompense for what they used to earn﴾ [al-Tawbah: 82], and the like. And it would follow from their argument that every path and every creed would be correct, since all of them would not exist had God the Exalted willed.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Some of the exegetes said: this statement from the polytheists was by way of mockery; and this is weak.

(p-487) The Mu'tazilah clung to this verse and said: God the Exalted has condemned this statement of theirs; and He condemned it only because their disbelief is not by God the Exalted's will, but is rather a creation of their own.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The matter is not as they claimed. God the Exalted condemned the polytheists' supposition that what God the Exalted wills does not incur punishment; as for His condemning their saying, "Were it not for the will, we would not have disbelieved," then no.

Then God the Exalted said, ﴿Likewise did those before them deny﴾; and there is an ellipsis in the speech indicated by the coherence of the speech; as if He, Exalted is He, said: "The polytheists say such-and-such; and there is no proof for them in that, nor anything that requires their denial; but likewise did those before them deny with a similar doubt, from their supposition that God the Exalted's leaving them is an evidence of His approval of their state."

And in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿until they tasted Our might﴾ there is a clear threat; and there is no explicit refutation in the verse of their saying: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated﴾; rather the refutation is left implied in the speech, due to its clarity and manifestness. And His saying, Exalted is He, "nor would our fathers," is conjoined to the pronoun of nominative case in "we associated"; and conjoining upon a nominative pronoun is not permitted by analogy, unlike the accusative; but Sibawayh deemed conjoining upon the nominative pronoun ugly, and the reason for its ugliness is that when the verb was made indeclinable it became like a letter of the verb, so conjoining upon it became ugly due to its resemblance to a letter; this is like your saying: "I stood and Zayd," because emphasizing it therein clarifies the meaning of nominality and removes from it the resemblance to a letter. And conjoining in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿we did not associate, nor did our fathers﴾ was good according to Sibawayh, since the speech was lengthened by "lā", so the meaning of nominality became clear, and "nor" required what is conjoined after it.

And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge?"﴾ and the verse; the meaning: "Say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers: Do you have any knowledge from God the Exalted, that you may state it, so that proof would be established by it?" The "min" in His saying, "min ʿilm" (any knowledge), is an emphasizing extra particle, and its extra occurrence came because the interrogative enters upon what is not obligatory. ﴿You follow nothing but conjecture﴾; that is: there is nothing with you but conjecture; and it is the most false of speech.

(p-488) Most of the people recited: "tattabiʿūn" (you follow), in the second person; while Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wththab recited: "in yattabiʿūn" (they follow), with the ya', as a relating of their speech.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is an irregular recitation; it is weakened by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"and you are not"﴾ and ﴿"you guess"﴾. Its meaning: you estimate, you conjecture, and you conclude.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 149–150:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive proof. So if He had willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ ﴿Say: "Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this." And if they testify, do not testify with them, and do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and they ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

Then, exalted is He, following up on His command to His Prophet (ﷺ), had the polytheists brought to account regarding the point of their inability, by His command to him (ﷺ) to say, clarifying and making plain: ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive proof"﴾. He means: the conclusive proof that reaches the utmost aim in the matter over which argument is made. Then know that if Allah, exalted is He, had willed, He would have guided the entire world.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This verse refutes the Mu'tazila in their saying that guidance and faith come only from the servant, not from Allah, exalted is He. If they say: the meaning of "He would have guided you" is "He would have compelled you to guidance," this is refuted by their belief that the faith which Allah, exalted is He, desires from His servants and rewards for is not that to which the servant is compelled; rather, according to them, it is only that which occurs from the servant alone.

As for "halumma" (هَلُمَّ), its meaning is "bring" (هَاتِ), and in that case it is transitive; and it may also mean "come forward" (أَقْبِلْ), in which case it is intransitive. Some Arabs make it a noun of verb (اسْمٌ لِلْفِعْلِ), like "ruwaydaka" (رُوَيْدَكَ), so they address with it the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine, in one uniform form. Some Arabs make it a verb, attaching pronouns to it, so they say: "halumma ya Zayd", "halummu ayyuha al-nas", "halummi ya Hind", and similar. Abu 'Ali mentioned both dialects in "al-Ighfal", and Abu 'Ubayda said: the first dialect belongs to the people of al-'Aliya, and the second dialect to the people of Najd. Sibawayh and al-Khalil said: its original form is "halumma" (هالُمَّ). Some said its original form is "halummum" (هالُمُمْ), and the alif was dropped because of the meeting of two sukun, so it became "hallumm"; then whoever said the original is "halumma" dropped (the second element), and whoever said the original is "halummum" assimilated (the letters), contrary to analogical rule.

The meaning of this verse is: "Say: Bring your witnesses to Allah's prohibiting what you claimed He prohibited." Then Allah, exalted is He, said to His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: ﴿If they testify﴾; that is: "If anyone among them fabricates and forges a testimony, or a report about prophethood, and the like, then you avoid that, and do not testify with them." In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿do not testify with them﴾, there is emphasis on describing their testimony as utter falsehood. ﴿And do not follow the desires﴾; he means: "Do not descend to the lusts of the disbelievers and agree with their statements." ﴿Those who do not believe﴾; this is a conjunction of one descriptive attribute upon another, as you say: "Zayd the generous and the intelligent came to me." This is the view of most people. Al-Naqqash said: it was revealed concerning the Dahriyya among the zanadiqa. ﴿And they ascribe equals to their Lord﴾; meaning, they make equals and place them on a par with Him. And even if it was revealed concerning the zanadiqa, their "equalizing" is other than this.
