**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 6, verse 151:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, show kindness to your parents, do not kill your children because of poverty, We provide for you and for them, do not approach indecencies, whether open or hidden, and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand.﴾

This is a command from God, Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he call all of creation to hear the recitation of what God, Exalted, has forbidden through the law of Islam, with which he was sent to the black and the red alike.

"Ta'alaw" means "come forward." Its root is from "al-'uluww" (height). Since the call is a command from the one calling, elevation of the one called is implied. "Ta'ala" is the reflexive (muṭāwi') of "'ala," just as "tafā'ala" is the reflexive of "fā'ala."

"Atlu" means "I will recite and set forth clearly," from "al-tilāwah," which is the following of some letters by others. "Mā" is in the accusative governed by the verb "atlu," and it is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which). Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that the verb "atlu" be suspended from acting (mu'allaq 'an al-'amal), and "mā" is then in the accusative governed by "ḥarrama" (forbade).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This view is unsound. The "an" in His saying "allā tushrikū" may be in the nominative position (fī mawḍi' raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (bi'l-ibtidā'), with the implied meaning "the matter is that..." or "that is that...". It may also be in the accusative position as an apposition (badal) for "mā," as Makki and others have said.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The meaning refutes this, so consider it carefully.

It may also be a purpose clause (maf'ūl min ajlih), with the implied meaning "for the sake of not associating anything with Him." However, this interpretation removes "allā tushrikū" from the recited content and makes it a cause for the recitation of the forbidden things.

"Tushrikū" may be in the accusative governed by "an." It may also be in the jussive mood governed by the prohibition, and this is the sound reading in the intended meaning. "An" may be connected to what it governs in the accusative, and it may also be connected to the jussive verb of command or prohibition. "Shay'an" is general, and what is intended by it is every deity other than God, Exalted.

"Iḥsānan" is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar), and its governing verb is an implied verb of the same root, the implied sense being: "And show kindness to the two parents."

The forbidden things are, in meaning, separable from these mentioned matters, and they are: associating partners with God (ishrāk), disobedience to parents ('uqūq), approaching indecencies, and killing a soul.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "These verses are the opening of the Torah: (In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾; to the end of the verse)." Ibn 'Abbas said: These verses are the decisive verses (al-muḥkamāt) which God, Exalted, mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran, upon which the laws of all creation agree, and which have never been abrogated (naskh) in any religious community. It has also been said that they are the Ten Words (al-'asharah al-kalimāt) revealed to Moses, peace be upon him.

If someone objects, saying that "tushrikū" is in the accusative governed by "an," with the jussive verbs coordinated upon it, this exists in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Tabari cited as proof for this the following verses:

"He performed the pilgrimage and bequeathed to Sulayma the slaves, / That you should not see [her], nor speak to anyone,"

"And her drink should never be cooled."

His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not kill your children﴾, to the end of the verse, is a prohibition against the custom of the Arabs of burying daughters alive (wa'd al-banāt). The word "walad" (child) includes both male and female among the offspring.

"Al-imlāq" means poverty and lack of wealth. This is what Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It is said: "amlaqa al-rajul" when a man became poor.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It seems that its meaning is "amlaqa," that is, "nothing remained for him except al-malaq," as they say "atraba" when nothing remained for him except dust (turāb), and "armala" when nothing remained for him except sand (ramal). "Al-malaq" means black stones, and its singular is "malaqah." Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned that "al-imlāq" means spending, and it is said: "amlaqa mālahu," meaning he spent his wealth. He also mentioned that 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said to a woman: "Spend from your wealth as much as you wish." Al-Naqqash related from Muhammad ibn Nu'aym al-Tirmidhi that it means extravagance in spending. Al-Naqqash also related from Mu'arrij that he said: "al-imlāq" means hunger, in the dialect of Lakhm.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not approach indecencies, whether open or hidden﴾, is a general prohibition against all kinds of indecencies, which are sins. "Open" and "hidden" are two states which encompass the categories of all things to which they apply. Some exegetes went in the direction that this verse intends specific things. Al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "What is open" is the notorious fornication of the brothels, and "what is hidden" is taking secret lovers (muttakhidhāt al-akhdān). They used to find only the open form abhorrent, so God, Exalted, forbade all of it. Mujahid said: "What is open" is marrying the wives of one's fathers and the like, and "what is hidden" is fornication. There are other such specifications which have no supporting proof, but are rather bare assertions.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not kill﴾, to the end of the verse, includes the prohibition of killing a Muslim soul and a soul under covenant (mu'āhad). The meaning of the verse is: "except by the right which requires its killing." The Shari'ah has specified this, and it is: disbelief in God, Exalted; killing a soul; fornication after being married (iḥṣān); armed robbery (ḥirābah); and what branches off from these.

"Dhālikum" refers to these forbidden things. "Al-waṣiyyah" means a binding and established command, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Did you truly not hear the charge of Muhammad, / the Prophet of God, when he charged and bore witness?"

His saying, Exalted: "la'allakum" (that you may...), is an expression of hope (tarajji) from our perspective. That is: whoever hears this charge hopes that the effect of reason will follow it, and that he will distinguish benefits from harms in religion.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 6, verse 152:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity. And give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a relative. And fulfil the covenant of Allah. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be mindful.﴾

This is a prohibition against approaching (the orphan's property) in any manner of disposal. It includes *sadd al-dhari'a* (blocking the means that lead to harm). Then He made an exception for what is good, which is investing and seeking its growth. Mujahid said: "*Allati hiya ahsan*" (in the best manner) means trading with it. For the guardian who has no property of his own by which he lives, the best course, when the orphan's property yields profit, is that he takes no maintenance, wage, or anything else from it. As for the guardian who has no property and cannot manage it without spending on himself from the profit of his management, or else necessity compels him to leave the orphan's property unmanaged, then the best course is that he manages it and eats in a reasonable manner (*bi'l-ma'ruf*). This was said by Ibn Zayd.

And "*al-ashudd*" is the plural of "*shadd*" and of "*shidda*". Here it means firmness, consideration of affairs, and good management of them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not the *ashudd* connected with reaching forty years of age; rather, this (maturity) occurs at a young age among many people. That *ashudd* refers to experience and a mind that has been tested and refined. But the exegetes have mixed the two. Rabi'a, al-Sha'bi, Malik (according to what is narrated from him), and Abu Hanifa said: reaching *ashudd* is puberty together with the absence of proven foolishness (*safah*). al-Suddi said: *al-ashudd* is thirty years. A group said: thirty-three years. al-Zajjaj related from a group: eighteen years, but he considered this weak, and preferred that it is puberty together with rushd (sound judgment). al-Naqqash related that *al-ashudd* here is from fifteen to thirty years. The jurisprudential view is what al-Zajjaj preferred, and it is the opinion of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him: *rushd* (sound judgment) and the removal of foolishness, together with puberty.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the most correct of the opinions and the most suitable to this context.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And give full measure and weight﴾ (up to the end of the verse): it is a command to moderation in taking and giving. "*Al-qist*" means justice. His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, implies that these commands apply only to what falls within human ability, in terms of guarding and taking precaution, and not that one is required to achieve absolute justice in the very thing being disposed of. Al-Tabari said: Since the one who gives less exerts himself in hardship, and the one who gives more also exerts himself similarly, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, lifted the command to equality so that neither of them would be burdened with hardship.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾, it includes testimonies, judgments, mediation between people, and other matters; that is, even if the truth goes against your relatives.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the covenant of Allah﴾, it may mean everything that Allah, Exalted is He, has entrusted to His servants, and it may mean all of that together with everything agreed upon between two people. The covenant is attributed to Allah, Exalted is He, because He has commanded its preservation and fulfilment.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "*la'allakum*" (that you may), it expresses hope, according to our understanding.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "*tadhakkarun*" (تَذَّكَّرُونَ) with the doubling (*tashdid*) of both the *dhal* and the *kaf*. Likewise "*yadhdhakkarun*" and "*yadhdhakkaru al-insan*", and whatever occurs of this kind, all with doubling. Nafi', 'Asim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him), and Ibn 'Amir recited all of these with doubling, except His saying, ﴿Does not man remember?﴾ (*awa la yadhkuru al-insan*), which they recited with lightening (*takhfif*). Aban and Hafs related from 'Asim: "*tadhkurun*" with a light *dhal* throughout the Qur'an. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "*tadhakkarun*" with a light *dhal* when the verb is in the second person (with *ta'*), and when it is in the third person (with *ya'*) they recited it with doubling. Hamza alone, in Surat al-Furqan, recited "*liman arada an yadhkura*" with a sukun on the *dhal* and a light *kaf*. al-Kisa'i recited that with doubling of both and with fatha on both.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 153:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] ways, lest they scatter you away from His way. That is what He has enjoined upon you, so that you may be mindful.﴾

The demonstrative refers to the sacred law (shar') that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought in its entirety. Al-Tabari said: the demonstrative refers to these injunctions that preceded it, from His saying: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ [al-An'am: 151].

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read "wa-anna hadha" with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun, and "sirati" with a silent ya'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-inna" with a kasra on the alif and a shadda on the nun. Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibn 'Amir, among the seven, read "wa-an" with a fatha on the hamza and a sukun on the nun, and "siratiya" with a fatha on the ya'. As for the one who reads with a fatha on the alif, the meaning for him is as if he said: "And because this is My path, straight, so follow it," that is: "Follow it because it is such." On this reading the waw conjoins one clause to another. It is also possible to take it as conjoining with "alla tushrikû" (that you associate nothing with Him), and then what is forbidden is following the [other] ways and deviating from the most upright path. Whoever reads with a light nun conjoins it to His saying: ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 151]. Sibawayh's view is that it is the light form of the heavy (anna), and that the implied reading is "wa-annahu hadha sirati" (and that indeed this is My path). Whoever reads with a kasra on the alif and a shadda on the nun has, as it were, begun a new sentence and cut it off from the first. In the codex (mushaf) of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is "wa-hadha sirati," with "anna" omitted.

Ibn Mas'ud said: God, exalted is He, made a way, a straight path, whose one end is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his law, and whose final destination is Paradise. Other paths branch off from it. Whoever keeps to the main road is saved, and whoever leaves for those other paths, they lead him into the Fire. He also said: One day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) drew a line for us, and said: "This is the path of God." Then he drew lines to the right and left of that line and said: "These are paths; on each path there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: This verse encompasses the people of desires, innovations and deviations in the branches [of law] and otherwise, and the people of excessive hair-splitting in disputation and immersion in theological speculation. All of these are liable to slip, and are a cause of corrupt belief.

The discussion of ﴿That He has enjoined upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 151] and of His saying "la'allakum" (so that you may) has already been given. Since the first prohibitions are such that no sensible person who has used his intellect would fall into them, the expression is ﴿so that you may understand﴾ [al-An'am: 151]. The remaining prohibitions concern desires, and some sensible people may fall into them without remembering, so the expression is ﴿so that you may remember﴾ [al-An'am: 152]. Then, since adhering to the complete main road involves performing the virtues, and that is the rank of piety, the expression is ﴿so that you may be mindful﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 154:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Then We gave Moses the Book, complete, upon the one who did good, and as a detailed explanation of all things, and as guidance and mercy, that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord.﴾

"Then" (thumma): In this verse, its function is only to indicate sequence in the ordering of the speech that Muhammad (ﷺ) was commanded to deliver; it is as if He said: "Then, among what We have decreed, that We gave Moses the Book." What supports this is that Moses (peace be upon him) is earlier in time than Muhammad (ﷺ), and in his recitation of what God the Exalted has forbidden. "Al-Kitab" (the Book): the Torah. "Tamaman" (complete): it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar).

(p-496) As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿upon the one who did good﴾: its meaning is disputed. One group said: "alladhi" (the one who) means "alladhina" (those who), and "ahsana" (did good) is a past-tense verb serving as the relative clause of "alladhina". The sense of the speech is: "And We gave Moses the Book as a favour upon the good-doers among the people of his religion, and as a completion of the blessing upon them." This is the interpretation of Mujahid. In the codex of 'Abd Allah: "complete upon those who did good" (tamaman 'ala alladhina ahsanu), and this supports that interpretation. Another group said: "alladhi" is not a relative pronoun, and the meaning is: "complete upon that which he did well of the worship of his Lord and the undertaking of the affairs of his prophethood," meaning Moses (peace be upon him). This is the interpretation of al-Rabi' and Qatada. Another group said: the meaning is "complete, that is, as a favour and perfection, upon the one to whom God the Exalted did good towards His servants, through the prophethoods, the blessings, and other things." So "alladhi" in this interpretation too is not a relative pronoun. This is the interpretation of Ibn Zayd.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi Ishaq read: "tamaman 'ala alladhi ahsanu" with a damma on the nun, making it a comparative adjective (sifat tafdil), and in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "upon the one who is best." Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) considered this reading weak, because of the ugliness of omitting the returning pronoun of the subject. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: it is permissible for "ahsana" to be an attribute of "alladhi," inasmuch as it approaches the definite, since the definite article (al-) does not enter it, as the Arabs say: "I passed by the one who is better than you (marartu bi-alladhi khayrin minka)," but it is not permissible to say "bi-alladhi 'alimin." Al-Zajjaj rejected this Kufan view.

"Tafsil" (detailed explanation) means: clarification and division. "La'allahum" (perhaps they): an expression of hope, with respect to mankind. "Bi-liqa' rabbihim" (in the meeting with their Lord): that is, in the resurrection, belief in which is the culmination of the affirmation of the prophets (may the blessings of God be upon them), since reason does not necessarily compel it by its own essence; it is established only by revelation, while reason permits it.

**The Qur'anic verses:** ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿Lest you should say, "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say, "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. Who, then, is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them? We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with a terrible punishment, for what they used to turn away from.﴾

**Commentary:**

"This" refers to the Qur'an. "Blessed" describes what it contains of expansion (*tawassu'at*), the removal of the rulings of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) and its prohibitions, the unification of the word of the Arabs, and the unity of the hands of its followers, and what God the Exalted opened for the believers through it. Its meaning is: its good is abundant and its increase is multiplied. *Al-barakah* (blessing) means increase and growth. "So follow it" is a call to the religion. As for "and be mindful of God" (*wa-ttaqu*), the more apparent reading is that it is a command to general God-consciousness (*taqwa*) in all matters, supported by His words ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾.

The "an" (that/lest) in His words ﴿an taqulu﴾ is in a position of accusative (*nasb*), and its governing verb is "anzalnahu" (We sent it down). The implied meaning is: "This is a Book We sent down lest you say..." This is the most correct of the opinions and the most precise in conveying the intended meaning. It has been said that the governing word of "an" is His words "wa-ttaqu" (be mindful), as if He had said, "Be mindful lest you say..." This is an interpretation that can be read as meaning: "Be mindful lest you say such-and-such, for you have no proof in it." However, a difficulty arises in it because of His words during that passage, ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾. In the first interpretation, the structure of the verse is coherent.

"The two groups" are the Jews and the Christians, by the consensus of the interpreters. *Al-dirasah* (study) means reading and learning from it. The *in* in His words ﴿wa-in kunna﴾ is the lightened form (*mukhaffafah*) of the heavy *inna* (indeed). The *lam* in His words "la-ghafilin" (we were indeed unaware) is the *lam* of emphasis. This is the view of the Basran grammarians. Sibawayh reported from some Arabs that they lighten it and keep it in its governing function, and from this is the reading of some people of Madinah: "wa-in kullan" (where *kullan* is in the accusative). As for the well-known usage, when it is lightened it reverts to a particle of initiation and does not govern. As for the view of the Kufan grammarians, the *in* in this verse has the meaning of the negative *ma* (not), and the *lam* has the meaning of *illa* (except), so it is as if He had said: "We were not unaware of their study except..."

The shaykh Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: The meaning of this verse is to remove the proof from the hands of the Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs, in that they had no Book. It is as if He had said: "This Qur'an, O assembly of the Arabs, has been sent down as a proof against you, so that you do not say: The Torah and the Gospel were only sent down in a language other than ours, to others, and we did not know of that. So this is a Book in your language, and with a man from among you."

His words ﴿"or lest you say"﴾ form a clause conjoined to the first clause. It shares its purpose, which is argument against the disbelievers and cutting off their pretext on the Day of Judgment that Books were only sent down to others, that they were heedless of study and reflection on the Law, and that if a Book had been sent down to them they would have been quicker to guidance than all people. So it was said to them: "There has come to you a clear proof from God the Exalted, and guidance and mercy."

Since it has been established that the clear proof has come and the argument has been established, it is fitting after that for the rebuke to occur with His words: ﴿"Who, then, is more unjust than one who denies these clear signs?"﴾

"*Sadafa*" means: deviated, turned aside, and turned away. Yahya ibn Wathhab and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *kadhaba* (without doubling the *dhal*), while the majority read *kadhdhaba* (with doubling the *dhal*). His words ﴿"We will repay those who..."﴾ are a threat. A group read *yasdifuna* with a kasra on the *dal*, and a group read *yasdufuna* with a damma on the *dal*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 158:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of the signs of your Lord should come? On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, its faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or earned no good through its faith. Say: "Wait, we too are waiting."﴾

The pronoun in "yanzurun" (they await) refers to the group to whom it was said earlier: ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 157]. They are the Arabs who associate partners with their Lord, and most of the verses of the surah have passed in dispute with them. "Yanzurun" means "yantazirun" (they wait for). "The angels" here is intended to mean the angels of death, who accompany 'Izra'il (ʿIzrāʾīl), the one specifically charged with seizing souls; this is said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. It is also possible that it means the angels who carry out affairs at the establishment of the Hour (al-sa'ah).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "illa an ya'tiyahum" with a ya' (yā'), while the rest recited "ta'tiyahum" with a ta' (tā') from above.

As for His saying, ﴿or your Lord should come﴾, al-Tabari said: "for the standing of reckoning on the Day of Resurrection," and he attributed this to Qatadah and a group of the interpreters. Al-Zajjaj relates that what is meant by His saying ﴿or your Lord should come﴾ is: "the punishment which Allah, Exalted is He, sends down in this world upon whom He wills of His servants, such as the cries, the quakings, the sinking of the earth, and the like."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This statement, on every interpretation, requires the omission of a modifier (mudaf); its estimate is: "the command of your Lord," or "the seizing of your Lord," or "the reckoning of your Lord." Otherwise, the coming understood from the language is impossible with regard to Allah, Exalted is He. Do you not see that Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Then Allah came to them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]? This is a coming that has occurred, and it is by way of metaphor and the omission of the modifier.

As for His saying, ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾, the apparent meaning of the wording, if we stop with it, requires that He threatened them with the well-known, dreadful portents of the Hour, without singling out any one of them. He intends by this the ambiguity which leaves the hearer with the strongest imagining. But when He said after that: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, its faith will not benefit a soul﴾, and the sound reports in al-Bukhari and Muslim clarified that the sign accompanied by this condition is the rising of the sun from the west, he strengthened the view that the indication in His saying ﴿or your Lord should come or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾ is to the rising of the sun from its west. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others held this interpretation. It is also strengthened that the indication may be to the death-rattle (gharghara) of a person at death, or what occurs in its place, for one who has not yet reached the death-rattle; for in the hadith it is reported that the repentance of the servant is accepted so long as he has not reached the death-rattle. This is a consensus, because whoever has reached the death-rattle and witnessed (the angels) is among the dead. And the person's being in this state is among the signs of Allah, Exalted is He; this is according to the view of those who see the angels who carry out affairs at the establishment of the Hour.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The purpose of this verse is to threaten the disbelievers with states from which they cannot be free, as if He said: "Do they await, while persisting in disbelief, anything but death, after which is the most severe punishment, and the known seizings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; or the signs which cut off repentance and make known the nearness of the Resurrection?"

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is also valid that by His saying ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾ He intends all that is certain to occur of the portents of the Hour; then He specified afterwards, by His saying ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾, the sign with which repentance is cut off; and the hadiths have clarified that it is the rising of the sun from its west.

Zuhayr al-Furqubi recited "yawmu ya'ti" with a raised (ḍammah) dal (the subject), and this is on the basis of the inceptive (ibtida'); the predicate is in the clause "la yanfa'u" (does not benefit) up to the end of the verse; and the returning pronoun from the clause is omitted because of the length of the speech. Ibn Sirin, Abdullah ibn 'Amr and Abu al-'Aliyah recited "la tanfa'u" with a ta' (tā'), making faith feminine, because it is added to a feminine noun, or because it was treated as the equivalent of repentance (tawbah). Most of the people of interpretation, as has preceded, said: the sign by which repentance from shirk, or from sins after it, is not benefited, is the rising of the sun from the west. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it is one of three: either the rising of the sun from its west, or the emergence of the beast, or the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This has room for examination, because the hadiths refute it and specify the sun. It is reported in a hadith that the sun runs every day until it prostrates beneath the Throne and seeks permission; permission is granted for it to rise from the east; and when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills to close the door of repentance, He commands it to rise from its west. Ibn Mas'ud and others said, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Then it will rise, and the moon with it, like two paired camels," and the examination is also strengthened by the fact that the death-rattle is the sign by which repentance is cut off.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿or earned no good through its faith﴾, means all deeds of righteousness, obligatory and voluntary; and this distinction pertains to the sinning believers, just as His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He, ﴿had not believed before﴾ pertains to the disbelievers; and the sign referred to cuts off the repentance of both categories. Abu Hurayrah recited: "aw kasabat fi iymanha salihan" (or earned in its faith something righteous).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "Wait, we too are waiting."﴾ contains a warning; that is: "you will see who it is whose word is true, and what he informed of will become clear."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verses 159–160:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects — you have no part in them at all. Their affair is only with Allah; then He will inform them of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, the Companions, and Qatadah said: what is meant by "those who" is the Jews and the Christians; that is, they divided the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham), the ḥanīfiyyah (pure monotheism). The religion is attributed to them from the standpoint that they ought to adhere to it, since it is the religion of Allah, the Exalted, which He imposed upon the servants; thus it is the religion of all people in this sense. ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "fāraqū" (they separated from), and its meaning is "they abandoned." Then His saying "and became sects" clarifies that they also divided it. The shiya' is the plural of shi'ah, which is a faction, according to the aim toward which they rally together.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿you have no part in them at all﴾: that is, "you do not intercede for them, and there is no connection between them and you." This applies absolutely to the disbelievers, and in the sense of emphasis to the sinners and to those who are excessive in religious matters, because they have a share in dividing the religion.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: this interpretation requires a chain of transmission that cuts off excuse.

Another group said: this verse applies to the whole community; that is, Allah, the Exalted, multiplies a good deed tenfold; then after this guarantee He may increase what He wills, and He may also increase for some deeds, such as the expenditure for jihad. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 6, verse 161–163:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion, the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿He has no partner. And with that I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims.﴾

This is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet (peace be upon him): to proclaim His sharia, to reject what is other than it from their falsehoods, and to describe the sharia by what it has of goodness, excellence and uprightness. "Hadani" (guided me) means: He guided me by creating guidance in my heart. "Al-Rabb" (the Lord) means: the Owner. Its wording is a verbal noun (maṣdar), from your saying "rabbahu, yarubbuhu." It is like "ʿadl" (justice) and "riḍan" (contentment), in that it is a verbal noun used as a description. Its original form was "dhu al-rabb" (possessor of lordship); then the annexed noun was deleted and the annexed-to noun was put in its place, so it was said "al-Rabb."

"Al-ṣirāṭ" means: the path. "Dīnan" is in the accusative governed by "hadānī," the implied verb indicated by the first "hadānī." This pronoun connects directly, without needing to supply "ilā," since "hadā" connects by itself to its second object, and also with a preposition; so it is a verb that is used in two ways. It was also said: "dīnan" is accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being "ʿarrafanī dīnan" (He made me know a religion), and it was said: its estimate is "fa-ittabiʿū dīnan" (so follow a religion), or "fa-ilzamū dīnan" (so adhere to a religion). It was also said: it is accusative as an apposition (badal) to "ṣirāṭ," on the basis of the place, because its estimate is "hadānī rabbī ṣirāṭan mustaqīman" (my Lord guided me to a straight path). "Qiyaman" is an attribute of "dīn," and its meaning is "upright, balanced."

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr read "qayyiman," with a fatḥa on the qāf, a kasra on the yāʾ and its shadda. Its original form is "qaywaman," and it was treated by the same reasoning as "sayyid" and "mayyit." ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "qiyaman," with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the yāʾ, on the pattern "fiʿalan." The original would seem to be "qiwaman," like "ʿiwaḍ" and "ḥiwal," except that it is irregular, like the irregularity in their saying "jiyād" as the plural of "jawād" and "thīra" as the plural of "thawr."

"Millata" is an apposition to "al-dīn." "Al-milla" means: the sharia. "Ḥanīfan" is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "Ibrāhīm." "Al-ḥanaf" in the speech of the Arabs means: inclination. It may be an inclination toward corruption, as in "ḥanafa al-rajul," and as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"fa-man khāfa min mūṣin janafan"﴾ [al-Baqara: 182], according to the reading of the one who reads with an unpointed ḥāʾ, and similar. It may also be an inclination toward righteousness, as in his saying (peace be upon him): « "al-ḥanīfiyya al-samḥa" » (the tolerant ḥanīfiyya), and "al-dīn al-ḥanīf" (the ḥanīf religion), and similar. Ibn Qutayba said: al-ḥanaf is uprightness. The name "al-Aḥnaf" was given to a man as an optimistic omen for him.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a negation of any deficiency in him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer﴾ and the verse: it is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that he proclaim that his aim in his prayer, his obedience, including sacrifice and other things, his conduct throughout his life, and his state of sincerity and faith at the time of his death, is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic alone, seeking His face and seeking His pleasure. In the Prophet's proclaiming (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) this statement there is what obliges the believers to emulate him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), so that they commit in all their deeds to seeking the face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also possible that by this statement he means that his prayer, his sacrifice, his life and his death are in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who directs him in all of that as He wills, and that He has guided him in that to a straight path. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"wa-bidhālika umirtu"﴾ (and with that I have been commanded), according to this interpretation, refers only to His saying ﴿"lā sharīka lahu"﴾ (He has no partner); or it refers to the first statement. According to the first interpretation it refers to everything mentioned, including prayer and other things, meaning: I have been commanded to intend the face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in that, and to commit to acting.

The majority of readers read "wa-nusukī" with a ḍamma on the sīn. Abū Ḥaywa and al-Ḥasan read it with a sukūn on the sīn. A group said: "al-nusuk" in this verse means: sacrifices.

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: What makes the specification of the sacrifice by mention in this verse good is that it was revealed, its mention has already preceded, and the dispute about it is in the surah. Another group said: "al-nusuk" in this verse means: all acts of obedience, from your saying "nasaka fulān, fahuwa nāsik" (so-and-so worshipped, and he is a worshipper), when he devoted himself to worship.

The Seven Readers, except Nāfiʿ, read ﴿"wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātī"﴾ with a fatḥa on the yāʾ of "maḥyāya" and a sukūn on the yāʾ of "mamātī." Nāfiʿ alone read "wa-maḥyāy" with a sukūn on the yāʾ. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: it is anomalous in analysis, because it combines two sākin letters, and anomalous in usage. Its justification is that it has been heard from the Arabs: "iltaqat ḥalqatā al-biṭān" and "li-fulān thuluthā al-māl." Abū Khulayd related from Nāfiʿ: "wa-maḥyāyi," with a kasra on the yāʾ. Ibn Abī Isḥāq, ʿĪsā and al-Jaḥdarī read "wa-maḥyayya," and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. From it is the saying of Abū Dhuʾayb:

"They outran my desire and overpowered their own desires, so they were struck down, and for every side there is a place of falling."

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "ṣalātiya wa-nusukiya wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātiya," with a fatḥa on the yāʾ in all of them. This was also transmitted from ʿĀṣim.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"wa-anā awwalu al-muslimīn"﴾ (and I am the first of the Muslims): that is, of this community. Al-Naqqāsh said: "from the people of Mecca."

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The meaning is one; rather, the first is more general and better. A group read "wa-anā" with lengthening of the alif, while the majority of readers read "wa-anā" without lengthening. All of this is in connected speech.

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Omitting the lengthening is better, because it is an alif of pause; when speech is connected it is dispensed with, especially when a hamza follows it.

This pronoun connects directly, without needing to supply "ilā," since "hadā" connects by itself to its second object, and also with a preposition; so it is a verb that is used in two ways. It was also said: "dīnan" is accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being "ʿarrafanī dīnan" (He made me know a religion), and it was said: its estimate is "fa-ittabiʿū dīnan" (so follow a religion), or "fa-ilzamū dīnan" (so adhere to a religion). It was also said: it is accusative as an apposition (badal) to "ṣirāṭ," on the basis of the place, because its estimate is "hadānī rabbī ṣirāṭan mustaqīman" (my Lord guided me to a straight path). "Qiyaman" is an attribute of "dīn," and its meaning is "upright, balanced."

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr read "qayyiman," with a fatḥa on the qāf, a kasra on the yāʾ and its shadda. Its original form is "qaywaman," and it was treated by the same reasoning as "sayyid" and "mayyit." ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "qiyaman," with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the yāʾ, on the pattern "fiʿalan." The original would seem to be "qiwaman," like "ʿiwaḍ" and "ḥiwal," except that it is irregular, like the irregularity in their saying "jiyād" as the plural of "jawād" and "thīra" as the plural of "thawr."

"Millata" is an apposition to "al-dīn." "Al-milla" means: the sharia. "Ḥanīfan" is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "Ibrāhīm." "Al-ḥanaf" in the speech of the Arabs means: inclination. It may be an inclination toward corruption, as in "ḥanafa al-rajul," and as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"fa-man khāfa min mūṣin janafan"﴾ [al-Baqara: 182], according to the reading of the one who reads with an unpointed ḥāʾ, and similar. It may also be an inclination toward righteousness, as in his saying (peace be upon him): « "al-ḥanīfiyya al-samḥa" » (the tolerant ḥanīfiyya), and "al-dīn al-ḥanīf" (the ḥanīf religion), and similar. Ibn Qutayba said: al-ḥanaf is uprightness. The name "al-Aḥnaf" was given to a man as an optimistic omen for him.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a negation of any deficiency in him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer﴾ and the verse: it is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that he proclaim that his aim in his prayer, his obedience, including sacrifice and other things, his conduct throughout his life, and his state of sincerity and faith at the time of his death, is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic alone, seeking His face and seeking His pleasure. In the Prophet's proclaiming (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) this statement there is what obliges the believers to emulate him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), so that they commit in all their deeds to seeking the face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also possible that by this statement he means that his prayer, his sacrifice, his life and his death are in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who directs him in all of that as He wills, and that He has guided him in that to a straight path. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"wa-bidhālika umirtu"﴾ (and with that I have been commanded), according to this interpretation, refers only to His saying ﴿"lā sharīka lahu"﴾ (He has no partner); or it refers to the first statement. According to the first interpretation it refers to everything mentioned, including prayer and other things, meaning: I have been commanded to intend the face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in that, and to commit to acting.

The majority of readers read "wa-nusukī" with a ḍamma on the sīn. Abū Ḥaywa and al-Ḥasan read it with a sukūn on the sīn. A group said: "al-nusuk" in this verse means: sacrifices.

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: What makes the specification of the sacrifice by mention in this verse good is that it was revealed, its mention has already preceded, and the dispute about it is in the surah. Another group said: "al-nusuk" in this verse means: all acts of obedience, from your saying "nasaka fulān, fahuwa nāsik" (so-and-so worshipped, and he is a worshipper), when he devoted himself to worship.

The Seven Readers, except Nāfiʿ, read ﴿"wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātī"﴾ with a fatḥa on the yāʾ of "maḥyāya" and a sukūn on the yāʾ of "mamātī." Nāfiʿ alone read "wa-maḥyāy" with a sukūn on the yāʾ. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: it is anomalous in analysis, because it combines two sākin letters, and anomalous in usage. Its justification is that it has been heard from the Arabs: "iltaqat ḥalqatā al-biṭān" and "li-fulān thuluthā al-māl." Abū Khulayd related from Nāfiʿ: "wa-maḥyāyi," with a kasra on the yāʾ. Ibn Abī Isḥāq, ʿĪsā and al-Jaḥdarī read "wa-maḥyayya," and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. From it is the saying of Abū Dhuʾayb:

"They outran my desire and overpowered their own desires, so they were struck down, and for every side there is a place of falling."

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "ṣalātiya wa-nusukiya wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātiya," with a fatḥa on the yāʾ in all of them. This was also transmitted from ʿĀṣim.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"wa-anā awwalu al-muslimīn"﴾ (and I am the first of the Muslims): that is, of this community. Al-Naqqāsh said: "from the people of Mecca."

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The meaning is one; rather, the first is more general and better. A group read "wa-anā" with lengthening of the alif, while the majority of readers read "wa-anā" without lengthening. All of this is in connected speech.

The judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Omitting the lengthening is better, because it is an alif of pause; when speech is connected it is dispensed with, especially when a hamza follows it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, when He is the Lord of all things? No soul earns [sin] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about what you used to differ over."﴾ ﴿And it is He who made you successors (khala'if) on the earth and raised some of you above others in degrees, to test you in what He has given you. Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

Al-Naqqash related that the disbelievers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Return, O Muhammad, to our religion; worship our gods; leave what you are upon, and we will guarantee you against every consequence you fear in your worldly life and your Hereafter." So this verse was revealed. It is an interrogative that implies affirmation (taqrir), censure (tawqif) and rebuke (tawbikh). "Abghi" means "seek". So it is as if He said: "Is it fitting in your view that I seek a god other than Allah, the One who is the Lord of all things? What you mention of your guarantee does not hold, because the matter is not as you suppose. Rather, each soul's earning of evil and sin falls upon itself alone." "Wa la tazir" means "does not bear," and "wazirah" means "one who bears," the burden (himl) and weight (thiql) of another. The root meaning of "wizr" is weight; then it was used for sin, because it breaks the back, as a figurative extension and metaphor. From it one says: "wazara al-rajul, yazir, fa huwa wazir," and "wuzira, yuzar, fa huwa mawzur."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ is a threat and a warning. "Fa yunabbi'ukum" means "He will inform you," i.e., that punishment for deviation is a clarification of the place of truth. His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿about what you used to differ over﴾ means, as some of the interpreters (mutawwilun) related, "concerning my affair: some of you say, 'He is a sorcerer'; some of you say, 'He is a poet'; some of you say, 'He fabricated it'; some of you say, 'He had it written down'; and the like."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is fitting in this context, though the wording encompasses all kinds of differences: differences in religions, creeds, schools of thought, and other matters.

"Khala'if" is the plural of "khalifah," i.e., some of you succeed others.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This can be conceived for all nations and all kinds of people, since whoever comes is a successor to those who passed. But it is fitting that the people of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) be called, collectively, successors to the nations, while they have no one to succeed them, since they are the last of the nations and the Hour will come upon them.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: « "You will complete seventy nations; you are the best of them and the most honored by Allah." It is also narrated: "You are the last of them and the most honored by Allah." »

His saying: ﴿"and raised some of you above others in degrees"﴾ is a general term covering wealth, strength, status, the quality of souls and minds, and other things. All of that is only so that Allah tests creation and sees the good-doer from the wrongdoer.

When He, Mighty and Majestic, informed of this, opening the field of action for people and urging them to race towards good, He threatened and promised, as fear and hope from Him, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾. The swiftness of His punishment is either by His seizing [people] in this world or by the punishment of the Hereafter. It is fitting to describe the punishment of the Hereafter as "swift" since it is certain, its coming and occurrence guaranteed, for every thing that is coming is judged to be near and is described as such. And ﴿Indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ is hope for the one who has sinned and wishes to repent. The combining of threat with promise is frequent in Allah's Book, as a kindness from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to His servants.

The commentary on Surat al-An'am is complete. Allah is the One sought for help, He is sufficient for me, and how excellent a Disposer of affairs He is.
